entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part I. August 8, 1990 Interview

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Neil Vanderburg, after a grueling interview regarding his family's history and his memories of the Berry Creek area during the 1930s. Neil is pictured on August 8, 1990 at the home of Bob Zybach, Corvallis, Oregon.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. Family History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My, both sets of my grandparents, [Elton Dorr and Dorothy Louise Rose Vanderburg, and William de Ruchie and Nellie Wilson Rose] were quite well to do. My mother's family had servants. And she had never cooked or washed a dish until she got married, so
bracketed_corrections: Elton Don and Dorothy Louise Rose Vanderburg, and William de Ruchie and Nellie Wilson Rose

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Let's see. This is Neil Vanderburg. We're at 530 NW 15th on August 8, and we're talking about his family history. So we start with your mother's family, and they are well to do. Do you know who your great grandparents were on your mother's side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No I don't and it can't be traced because my mother was born in Canada and you can't trace your family tree through Canada unless you are one of the people in there so my daughter [Mary Stone] has not been able to go back. My grandfather and grandmother were both French [Editorial Note: These are Neil's great grandparents. A few of Neils other memories regarding family history contain minor errors. Please refer to Appendix A for a detailed history and genealogy

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: over from France, into Canada, and my grandfather's name was William de Ruchie Rose, changed to Rose after the family came to the United States, and my mother's name was Dorothy Rose. But they, he did a lot of investing in real estate and they were financially capable so that they went down into the Buena Park area which is down by Knotts Berry Farm, they had a whole city block there for their home and their servant's quarters. I have seen it but it is now in part of a freeway. And anyway they would go down there in the winter time and in the summer time they went back to Canada each year. So my mother went back and forth and she never became a citizen of the United States actually, except through marriage. My mother had a brother who was about her age who was, we called him Bud Rose, his name was Clarence, and he was an artist and a painter. He and my mother were, oh, about 7 or eight years older than their three younger sisters. And I don't, I'm not positive whether they had the same mother or not [They did.]. My grandfather had three different wives through death, he never had a divorce, it was through death, but anyway there was a gap between the two older ones and the three younger ones. Strangely enough, the three younger ones are all still alive and they are up over 85 now, so

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your mother was one of the two older ones?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Bud and she were the oldest ones.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now your great grandfather and grandmother Rose both were French?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but they came from, one came from northern France and one came from southern France, and they could hardly understand each other in their French language.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they met in Canada?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. [Story deleted here: See Appendix A]
bracketed_corrections: Story deleted here: See Appendix A

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your sister is the one doing a family history.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No that's my daughter [Mary (Vanderburg) Stone].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Daughter is doing a family history.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My sister [Ruth (Vanderburg) Monroe] lives up in Canada now. She loves it and lives up the Kamloops area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that where your grandparents are from? The Kamloops area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were on north another 150 miles or so, and she went on up to where they had lived. I have pictures of the mine that my dad took. Whether I could find them after the move or not, it would be a little hard probably. Anyway, that about covers my mother's side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now when they were in Canada, then they came down to the United States, do you know why they moved down to the Knotts Berry Farm area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think probably for climate.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they had just gotten tired of Canada. . Do you know what year they moved down to the

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: United States?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I understand my mother was born Christmas before the turn of the century. Seven days before the turn of the century. And I understand that her first trip to California she was two years old, supposedly. But they made that trip back and forth and I think probably they didn't like the winters in Canada. And they had the money so they didn't have to stay up there in that. . . cause that's pretty far north there and pretty cold, and inland far enough to make it colder yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So she was born Christmas Day, 1899. She had an older brother?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that would have been by your grandfather's first wife. Then about 1901 the family started going back and forth between Canada and the United States. So when did your grandfather's first wife, [See Appendix A] your grandmother, when did she die?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I. . . let's see I would have to figure back by my. . . one of em died about, around 1920 [Feb. 2., 1918], right in there, because when she died, my aunt Esther came to live with us, and she was in the home when I was born. So I was always like her son, because she later had three daughters, so I was always really important to her, because I was her son, and am to this day, and that's another story, of course.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would have been one of her younger sisters?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. That was her youngest sister.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, if somebody wanted to get the genealogy from your daughter, what is her name and address?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Her name is Mary Stone, and she lives right here in Corvallis, and the easiest way to get ahold of her is she operates the Bible book store [Christian Supply Store] here in Corvallis across from Fred Meyers there on Fillmore Street.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And she's got the genealogy of your family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So anybody that wanted to find out when your grandparents were born, when they got married, when you kids were born, where your parents. . . where they lived, she'd be the person to talk to.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Good, that'!! save us some tape space here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She has traced my father's side to a Vanderburg that came across, and well at that time it was three words and "h" on the end of our name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now when your great grandfather came back out to California, was your grandfather already born, or was he a native of California?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea back in that history. You know, my grandfather had a brother. And I met him one time when I was probably 5 years old. And that's really all I know about my, on my grandmother's side, her mother was still alive, she broke her hip when I was probably 3 years old, and I remember her in bed, that's all I know about anybody further back than my grandfather and grandmother. My grandfather and grandmother [Lester and Jennie Hiserodt Vanderburgh}, if you put them in a shower and got 'em soaking wet, and put them on the scales, the two of them together wouldn't weigh 200 pounds.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Small people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, my grandfather was 5' Il", my grandmother was. . . or I mean 4' 11", my grandmother was 4'9".

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think the most riy grandmother ever weighed was 84 pounds.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those were the Vanerburgs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the V. derburg side. And so they were all . . everybody was quite

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: surprised that no e of us ended up that small. As you can see, I'm not small. But I do have 2 daugh ers that are only 5'2". But. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now Vanderburg, your randfather, may have been brought over with his father to California,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very likely. [See Appendix A]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or he could have been born there in California.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well you see my dad . . . yeah, he was probably born in California because my dad was born in 1896, so 1876, it'd been probably . . . I think my granddad was at least 30 when my dad was born, so that wouldn't go back to 1949, so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I mean 1849. So there had to be a generation in there, so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he'd be native CaIfornian quite a ways back.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now then, your grandmother, what was her maiden name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was Heisert.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how her family got to California?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea [See Appendix A]. I know that the Heisert family was kind of more bullish than the Vanderburg side, because my dad had a cousin and he was always restless in church, and so his mother asked my grandmother how she kept my dad quiet in church, and she says "I just reach over and pinch him." So the next Sunday, well, while I'm talking here I'm thinking I'll come up with my dad's cousin's name, but I haven't anyway, right in the middle of service he just stood up and he says "Now you quit pinching me!"

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it didn't work for that side of the family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not at all. But I knew him and he was that way. But anyway, then all of my dad's children, he had six, and five of them were born in California, and my youngest brother was born out there at Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there's six kids in your family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then your mom, from about 1901, she's going to California during the winters and going to school there. And your dad, when was he born?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was just a few years older than.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Four years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they meet?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think they probably met at school. Because in these annuals I see both of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But he's a few years older than her.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He's a senior and she's a freshman.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. So, when did they get married then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They got married in 1917. [May 1, 1918]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So she was just about graduated from high school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. She was a year out of high school and of course this wa, my dad went into the service in 1917. See he was, well he would have been 21 en, but he, I don't know, he was going to college I think or something and they ap iarently didn't draft him until, I believe it was 1917, and he was drafted. And they ot married about the time that he got drafted. And he spent his World War I time up in Washington in a sawmill. And it was a sawmill because his eye sight was very oor. Actually, he was a wonderful accountant, and you could read his figures from cle across the room when he wrote 'em. But he had one eye that was blind and act ally he worked for Union Oil Company when I was real small as an accountant and he had to give up because his eyes were really going down hill and they didn't ha e the doctors they do now. And I remember when I was about 4 years old, well one ight he was working

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: graveyard and my mother was doing something so he took me to work with him, and his job then was storekeeper in Union Oil warehouse, ordering parts and all the valves and all the stuff they use in the well drilling down there. And that was his job. He put me to bed on a bench there but I had one eye open watching what was going on all the time 'cause I was always a mechanic from the time I was a little bitty person. I was interested. Now, I got lost, where am I?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see. Your mom and dad got married, and then he got drafted in the war and sent to the sawmill, but to back up just a little bit, what did his parents do for a living? Your grandmother's were wealthy real estate.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My grandfather on his side was into real estate, too. And he bought homes, fixed them up and sold 'em. He was a good carpenter and painter and had a good eye for what he could make money at. And he really got creamed in the Depression because he had a bunch of houses sold on contract and people didn't make their payments, so they lost 'em back to him and he lost 'em to the bank, and so he went from a rich man to quite a poor man. However, he did have 160 acres of walnuts in downtown what is now Fullerton, just right off of Chatsworth, and when my grandmother died, before she died, I was up to see her one time, and Chatsworth was four-lane street, probably 50 mile an hour street, and she'd walk out her back door and just walk right over to Alpha Beta market right across that four-lane highway and never look either way because she was just walking the back place there. She never realized that the town had built up and she thought she was walking on the farm. And I was very surprised she lived to die of old age, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the Vanderburgs, how many kids were there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In my dad's family there was Clarence, his older brother, and his sister Velma, and him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the three of them as small as their folks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Velma was. Velma was very small. And she was almost totally blind before she died. They all had glaucoma and they didn't know what to do about it in those days, and so it took their sight, and, yes she was small. But my dad was about 5'7" and so was Uncle Clarence, and that was smaller than average but big enough so I couldn't wear my dad's pants when I was in the eighth grade.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, he married your mom, and then he got drafted. Do you know what town that sawmill was in that he served his time in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he was in the Vancouver Barracks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In Vancouver, Washington.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's where he lived, and they transported him to the mill, so I suppose it was probably down along the Columbia River. Vancouver Barracks isn't in Vancouver, though, is it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well yeah, basically, but they had the spruce mill, say in Toledo, Oregon was controlled out of Vancouver Barracks. So they had the whole spruce division going, I think, from that area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I can't say where he.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But he was stationed at Vancouver Barracks and he worked in a sawmill out of there until the war ended?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then, then what did your folks do for a living?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was one other thing that might be of interest. My mother got the World War I flu. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, that influenza epidemic of 1918?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And she almost died, and she was pregnant with my oldest sister [See Appendix Al. So they decided they had to take the baby to save her life and so they did, and my oldest sister lived. And at that time she was the smallest baby that had ever lived on record.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there any kind of clippings or newspapers in your family about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. My dad said she'd fit into the palm of his hand and her head would come up to about here. And he wasn't a very big man. And so she was pretty premature. But anyway, that was one of the highlights of their early marriage. My mother, when she came to, she didn't believe she had a daughter, and she didn't know it for a week or two for sure until they could finally bring her in to see her. But she did recover from the flu.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many children. .. was that the first child then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the first child.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then how many more children?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was three girls older than I am, and then me and then my sister that's in Canada [Ruth] and then my youngest brother who is an electrician out here at Leading Plywood in Philomath.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so you have got quite a bit of your family in the Corvallis area now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have a sister in Washington. My second sister [Wilma] died many years ago and that is the one whose husband married the daughter of the first forest ranger in Oregon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. It's a.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Orval Cummings.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. He's the one that took the deer into the Smith area, the Greenberiy Smith area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. He took them in there apparently about 1934. He got a couple fawns. He worked for Doc Howard in Corvallis. Doc Howard ran a bunch of sheep and my brother-in-law lived up in the Alsea area and herded sheep for Doc Howard, made fence and so forth, and he, when we moved to Oregon we were pretty hard up so he decided we needed some help eating and so he took my dad up there on the south fork of the Alsea River with a pitchfork and cork boots and he brought back about 30 salmon and smoked them and since they're not traceable, I can tell that story. But we had smoked salmon that year to winter us over because we were really hard up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's go back to 1918, World War I, and your dad came home. Was he there when your oldest sister was born?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, my oldest sister was born in Fullerton. My next oldest sister Wilma was born in that area some place. Then my dad bought a ranch out in the Mojave desert out there by Lancaster, and it had an artesian well on it. And my sister Audrey was born there, and the story on that was that no telephones, of course, and my dad got in the Model T and headed for town to get the doctor and he hit a chuckhole and the wheel went like this and the Model T tipped over and by the time he got it tipped back over on its wheels and got the doctor and got there my sister was already born. But anyway, and then they moved to Baldwin Park where I was born, and I don't know what he was doing at that time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year were you born?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was born in 1923.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So in just five years there he had. . . do you know what he was doing while he was still

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: living in town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, he was tied in with Union Oil Company, I believe, from the time he got out of the service until we moved to Antelope Valley the second time, which was in 1929.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's the area in the Mojave Desert?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big a place did he buy there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The first time he had 40 acres right on, near on Dry Lake. But I think he worked in town for Union Oil, I don't think he farmed that. Then, when I was born in Baldwin Park, he was farming. That Baldwin Park of course is all city now. It's between Los Angeles and San Bernardino. Then he moved to Chino, when I was fairly, pretty young, and he left Chino when I was two. My mother one time realized that I had a fantastic memory and she asked me what I could remember furthest back. And I told her, well, I could remember my dad out plowing with a team of horses and they had these pushers that they pushed the laundry in when they boiled it. I was riding one of those for a horse and I had a black and white and brown dog and I was following my dad down the furrow. I said there was a big corral there, I think it was probably a bull pen and some cows, but that's all I can remember. And she says, well, she says "That was Chino and we left there quite a bit before you were three years old." So, anyway...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of crop was he raising?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had milk cows. He had a big dairy there. And he [his cows] got hoof and mouth disease and lost the whole thing. And so then, from there he went to Brea, California, and he was back working for Union Oil Company then, that was the time when I remember sleeping on the bench at Union Oil. And, by the way I can drive right up to the house we lived in Brea and we lived there when I was four.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The house is still there then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you can remember where it's at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, my wife and I when we went on our honeymoon, we were driving through Brea and all at once I made a turn, and she says "Where in the world are you going?" and I said "I think this is the street I used to live on." Drove right up and I says there's the house. When I was four years old! So anyway, then in 1929 of course my grandfather lost about everything he had and my dad kind of took the tumble with him. And I do know that my dad before he got married bought 40 acres and planted it to an orange grove, and he made quite a bit of money off of that when he sold it, but he could have made more money off of it because it was right in the Disneyland parking lot now. I told him he should have kept it and he says "I couldn't have paid the taxes on it all those years."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the . . . so your grandfather Vanderburg lost pretty much everything in the stock market crash in 1929?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, actually, it wasn't the stock market, it was real estate loss.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that kind of related?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was all related, everything fell.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about your grandfather Rose?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh, I don't really know. He died just about 1929 [February 11, 1930]. Cause I was. well he died jUst after we moved to Lancaster. And we moved to Lancaster in '28 I believe it was. And we just got moved up there and my folks took my sister and I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: down so they could see my grandpa in the hospital and he died very shortly after that. That was before I was going to school. Because the kids that were old enough to go to school, they didn't go down with us. So he would have died just about the time that everything fell. But apparently there wasn't much left of his fortune, because I never heard much of anything about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Probably would have had an impact on your mother and the rest of your family, or you would have known.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But his third wife. Was she still alive?

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 2. California Homestead

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anyway, she lived up into the, I'd say about 1950. My mother had a great dislike for her, so I had no tie with her at all until, actually, probably, well about the time my mother died, I went to a family reunion down there and she was there, and got acquainted with her, but at that time her mind was going and she didn't even know who I was and so. . . But anyway, the reason we moved from Brea of course was hard times hit and about the same time my dad got a chance to, what do you call it when you got 320 acres for nothing by proving up on it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Homestead?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Homestead, yeah. He got a chance to homestead 320 acres up there 32 miles out of Lancaster at Wilsona. Out in the desert, and not too far from what is now called Los Angeles Lake, which was Lovejoy Lake when I was there, and this Lovejoy Lake was full of Indian artifacts. And we used to go there and swim and look for arrowheads and one time one guy found a perfect set of Indian beads. And he took them over and washed them in the Lake and all he had was the thong. They all dissolved. But anyway, that was in the area where we lived and we built a house there and by that time my dad had five children and he built a two-room house. But there

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did your mother handle that? Just having been raised by servants and all of a sudden having five kids and a poor family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was very adaptable to any situation. My mother was always adaptable. I mean, she was, she was . . . when Hatfield was running for office she had her picture taken with him in his campaigns and so forth, she was into . . . she was Oregon Mother of the Year twice, she was . . . but she adapted to whatever the situation was. And in that case, well, we slept outside because, well, once in a while we'd get snow on the ground but most of the time by 8:00 it was warm anyway. Of course, there was a lot of rattlesnakes there, we'd get up and find tracks under our beds in the sand where the snakes crawled under our beds at night and so forth. And once in a while we'd find the snakes in the sheet under our bed!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Depression to you kids was more kind of like a camping out adventure, in a way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Basically, we didn't really know it except that I can remember the first steak I ever saw when my dad got a new job and my mother went out and bought him a steak out of the first paycheck, and we got to smell it. [Laughs]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. What year was that, about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I suppose it was about '34, or something like that, he'd gotten back on at Union Oil Company.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you just got to smell the steak!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Smell the steak! Anyway, but times were hard, I mean, there wasn't, in that country, there was nothing you could go out and shoot, a deer or anything like that, to get something to eat and so we ended up we were on welfare for a year or two there, and the thing I remember about welfare was that they, the story went that our government officials decided that they were going to put a big herd of cattle out there in the desert and pasture them, so they got all these cows and were gonna make meat for the starving people and turned out that they figured that you got a cow you gotta have a bull for the cow. So they had as many bulls as they did cows, then somebody told them that wasn't necessary, so they made these big old bolognas about that long and about that big around and all the welfare people, every time you went for welfare you got those bolognas! And that was all bull meat from the surplus bulls!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think that story was true?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I kinda think it was 'cause I heard it from several different people. But it's very possible! And, anyway, but then my dad then got a chance to trade that place for a place on Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was. . that's kind of how the Hanishes came up. He was able to trade his real estate in California, that he was homesteading, for a place in Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, except that he [Hanish] also had property back in the midwest. And that was at the time of the dust bowl. And he traded for some property about, probably two miles, I don't know if you ever got to the Chaffin place up there not, but I think probably the fireplace is still standing. They were way back off the county road. And he had 100, he traded 160 acres of farmland back there in, I thought it was Nebraska, but it could have been Kansas. And he traded it for some 160 acres of ground in Oregon. He says, boy he sure thought he'd pulled the wool over the guy's eyes. He says he got out here and he said he found out his farm was all covered with trees!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And so that was what he was logging. And that was probably a mile and a half from where they lived. And I don't know if Jim even knew that, but his dad told me, you know, I told you that I worked for his dad on Saturdays helping him fall trees to keep him busy the rest of the week, and he told me that. And he was kinda mumbling and grumbling about trading his farm back there in the midwest for a bunch of trees, and they weren't worth anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he ever change his mind after he started logging, or..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so, because at that time, you see, he was selling stumpage for 50 cents a thousand, and Orval, my brother4n-law, cut wood on his place, and he paid 50 cents a cord stumpage for the wood and it, those trees were probably 30 inches across the stump and no limbs up there for 150 feet and you'd just haul them. And of course in those days you didn't have power saws so you cut it in four foot lengths and split it and then they came in with power saws and sawed it. Not power saws, but buzz saws. And it was. . but anyway, it was 50 cents a cord or 50 cents a thousand for that timber and that was worthless as far as he was concerned because a good man could make a dollar and a quarter a day, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So a #1 peeler now was just firewood then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. We made a lot of firewood. Anyway, that's off on a different subject, but you did mention the F{anishes and I do know that he traded that farm back east.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about your dad? flow did he feel on his trade?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He felt real good about it. But he was too slow getting his feet under him to make payments on it. And he lost it in '40.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 3. Land of Milk Nickel Trees

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But in '35, . . . why did you decide to come to Oregon? Nothing going on at home there, or. 2

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was, actually, his farm down there in Wilsona had water at 50 feet, all that you could use, and he pumped it with an old Hudson motor but that old sandy soil, it took a lot of water and he never got financially capable of planting enough alfalfa to make a living off of it, and, so, he was always watching newspapers and, you wouldn't know it, but I remember when I lived down there that when my dad worked on WPA, during lunch time, well all they talked about was Oregon. And everybody wanted to go to Oregon. And of course one reason for wanting to go to Oregon was there was berries, and there was wild fruit and there was wild animals and so forth that you could supplement your diet with, which was quite a difference when we moved to Oregon. The fact that we could eat berries and there was wild plums and, you know, we never did shoot a deer cause we never did see any deer in that country at that time. Maybe we'd see two deer a year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In the Berry Creek area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But even down in Southern California, families were made poor by the Depression, there was a lot of talk of coming to Oregon, just because of the ability to live off the land, support yourself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: More or less, yes. Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's interesting.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I remember, there was guy by the name of Andy Anderson worked on WPA and during his lunch breaks, he was quite an artist, and my dad used to take me with him sometimes cause we were real close, and Andy Anderson, every lunch hour, he was drawing a picture of Oregon and I remember, of course I was probably 5 years old, and right in the middle of the picture he had a big picture of a milk nickel tree. Well the milk nickel was an ice cream bar. And he thought that they had milk nickel trees in Oregon, just pick the milk nickels off the trees! But that's the way the gist of the thinking was running in that time frame there out in the desert where we were, was the fact that you could pick most anything off of the tree and, you know, life, and so my dad felt that we had an opportunity there and he got help from the FHA buying ten head of cows and to buy some farm machinery. But, he couldn't buy any tractors because tractors were not feasible. He had to buy a team of horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They didn't use those in 1935.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the help was on the farm up here, not down there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the name of the real estate dealer or the land owner that he traded with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dollarheide was the realtor in Albany. He was right at the foot of the first bridge there on the left across First Street or Second Street there, whatever it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the name of the land owner that was engineering th trade?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know because Dollarheide made the trades, our place for his place, and we never saw him. We dealt through the realtor. The guy that owned it didn't live on it. When we moved in the renter lived on it when we moved in. And so that, anyway, we moved up here..

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 4. Migration to Oregon

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you remember anything about the move? Your dad.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was just gonna say, my dad was on WPA and you weren't allowed to save any of your wages, you were supposed to spend it all to help the economy. So when he made the trade the he bought a 1923 Dodge truck that had been a garbage truck, $25.00. And we overhauled it. I say we did, because my dad wasn't much of a mechanic and even though I was only ten years old I did most of the work overhauling it. And we overhauled the truck there in the yard, and then we loaded the thing up with everything we owned, and we pulled out one morning and we got four miles down the road to where the pavement was and we couldn't get up onto the road because our load was so heavy the body'd come down on the tire and then it would stop us. So we had to back up and go to the people that had the post office and store there in Wilsona and we left a bunch of our furniture there and we never got anything for it, I'm sure they sold it but we never heard from them. We had to get some weight off that truck because the springs weren't strong enough to get us up onto the road. So then we took off and there was a bolt sticking down from the bed and it started rubbing on the tire and it started getting a hole in it and so we had to stop and with a chisel and a hacksaw cut that bolt off down underneath the bed, between the bed and tire. And it was ultimately, took us five days to drive that thousand miles from there up to our farm and when we came in to Berry Creek we had to come in from, that town between here and Monmouth,.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Folks? Airlie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, on the highway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, between here and Monmouth?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the one where the service station store is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, it's Adair now, but it would have been.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, clear on past there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Suver?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Suver, yeah. Suver. We had to go in to Airlie through Suver because the road didn't go across from Berry Creek to Soap Creek at that time. There was no road through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From Berry Creek to Soap Creek, there was no road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was no road. The road went to Berry Creek school, and to the turnoff to Bill Coote's old mill, which he had abandoned before we moved there. And then, when he built the mill up on top, they had to come in from the Soap Creek side with their trucks and stuff, and ultimately that was what made the road be pushed on through between Berry Creek and Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, that road in there dates back to the /850's. But when you were in there, it had been pretty much abandoned, and wasn't in use anymore?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It didn't go through. The, right this side of where the school was, was a real steep

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: hill, and no possible way you could get up that hill in the wintertime. In the summertime, we could get through. But when we first moved there, Dorsey Bus Company had to come in through Suver and then back to our place, because we lived in Benton County. Most of our property was in Polk County, but we lived in Benton County. So the bus at driver lived at our house and the bus stayed at our house. We had a 1935 Diamond T bus which was practically brand new -- the pride of the Dorsey Bus Company. I mean, at that time he had six buses. And, but anyway, so we took off from our place and went toward Airlie, and then came up the Suver road until we got almost to Suver and then we started picking up people in that area and I don't know why we were picking them up in Polk County. Because we picked up, oh, Wesley Voss, he's still alive, and a bunch of the Kesters and one thing and another coming out to Suver. Then we went down Highway 99 until we got to what is now Camp Adair, and then we went across over to, I think they call it Independence Road now, and then we came down Independence Road to Highway 20 and then came in and picked all the people up on Highway 20 into Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this was when you were going to High School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And then, while we lived there, then they came in and punched that road on through and graveled it. And then the bus started going the other way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was about, late 1 930's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, probably 1938, '37 or '38 that they pushed that road on through and at the same time just north of our house that was a steep road and they had to do quite a bit of blasting and they made about a four foot cut then, but most of the work was done with teams and horses and that sort of thing, so it was quite an undertaking to put that road on through.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you are saying north, you are talking about Brinkley's Hill there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what you call it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That little hill, just to the north of:

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right on the county line.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 5. Berry Creek Farm

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you think when you first got to Oregon? Was everybody happy to have the trip over, they liked the new place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oregon was beautiful. And everything was green and if you remember where our house was, our house set right behind those maple tees, and we had a. . . let's see, five bedroom home there with a front porch that went clear across the whole front of the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it one of the old farm homes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a farm home, but it was a well-built, nice home. And they actually moved it when the Camp Adair moved in, that was one of the few homes that they moved out of there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So is that home still in existence?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Somewhere, but I don't know where it went. But I was told that they moved that out of there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the home have a name to it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of. But then, to go on, it was a nice home and then we had, behind

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the house we had a porch across the back where we hung our clothes to dry and we didn't have any electricity, no telephones, and then we'd, behind that we had our milk house and behind that we had our woodshed, all hooked to the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, those were connected to the house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, all connected to the house. So we didn't have to get out in the mud at all from the house to the woodshed to the milkhouse. So once we got done with our chores and took off our rubber boots we could separate the cream and all that sort of thing without having to go back out into the mud again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a dairy farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was a dairy farm. I told you we bought ten cows through the Farm Home Administration, and we had 120 acres there and we had about 27 acres in pasture down along the creek. And then we had oats and vetch down along the bottom land and we raised oats and some wheat and some barley up on the hill. But mostly we raised ferns, because we didn't have sprays, herbicides, to kill the fern and they we tried clean cultivating, we tried everything in the world to try and kill those fern but the more you plowed them the thicker they got. And now its pretty good farm there because they can control the weeds and so forth. And we also had Canadian Thistle that was a big problem. Mostly up on the hill ground. But.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, your land, was that to the east of Berry Creek Road there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it would sit down well away from the forest land.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Actually, our property was on both sides of Berry Creek. Once you went. when Berry Creek went about, oh, 500 feet past the road there, across over, it was in our property all the way down to the back except our property was kinda L shaped and Forest Tandy lived in this L back there. And Forest Tandy had water rights on Berry Creek and he was a good truck farmer and he raised a lot of fruits and vegetables and stuff back there. And he built a beautiful barn back there also. I don't know if that barn is still there or not but I didn't see it when I was there last time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There is a barn still standing right next to Berry Creek, pretty close, was that Tandy's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the road?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Forest Tandy's father-in-law built that. Mr. White built that. And he built that while we lived there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tandys lived right next to Berry Creek. Wasn't there another family on the other side of Berry Creek from Tandys?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well Tandy lived behind us. Tandy lived east of us. He lived just directly east from our house. See we went. . . our property came like this and Tandy set right in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If. . here's a little drawing of. . if this is Berry Creek, and here is the Coote's house .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: here, and Hanish is back here, and Dickeys are right there. . . fsee map on page.. - . .1

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, Dickeys are over here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And then, we were right straight across from that house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's the Vanderburgs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. And then, our property, this is Berry Creek, well Berry Creek goes like this and Tandys had road went right along the creek here and then across the creek right here, and that's here the creek came into our property, and then Tandys lived back here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Tandys were. . now, wasn't there somebody living about right there on the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was four people lived in there while we lived there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Was there two houses, one on either side of the creek, or just one on.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just one over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And there was two houses back here. Tandy built two houses there, one for himself and one for the Whites.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the Whites was his father-in-law.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Was his father-in-law, yeah. And they both lived together back here and this was just strictly a summer road. And the school teacher lived back there and it was about a half mile walk out for her through the mud to get to school every day. I was talking to Mrs., or Miss Ramona (Moehnke) Dodson, here last week, and I said "Remember walking that mud?" and she says, "I sure do!" But anyway, that was about the location and then on, see our property came down here and then it made an L and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it just excluded the Tandys there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and Tandy came out this way, his farm did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, Tandys had a fairly large place, too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'd say they probably had 150, 160 acres in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then somewhere over in here would be Joe Smith?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Joe Smith is back on the next road back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And Joe Smith owned this property right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he owned all the way up to the road here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He owned on this side of the road. He owned the Coote's place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he owned that whole hill that you said there was snakes on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I'm quoting Jim Hanish on that, so. . that hill, did you have a name for it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, Jim calls it Folk's Hill. Does that ring any bells? He says there was a Folk family right at the base of it that farmed it. And an old house and orchard in there in the / 930's. And there was an old road that goes around the base of it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the one right next to the [Berry Creek] school house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. The school house is over here, kinda against the base of the hill on that side of the road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, well when I lived there, Mr. Folks [Bert] lived in this house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I saw that on the map and I was thinking maybe he was forgetting "Folks" for "Polk", so

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Folk. Okay. And Folk had kinda the same job I did, he was on the Soil and Water Conservation Board of Directors, the same as what I was only back in 1936.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so he was with the Soil Conservation Service back when you were living there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, clear back in '36.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are any of his relatives still alive? Any of the kids that he raised or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ethan Folks was the only son that they had, and he went to Washington. And Mr. Folks sold the farm over there to Dick White and he moved over here on Highway 20. I don't know if you've been around here long enough to remember when there was a bull farm over there or not. Highway 20.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've been over in Lincoln County for 40 years, so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, you go out Highway 20, and you go down past that golf course and then you go up a little hill on the left, and that's where Mr. Folk lived when he died. Anyway, so it was "Folk" rather than "Polk" that he was talking about. But anyway, he wasn't farming this when I was there. Not up by the school, because I know that Mr. Smith had a bunch of sheep in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Smith was running sheep in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, on that hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There is an orchard right around the school house there. Do you remember anything about that orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you ever remember the name Berry Creek, or Berry Creek School -- I mean Savage Creek, or Savage Creek School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I just remember hearing it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not a thing. I didn't know it was in our area. I thought it was over on Soap Creek side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Soap Creek side they called it the Savage Creek. On your side. Okay, up against. . . on the other side where you called the "Cootes" rather than "Coonte's", there is in old mill site in there and there is some houses where the people that worked in that mill lived. Was that mill closed down by the time you

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mill was closed down but us kids played in it all the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything about that mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can remember one thing about it. All these workers' cabins, their outhouses were built over the creek so they didn't have to dig holes for them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. They weren't so worried about pollution in those days.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. We would go from the school, and this was all clear fields over here, and there as a great big barn across from the school, it was put together with pegs. Wooden pegs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A real old barn, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And it withstood that 3 foot of snow we had in '36.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 6. Snowstorm of 1937-1938

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, it was the '36 snow? I've heard '37, but it was a 1936 snow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Might have been '37 [According to Eugene Glender, the snowstorm began on January 1, 1937 and continued for 2 or 3 weeks], but it was while we lived there. And we had three feet of snow there and we'd like to have never have got that Diamond T bus started after that snow.
bracketed_corrections: According to Eugene Glender, the snowstorm began on January 1, 1937 and continued for 2 or 3 weeks

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did that snow stay on the ground?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, but I know we didn't get that bus started for over a week. 'Cause it just had a 6 volt battery in it, and old Mr. Dorsey he carried a battery in on his shoulder from over there toward Airlie someplace as far as he could get with his car. Of course there wasn't any such thing as pickups in those days. And he carried that on his shoulder. And then he took all the spark plugs out and put them on the heater to try and warm them up. And he ended up, he carried two batteries in there before we finally got it started; course no electricity, no battery charger. And he couldn't get

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: a car in to put a jumper cable on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything else. . . were the people surprised about that snow, or was there any...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. That came fast. I went to bed, and there was no snow. And when I got up the next morning there was 3 feet on the ground. And our machine shed had gone down, and all of our tools and stuff. And the machine shed was a lean-to on our granary, and it tore lose from the granary and it went down and as I remember in this house where the barn is still standing

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: . make sure the thing's running, I don't like to redo my errors. Okay, we're on the '36 or

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: '37 snow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, uh huh. Yeah, anyway, when that snow came, well of course we were milking cows, and no place to put the milk anyway because the milk truck couldn't get through, but I always took a gallon of milk to Elmer Tandy on my way to school and so my mother insisted that I take a gallon of milk to him that morning through three feet of snow. And of course I was about, well, 14, and traveling through that three foot of snow was pretty tough going, I'll tell you! Cause it was clear up above my knees, you know. And you couldn't push the stuff and you couldn't get on top of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they close the school because of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah. Yeah, the school teacher couldn't walk that. See, she walked over a mile and there was no snow plow or anything ever came in, cause of course this road didn't even go through at that time, so

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When it melted did it create any flooding problems?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No to my knowledge. Flooding in our area was flash floods pretty much on Berry Creek because it's such a short ways to the top of the coast range there and it, if we got heavy rain all night well a lot of times you could hear it roaring when you woke up in the morning, but we never had any floods, you know, that amounted to anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Have you ever seen any snows worse than that snow since you lived in this country?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Had the same thing south of town here, in 1969. Had three feet of snow there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Happened just as quick?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But I had four-wheeled drive then, an International, and I went out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the old timers that were in the Berry Creek area when that happened? Do they remember, did they talk about worse snows, or ....

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never heard anything to that effect. Like I say, they did say that Pedee had 14 [four!] feet. I don't know what area in Pedee or what, whether it was drifting, or what it was, but it was pretty good snow and one thing about it, we had lots of milk so we had lots of ice cream and rice pudding to eat! Till the snow melted off. But my folks only went to town once a week anyway, because. . . you know, people nowadays if they've gotta have something they run to town and get it. But in those days a half a gallon of gas was too much to spend just to go to town, after all it cost 12 cents a gallon, you know. 0

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 7. Bennett's Mill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have the same vehicle, the old garbage truck was your main vehicle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we also had a '27 Dodge Sedan that we drove up at the same time. And that was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the car we drove for a limited amount of time, and then after it kinda tuckered out, then we got a '29 Nash, and went on up through the ranks. But I did take that. . . I mentioned this Bennett's Mill, there was a man by the name of Jack Green that lived over by, just over the hill from Suver, that was in the wood business. And anybody cutting wood over in the Berry Creek area he bought it, and so he made a deal with the Bennetts for their slab wood. So I had that old Dodge, or my dad did, and so they offered us, if we would buy the slab wood for 50 cents a cord from Bennetts Mill, cut into four foot lengths, and we would load it and bring it down to Berry Creek Road and stack it 8 feet high and Jack Green would pay us $1.50 a cord for it. So we got 75 cents a cord for hauling that stuff out of the mountains. I mean, real steep mountains.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We got 75 cents a cord for it for stacking it down on the county road. And so we took the bed off the truck and we would stack that stuff on the frame and come down the hill, and of course in those days only rear wheel brakes to start out with and not much of that, and low gear and down the hill we'd come. And anyway, I did most of the work on it, cause like I say my dad wasn't much of a mechanic and he was farming, and so that was my job for one year. Anyway, I made enough money I bought a 1933 Chevrolet truck then, so I was in the trucking business then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So how old were you about that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fifteen. I didn't have a driver's license then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you were in the trucking business anyhow!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I got a learner's permit and every time I had to get out on the road my dad had to go with me. But Cooper's Mill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now where was Bennett's Mill located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bennett's Mill was in back of Hanish's house. On up the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And. okay. There was a road that went up. . did you know where Forest Peak was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. There was a road that.. . did you have a different name for the creek that came by the old Coote Mill site? Did you call that any

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We called that Berry Creek, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you call it lefthand, or south, or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Really, we didn't. It was just Berry Creek, we went up this fork or this fork. I imagine we would probably call it the south fork or the left fork of Berry Creek, you know if we'd have been trying to identify it, but I never heard it identified, actually. For the most part we called the Berry Creek that went past the school, we called that Berry Creek, and we didn't have much reason to even call the other one by name because it wasn't all that big.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's a road that went back up along the base of that hill there. There's some apple trees in there. Do you know anything about that orchard in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, that's going past the sawmill site?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just in the sawmill, getting ready to move up the hill, because I wanted to kind of tie that into Bennett Mill there, if that was the road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's what they call the 100 road now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you turn down here right there where that barn is that's standing by itself.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About 100 feet this side of that there was a road went back. And that was the road that went back to Hanish's house. And we took that road and we just kept right on going past Hanish's and right on up to Bennett's Mill. And it was a steep road. I mean, it was. . . that's why Jack Green wasn't taking his truck up there, cause it was practically a cat road.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 8. Coote's Sawmills

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So, then you said there was a pond in back of the Coote Mill. Is that the place that you were telling me that they had a flume?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, where the Coote Mill, the one you were talking about, if you went on around the corner and probably I would guess probably, oh, maybe a half mile, right on Berry [Savage] Creek, just follow Berry Creek up, Bill Coote had a dam in the creek there, and his mill was on this side of the creek and he had this flume on a pretty steep hill over on this side. And he pulled the logs down the ridge of the mountain, or hill, and then shot them down this flume he had. There was water up there on top that he got in there someway. And they pulled those logs in with team of horses and got them up to where the top of the flume was and then they'd unhook the horses and take a peavy and roll the log into the flume -- shoop -- down it'd go.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Straight into the pond.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But was his mill back by the pond then, or was it up here closer to the road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that one was back by the pond. He had three mills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so one of the mills he had was the one right by the road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then one was back by the pond.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was on around the curve of Berry Creek and back up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And then he had the one up on top of the hill. And the one up on top of the hill is what made em put Berry Creek [Road] on through.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, when he had that one on the top of the hill, there's a couple of small homesteads up there. Do you remember the families who lived in those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I can tell you a story about the one that's, I think there's still a house on the lefthand side right up on top of the hill?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think the house isn't there, but there's a couple of apple trees and an old pond up in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Okay. Well, I don't know who owned that, but the Gardners lived there. And Mr. Gardner, he was on welfare, and he lived there long enough so that he claimed squatter's rights and he got that away from the owner for nothing. And even in the Depression, everybody looked down on Mr. Gardner for getting free right, or free living, for seven years and then taking it away from the owner.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. Who was the owner? You don't. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. He was, could have been in California or anyplace, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was pretty curious why that got surveyed out. It's a real odd.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, well. . . Gardner got the house site and quite a bit of land by squatter rights. That would have been probably 1938.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Like a little local scandal, or something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah. Because he was, actually he was running a "turn a pull" road machine [He helped make the fill on Highway 99 over the rail road in Albany] and still drawing welfare so he was. . . there was a lot of scandal as far as he was concerned. He had a daughter, Charlotte, who had polio and she was older than I was and she just got where she could walk after we lived there, and she rode the bus when the bus started going past their place. But it was another interesting thing about that, when they first lived there the road didn't go past their place. So after they put the road in, well, every time you'd drive by there they'd hang out the window to see who was going by.
bracketed_corrections: He helped make the fill on Highway 99 over the rail road in Albany

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Gardners would?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they always. . . and of course, another scandal with them, they were never up till 8:00, and everybody was up by 5:30. So that was another scandal for them. They just laid around until 8:00 in the morning.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All the way till then. [Laughs]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But anyway, there is one thing more now, we've already gone around the corner here in Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep. Now let me ask one quick question here. When this mill was closed down was it still called the Coote's Mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and the old houses were there, but nobody was living in them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, people were living there when we first.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They were still living there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, were they working in this mill back here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this mill was the first one and this was the second one. And this was the.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the one back by the pond was the first one? With the flume.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So was that flume still operating when you were there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It wasn't operating but it was there. I climbed the hill beside the flume one time and it was steep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then this one here had even closed down by the time you lived there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but he'd just barely moved out of that. He hadn't started up the other one up here yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Okay, so but then we kind of backed off over there. The one that he started up on. this one here was the one you were telling me got repossessed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was the one on the top of the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so these down here he still owned but they weren't operating any more.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they weren't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and then he moved his operation up the hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up the hill, closer to the timber. He'd pretty much logged this out and moved up where there was. . . remember, when you're logging with horses you don't pull the logs very far.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You pull the mill to the logs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's basically . . I mean that's the same thing with Bennett's Mill. It was built up in the timber. Anyway, did you ever hear anything on the Chaffin place?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nope.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 9. The Chaffin Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, well if you went on up the creek here, probably a mile and a half, there was the Chaffin place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, would that be up this road here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not towards Bennett's Mill, but up past.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up this. . . see, there's a knob goes between this and this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The one that. . . Okay. Between the two Berry Creek forks there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You went up the south fork. And you went up there probably a mile and half, two miles. It was a pretty good walk. And the Chaffin place was built up there and I knew Ralph Chaffin, who was a child when they lived up there. And they never built a road up there, and all their stuff was done with horse and buggies. And when we moved there the Chaffins had moved out because Mr. Chaffin had had a heart attack riding back up in there. He rode horseback, in and out of the farm there, and one night he didn't come home and his wife went down and. . . I met his wife also. And she went down and found him dead. The horse came in and he didn't, and she found him dead. And so she and the boy moved out. But he had built a nice two-story house there with a two-story fireplace in there. And I had quite a bit to do with that because we were hard up and there was a meadow down below the house. And we moved our cows up there in the summer, and we pastured that meadow and milked up there at the Chaffin place. But one of the big memories I have was, here was all these buggies up there -- about five of them. And being the mechanic I was I took all the bodies off of them, and then I could ride on the wheels and reaches and ride down the hill full tilt. So I destroyed a lot of valuable wagons, buggies. And then one of them that I took down there we ultimately made a cart out of to move our milk cans on. My dad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long had the Chaffins lived up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. That's all I know about it, they were gone when we moved there. And they moved into Airlie. And where I met them for a short period while, we went to the, there was an Evangelical Church in Airlie, and we went to that church, Mrs. Chaffin and Ralph went to that church. And that's where I met them. But they never talked much about the history of that place. Of course, Ralph, he was kind of interested in my sister, too, all the single guys were around that area. But, anyway, I thought I ought to bring that in because I hadn't heard you mention the Chaffin place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I know where it is. And there is remnants and all this of an old homestead, we don't know...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is the old fireplace still there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That might be. They've got it marked from ten years ago. But to know the name of the family, and why they moved out, all that, the fact they had buggies there. .. Was the house still standing, when you were up there, pasturing up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But no families moved in there or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wasn't pastoring, I was pasturing. [Laughs]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, pasturing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we would stay there overnight. We had brought our bedrolls up there and we stayed overnight. And at that time, in the summertime, we could get in there with our old '29 Nash. And we would haul the milk out in the '29 Nash every morning, and then my dad and I would do our farming and stuff during the day, and then we'd go back up there at night and go find the cows, and.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it was called the Chaffin place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was the Chaffin place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Was there any other families back in there, or anything back up on that road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So from that on, all the way back to the Chaffin place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was a beautiful walk back there, because that was old growth and the moss was about that deep, and in the spring it was just covered with these lady slippers, I don't know if you know what they are or not, but anyway it was just purple with ladyslippers on that road up there because the timber hadn't ever been cut between where Bill Coote quit cutting and where their house was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember an orchard or anything associated with that house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah, there was an orchard in back of the house. A year or two later a family that lived in Airlie, her son was pasturing sheep up there, where we pastured our cows and there was two of them, two guys up there pasturing them, and the one guy got appendicitis and it had to come out, and so his mother asked my mother if I could go up there and stay with him so that he wouldn't be up there by himself. And so I went up there and stayed with him [Jerald McKibbenj probably ten days because it was a about a ten day recovery period for appendicitis at that time. And he had five dogs and he had built a holding pen for them at night and I hadn't ever seen dogs work much before that. And it was very interesting to punish a dog for not doing what it was supposed to. Hey, he had to stay with us all day. And that poor dog would just cry and fuss and whine and so forth all day long. The next day, it minded. But we would take those sheep out to a green patch, and then we'd find a shady ttee to lay under and watch those sheep all day, and whichever dog saw a sheep getting out of place, well it was the one that got to bring it back in, so they were all sitting there watching the sheep, and we were sitting there playing mumbly peg and one thing and another. Just to kill the time. And anyway, at night, we had a vee that came in to the pen and the dogs would get all the sheep up in this vee. We had 443 of them . . . no, 543. And so those dogs would line those sheep up around the vee that went into the pen, then one of us stand on each side and count the sheep as they went in and if there wasn't the right number then we sent the dogs out looking for them. So, it was real interesting to me to see how those dogs worked those sheep. We never herded sheep the whole time we were there, we just told the dogs what to do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were going through that old growth timber, but then you had all those sheep. So there must have been meadows or pasture .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was some big meadows around the Chaffin house. And actually we could go from the Chaffin house and go on around and end up in Hanish's timber place. And...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any other pastures or meadows up in that country there, or just around the Chaffin place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just around the Chaffin place. And they were natural meadows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They weren't anything that Chaffin graded or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, huh uh. There was no stumps, and in those days you'd see stumps because they didn't bulldoze them out in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you have any idea how big those meadows were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say there was probably 40 acres in one and about 7 in the other. And then there was a couple of little small ones, three or four acres that we could take the sheep out on for a couple of days, to pasture them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then on those meadows, can you remember any of the types of grasses, or plants, any trees growing in there or around those meadows?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a kind of a swampy area down in the middle of it, right down in the middle of it. Like there was a spring in it, probably more than anything. I think they had spring water piped into the house there. They had pipes running. And they had put a bunch of buildings up there, they had a milk house up there and so forth. I have an idea that he probably separated and sold his cream and, with the cream you only had to take it out twice a week, so probably he didn't have too much, could put it on a pack horse or whatever, and take it down to sell it. Anyway, that's all I can tell you about the Chaffin place. But I thought you might be interested in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I'm real interested. That's absolutely all the information we have on it. And we know where ruins are around the forest, but we don't know who owned them or what they did, or don't know how they herded sheep, so all this is the type of information that we're exactly looking for.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We were on horseback there herding those sheep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Doesn't sound like you needed them very much, sounds like the dogs did the work.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we just went out and back! But Gerald McKibbon was the guy I was herding sheep with, and he.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He's still alive, and I'm supposed to do an oral history with him.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he's back on the old McKibbon place now. He lived over in Lebanon for a number of years. And I knew his brother-in-law over in Lebanon. Today, but

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've been meaning to talk with him for some time. He's the person I'm supposed to interview. I've got two or three people I still haven't interviewed and he's one.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he could probably tell you some more about that Chaffin place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Good, and that's good to know, because I didn't even know to ask about that. I'm mostly concerned about Camp Adair with him, because he lived along there through Camp Adair. Okay, so we've covered the Chaffin, and Coote s Mill up on top, and the Gardner fr1mily there, and the two earlier mills that closed, so as we come around back towards Hanish's wood patch, and move back towards the highway, would Hanish's be the first place you'd run into then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Hanish's was the only habitable place in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, he mentioned finding back in the hills -- he didn't know the Chaffins, but he knew that there had been people living back in there. He mentioned that he found skulls of sheep with curved horns. Do you know anything about that at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were probably Chaffin's sheep, but I couldn't tell you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Anti you never heard of any other family living back in that country or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the only one that I know of that was back there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 10. Old-Growth

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On that timber that you describe as old growth. Jim [Hanish] and I looked at some trees on Forest Peak, and he said this is about the size of old growth on the hill. And it was about 30 inches and we counted the rings and it was about 75 years old. Is that what you were calling old growth in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so it could have been

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was calling it old growth right now. It's the first time I ever called it old growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you call it then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I didn't call it anything, but just the fact that the moss was so deep there made me think that it was probably old growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. But how big were the trees about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I would say they were 30, 36 inches. Same as Jim's dad, that's the way the timber on his place was. It would run 30 inches on the stump or so. But his was nice straight good stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But he said there was larger trees every so often, which they called the "grandfathers," and then he said they called them the "kids", the smaller trees. Do you remember anything about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we always figured that there had been a fire had gone through there many years ago and there was a few of them lived through it was kind of what we always assumed. And we called 'em grandfathers, just the same as what he.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so the trees that had seeded in those younger trees, you called the grandfather trees?

entries.speaker: A
