entries.text: Yeah, and we figured it was a fire that had. .. we always kind of figured the Indians had burned it. I mean, that was just our assumption, but. . . I worked in the woods, and what we called an old growth tree, was one with thick bark, It didn't necessarily have to be old. But it was this growth of bark on the outside that made it an old growth. Now I had trees down here on my place in Smith Loop that were old growths that weren't very big. I had some that probably weren't over 18 inches across the stump. But they had that big, thick bark and us old timers called those old growth, regardless of the size.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about, did you call them anything like "bastard fir," or "yellow fir," or "red fir?"

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we'd call red fir, red fir and white fir, white fir, clear back then. But the old growth were always called red fir, but they had a real coarse bark on them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you went by the thickness of the bark on them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the ones you called the grandfather trees? Would you call them old growth too, or would you just call them grandfathers for a different reason?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't believe they were. There was a lot of those that were white fir.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So grandfather just had to do with the fact that they seeded in all the younger trees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were bigger trees was all. But I wouldn't say that they were necessarily old growth, because see white fir had, at that time, had a quite a smooth bark even though they were three feet across the stump. Now these trees that Mr. Hanish was having me help him fall, we would fall them, he would cut them into 16 foot lengths, and then he would peel the bark off them, with a spud. And then they would log, take those logs into paper mills, with no bark on them. And, of course, they had to get them when the sap was up. They were big trees, but the bark wasn't more than an inch and a quarter thick. They'd be big enough to call an old growth, probably, but they were white fir, and that's what they wanted was white fir for paper mills in that

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: day because it made nice white paper, I guess. Less pitch in them, and so forth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they were easier to peel than the Dougs anyhow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you say Doug fir or did you just call them red fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We called them red fir.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the white fir would be what we call grand fir now, and the red fir would be the Doug fir, and the old growth would be the Doug fir with the thick bark?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You don't call white fir white fir anymore, huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, yeah, different names.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: White fir, the way you could tell them was that the limbs came from the trunk and went down before they went up. The red fir, the limbs went up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any hemlock in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, down lower.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not too much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, huh uh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about cedar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Not very much, though, really. We didn't cut any cedar, except usually you'd find the cedar down on the creek or something to make fence posts out of, and that was about all the cedar we cut. There wasn't really, I don't know, there wasn't enough cedar there apparently to make it worth bothering with because I did work west of Valsetz, down on the coast side, we cut quite a bit of cedar in there when I was logging. And I don't know if you ever wore a pair of corks in a logging show or not and stepped on a cedar, but it's a fast trip to the bottom of the

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, that bark kind of peels off a little quick and easy.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the bark gets in your corks and then you don't have corks and the next step you've got slick bark and away you go, and.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've worked a lot of that country west of Valsetz for twenty years.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I worked for Werner Timber Co., we went up the Siletz River and then went on up in there and most all of us had a scar on our back where carrying our old hand tools so it's get you in the back when you went down, rode down a cedar tree! When a man first went to work in the woods, well they would warn him about it and then they'd stand back to watch him to see when he was gonna do it! Cause nobody learned until he did it. A man that's pretty good could stay on there for two steps.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did .. . do you remember much oak or alder?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: None in that area there at all.

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Map of the tour of Soap Creek and Berry Creek with Neil Vanderburg on September 1, 1990.  Notice the juncture of the creeks to the east of Highway 99.  Modern U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) quadrangle maps have the junction in error, to the west of the highway.  Based upon a claim made by his father in the 1930s, Neil objected to the first draft of this map, which contained the USGS error.  After visiting and surveying the creeks with Neil during the fall of 1994, it was determined that his memory of his father's claim was indeed more accurate than current government maps.  OSU Research Forests maps and computer files were subsequently updated to reflect this new information.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part II. September 1, 1990 Interview

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Interview conducted September 1, 1990 by Bob Zybach.]

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: A. The Hildebrand Fire

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're at the [Homer H.J Hildebrand place, this second recording session with Neil Vanderburg, and today is September 1, 1990. And Neil, you want to tell me again how you found out about the fire here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I used to ride the school bus up here that came to pick up Bill Hildebrand, and one night when we brought him home we left him off here and the next morning we came to pick him up and all there was was some smoke coming out from little coals of the house that they lived in. And we later heard that Bill and his dad were the only ones that survived. Until I talked to Bob, I didn't know anything more about what happened to the Hildebrands or anything, so I wondered for this last 50 years or so what happened to them. So it was quite interesting to get back here and find out a little bit more about them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you say when you talked to Bob, you mean me?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. Now you said when you picked up Gene Glender after leaving this spot was the first you found out exactly what happened.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's when we found out that the two had survived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have a basement here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when it burned it was just down to bare ground.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just down to bare ground and some of the bigger timbers were still smoking but the main house was completely demolished. Nothing there but ashes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember where the house was located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not in this mess, it doesn't look the same as it did 50 years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's an old road down the east side over there. Do you recall where that might have gone?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Haven't any idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. The picture we looked at from 1936 showed a big barn down there where some pear trees are now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that barn was there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any old houses or anything down in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. I'm not sure, I had the impression that they weren't really farming here. Maybe had a few animals but that's about it. I don't know how they earned their living or what. But that would have been in about 1937 when that burned down, according to my calculations.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you said the school bus at that time couldn't come over the Tampico Road, they had to go all the way around?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, at this time we were coming over the hill there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then going down to Goviers down here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a mill going there at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A little later.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this mill wasn't quite going yet?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Leslie Gardner's husband worked there. Roif was his name. And he worked in that mill when they were building it, and that was after this fire had taken place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anything about the Hildebrands, what kind of people they were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Only that he was just kind of a small, light, fair type person. Nice looking kid and very quiet. He got on the bus and sat down and didn't say much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. Was this called the Hildebrand place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Far as I know. Of course, this was away from my old stomping ground, so all I knew was the kids that got on the bus. You know how kids are when they're on the bus, they're kinda flirting with the girls and all that stuff, they aren't much interested in scenery!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep. Can you recall any other thing about this site here, in particular?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, only I remember the house sitting out there in the clearing. I mean, all by itself basically. And we're standing here in front of a couple of fir trees that are probably 50 years old and if they were there they weren't as big as Christmas trees. And now they're big enough to saw. People that fight the clearcutting can't realize in a man's lifetime how big trees can get.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Well, all these silver maples here have just gone to weed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: B. The Marcks Place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're going by the old site on Marcks place. The school building on the left. And we're talking about Reese Mallow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Reese Mallow, I believe lived down in here someplace around the Dobrinins. We ran out of hay one year and my dad bought a big truckload of hay from Reese Mallow and later on he lived out there 8 miles south of Corvallis by where I moved in the late 1950's, but I didn't have too much to do with him. But he was always a cattle dealer and hay dealer. And that's about all I can tell you about him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: C. The Joe Smith Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay. I think this is probably part of Berry Creek. I can't get my bearings yet. But that marsh would be about where those trees right there are. Just the other side of that tractor, according to my memory. It might be over behind that barn. Probably more likely behind that barn over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're just south of the Joe Smith homestead.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Joe Smith home. I don't know whether it was a homestead or what, but that's where he lived when I lived here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And just north of Folks' place and we're looking due west.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just about due west.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so that grove of trees across the field there, maybe about a mile?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is where you think the old marsh was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well when we get up here on the Suver Road I can show it to you real plain.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But from down here . . . I was only down in here once. The Whites that did, well Charlie White and so forth, they moved here for a short period of time while we lived over there. And I came over here to see the Whites one time. It was the only time in my life that I was ever on this road before today.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh, it's the first time for me so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was about four houses in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In this area right here. Was just kind of a little. . . I don't know, Joe Smith was John's father. Joe was quite old when I left here in the late 30's. And John was farming t. I understand they both hit the bottle pretty heavy. But, like I say there was about four houses in here and there was a rental house apparently that old man White moved into, and this is, the slough area in here apparently that comes off of Berry Creek, I think that's probably Berry Creek in front of us, when we get onto Suver Road I can show you the back of our place from the road. I can show you our old fence line and from there we can tell where that was, because that marshy place started right at the end of our back field.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this slough here when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Joe Smith, did he have any reputation locally as a writer or a historian or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I knew. He was just a big landowner. Any time you talked about Joe Smith everything around here belonged to Joe Smith.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody put him together with Greenberry Smith, talk about Greenberry Smith at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't know about Greenberry Smith 'til I moved out on Smith Loop south of Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know anything about Joe Smith's politics or religion or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just that he owned a lot of land.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just that he was a big landowner and I heard rumors that he had a bottle hid in every corner.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did most people think he was pretty fair, the way he treated people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so. I never heard any complaints about him. I heard a lot of complaints that he didn't take care of his sheep very well. There was a lot of them died when we had snows and stuff like that. He just let them run and if they died, they died. And we saw a lot of dead after that three-foot snow we had, well there was snow all over Folks Hill over there, dead sheep and lambs and stuff. [Snowstorm in 1937-1938] It happened that snow hit in January and the lambs are always born about the middle of January, and so there was a lot of lambs that didn't survive.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now on the Folks, can you remember anything in particular about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Ethan Folks went to high school with my older sisters. He was older than I was. I met him a few times. Bert Folks had the position of the Director of the Soil and Water and Conservation when we left here, and that's what I had up until last December, and I hadn't thought about -- I thought he was a pretty big shot when he was the Director, but I didn't think too much about me being a Director! But anyway, that's basically all I knew about Bert Folks, was that he came to our farm and checked to see. . . well he didn't check too much about pollution but more about erosion and that sort of thing. We didn't have too much problem with erosion around here then because the fields were all so full of fern that the water couldn't get through them. And we had no sprays to get rid of them. And we tried all kinds of things to get rid of those fern, but the more you plowed them the more you spread them around. And we tried clean cultivating, we tried a lot of things, but we just were unable to get on top of them. And that was our biggest problem on our hill grounds here. Now, we had creek bottom ground that was Chehalis soil, it was very clayey, we were farming with horses, it was very hard to farm, very hard to work down. And my dad finally went down to California and got his brother's Fordson tractor, and we plowed with that and Mr. Hanish told us he wanted us to work in the woods for him so he told us that if we'd let that soil lay all summer in the fall we could work it down, it would just all mellow down. And so my dad took his word for it and so we plowed it in the spring and then in the fall when we tried to work it down our Fordson tractor would get high centered on a clod and we'd sit there and spin both wheels and then we had to either go get a team of horses or, of course in those days you had lugs on your wheels rather than tires so, we could take a fence post or a log and put across underneath the tractor and get it under the lugs and then the tractor would pick itself up and go to the next clot!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the advice didn't work too good!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it didn't work good at all. But he got us to cut wood for him that spring.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember. . that's Jim Hanish's father.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall his first name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not right now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just called him Mr. Hanish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that was who he was. He was an old man to me and he was hard to get along with, and kinda what you would picture a wife beater. I don't know if he did but that's kinda the picture you had of him. And he was a big man. But he was very dominating, and kind of a recluse. He, I don't think that we ever saw him away from his home. He never came down and got the mail, he never, you never saw him. I don't even know if they had a car. But he, his wife came and got the mail when the mail was picked up. And I don't know as I ever saw him where he wasn't either where he lived or up where his timber was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody come from Berry Creek down into this pond area here for swimming or fishing or picnics?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It wasn't that much of a pond then. Then you can see that this has been built up by bulldozers or something. It was . . . I came down, came through our back fence and came down through it and it was just marshy, muddy, with swamp grass and stuff. And it was pretty hard going for the horses, kind of grey looking soil where the horses threw it up. And it was not a place that I particularly cared to go to, it was just a

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: place you went around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this has been built up since the war then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm quite sure it has.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would this have been the furthest end of the swamp that we're talking about between here and Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would think so, I would think so, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you recall anything else about this particular area or the people that lived right through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Like I say, I was down in here once. And I know that there was just a little settlement in here. And I wouldn't be surprised if that white house over there wasn't here when I lived here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the brick house was here then, and the green house, both.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I know that and there were some houses on this side. Of course, this here is evident that it wasn't here. It's too new. Of course, they put some metal siding on it so they may have made it look a lot newer than it is, too. But they . . . this was always kind of a prosperous looking area, when you drove by it up there on Suver Road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now these houses are smaller than a lot of the older farm houses, and they're obviously newer, from the 1 920's or 30's, did anybody think that was odd that they built these newer style homes or smaller homes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We always felt the Smith's had money, you know. And of course, Joe Smith, all there was his wife and him by the time he built this house down in here I imagine, so he probably didn't have use for a very big house. And I never heard that John had any kids, I don't know if he did or not. But it was always just Joe and John was all 1 ever heard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now one more question. We're seeing birds everywhere. Can you recall if this, geese or ducks because of the marsh or swamp through here, if this was part of the flyway? Can you ever recall seeing any particular birds around here, or shag pope, anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think that it was part of the flyway. Geese once in a while would get up our direction, we'd hear geese. And when we would, it was enough of an oddity that we'd go out of the house to look at them. So, we wouldn't have been on the main flyway. And I don't think there was enough water in this. .. it was just too flat for it to be enough of a pond for anything like that, the land in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any eagles or hawks or cranes or egrets? Types of birds that might.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I can't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. We talked to Don Dickey the other day about it. . . can you recall any owls in the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't, no. Yes, I can. I can remember I went to Hanishes one night, after dark, which was going around the Dickey place, and I was walking through some timber there, and an owl hooted pretty close, and I really took off! It scared me to death!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they weren't real common, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so, but then, I was pretty young and there was a lot of things that I could have missed. But I do know that one owl was in that tree because it like to scared me to death!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall seeing bats around?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Quite a few, or just now and again?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just now and again. We had one in the house one time. Got in some way, and we were pretty concerned about getting it out. Yeah, there were bats in the barn, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, might as well go for one more animal while we're here. How about beaver? Can you ever recall any beaver along Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never saw a beaver on Berry Creek. I never saw a beaver dam until I was over with Jeff Garver above Sulphur Springs, that's the first beaver dam that I saw in this area. I had beaver over on my place south of Corvallis. And I tried to keep them around but there was always hunters, deer hunters that would see the evidence and come back and trap and so they . . . We also had fox over there. And people, well the hunters think the fox is terrible because it's gonna kill the pheasants and so forth. And to me, I kind of enjoyed the fox.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about nutria and possum in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nutria didn't come to this country, the United States, until after I left here. See the nutria were brought in right after World War II. They were brought in from South America.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the possum?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never saw any. I never saw any possum or coon or anything like that. But I wasn't looking for it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. Would you see many deer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very few. I think I put that in the recording before. I think I saw two deer in all the time I lived here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. And that's what, four. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Four years. Part of five years. But there wasn't that much browse for them. The fir trees were up there 75, 100 feet high and not very big around, but still there was nothing underneath them. There was an awful lot of ladyslippers up in around the [J. W.} Chaffin place, which is a form of orchid that is very beautiful. And my sister commented that she hated to see clearcuts cause she was afraid she'd never see any ladyslippers anymore and she always loved them so much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall other iypes of wildflowers in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. There was a lot of wildflowers. Bachelor Buttons. We had Bachelor Buttons like you couldn't believe. I mean the fields would be full of, just clear blue with Bachelor Buttons before the wheat would come up through. The first year we moved here my mother ordered some flower seeds for her little planter in the window, it turned out they were Bachelor Buttons, and the neighbors really booed her! They thought that was really funny that she'd send off for seeds of a . . . we didn't call them wildflowers, we called them weeds, so that's why I had to think a minute. And there was, yeah, there was quite a few wildflowers. But like I say we tended to think of them more as weeds than we did wildflowers, but they, because they were detrimental to the amount of crop we got because they'd draw the moisture from what we were trying to grow. And I'm not thinking too much of anything else, but I might later.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Camas in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what Camas is, I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And the type of fern, was that Bracken fern?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I suppose. Just one fern that'd shoot up and spread out then the roots go underground and there's another and here's another.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it's just a single stem per fern.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Single stem per fern.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it grow up about five or six foot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, not on our ground. They were up there about 18 inches, probably.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you think of anything else here? We kind of jumped ahead and got into fish and wildlife there a little bit, but.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I can't right off hand. Old Joe Smith doesn't look as old as he used to, does he? [Reference to younger man that has come into view]
bracketed_corrections: Reference to younger man that has come into view

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, it looks like he's gotten a lot younger. [Laughs]

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: D. The Cox Dairy

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is this College tees here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, this is Dunn Forest Road, going to the west, and we've just entered Berry Creek. . just

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: crossed Staat's Creek. Can you tell me about the dairy farm here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm not going to tell you what I told you about it a little while ago! But all I know about it was there was a pretty big dairy [Fred Cox] back there and we hauled some feed in to him one time and I think he probably lost the place and I think my brother-in-law's mother and father moved in there just before the war. And they got moved out just about as quick as they got moved in, I didn't know where they lived, but they lived north of Dickey some place, and I think this would put them right in there north of Dickey's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, now that draw there connects up to the Dickey's. The one that's running north and south towards Forest Peak there. Can you recall any other families living back through that country?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not at this point. Right up on top of the hill there's a house, you can see a roof sticking up, Gilbert Ennis used to own that. He lived there with his son and wife and he sent his wife home on a vacation and she's still on vacation. She got the fare to get home and she went home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did she live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, back in the midwest some place. But Gilbert was raising that boy, oh the last time I saw Gilbert his boy was in high school. He moved over to the Lebanon area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But down this road here there was just the one dairy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just the one dairy and it was a dead end road there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this was a dead end road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And Cooper's Mill would have been on back past the end of this road. And there wasn't any road that came here, you would have had to come in on that other draw there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so where Cooper's Mill was, then you came in, like you said from Airlie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: From Airlie, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you have gone past Maple Grove and come in on Maxfield Creek, maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And so the Cooper's Mill was actually on the Kings Valley side of this ridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, according to Donald, it was right over in back of his place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. But you just had to drive in from the Kings Valley side.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't any road that went through there. But we could hear. . . see, all these

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: mills were run with steam. And we could always hear three whistles, for 8:00, noon, and 5:00, because there was the Bennett Mill, the Coote's Mill and Cooper's Mill, and my dad always used to tell me, that's one thing about being a farmer, you don't have to quit when the whistle blows!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, on the mills here, did they have wigwam burners?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they keep slab fires going?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had some fires going, but at that time there was a lot of wood burned, and slab wood was good wood. And I think I told you that I had a contract with Bennett's Mill to haul their slab wood out. And they sawed their slab wood, cut it in four foot lengths, I hauled it out to the road, and a guy by the name of Jack Green had a buzz saw. And he cut it up in 16" lengths and hauled it in to Monmouth, Independence and Salem, out that way. He lived over in the next draw from Suver Road here. But he bought the wood from me, I bought the wood for 75 cents a cord and sold it for $1.25, and I earned enough money that year we had a 1923 Dodge Graham truck. And I earned enough money that year to buy a 1933 Chevrolet truck that was only 4 or 5 years old, but it had been a logging truck and it was well used. And actually, I went into the . . I would haul anything for anybody. I moved a lot of the people out of the Cooper's Mill area to Independence when they moved the mill to Independence.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, Cooper's Mill was like Coote's Mill in that they had a lot of people that worked there living right there at the mill site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and there was a lot of people in Airlie worked there, and Kenneth Dodson lived right over, just up this draw here, he worked there. There was quite a number.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, when you say Dodson lived up this draw, will we hit that on this road, or is that between.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We'll hit them, well I can show you where they lived from this road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Why don't we just go on to the next site then?

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: E. The Ennis Place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, we're at the first house on the right coming off of Berry Creek Road there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And this is where Gilbert Ennis lived, he and his son lived here. He was a pretty good farmer and he was very industrious, he cut wood and he did a lot of things to make a living. However, this hill here was mostly all covered with scrub oak, and he cut a good share of them out of here and sold them for wood. But he was always working.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know anything about that house back there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That house was not there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Even that older one wasn't?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. This is where Gilbert lived and there was a couple of barns out here and that was all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this house that's up here right now was the actual house he lived in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the house he lived in, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was his boy about your age?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh no, his boy was probably 8 years younger than I am, or ten.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had they lived here for quite a while?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well Gilbert and his dad lived over at this next place, where the Mulkey's moved in, and there was also a Gene Ennis and they farmed this hillside here where the Christmas trees are on this side of our place. And he, they farmed over there, and after the old man died the family just kind of disintegrated, and went their separate ways and Gilbert ended up here. Gene Ennis was kind of interested in my sister Audrey who was just older than I am. And when we were thrashing one time, well my mother made some biscuits and she stacked them very neatly in a pyramid, and they used their knives instead of forks, and the only thing forks were good for was to stab the slice of bread with and Gene stabbed the biscuits and the biscuits scattered all over and we all had biscuits in our lap! And he was embarrassed!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But they ate with knives?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so they were kind of primitive, in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the way, I guess, people from Germany or some place, it was quite common that they ate with knives. The only thing they'd use, they'd put honey on their knives to eat peas and roll the peas on with their fork or spoon. But the knife was the utensil that they put in their mouth all the time.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: F. The Dodson Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Dodson place, I think you went up this road here. You couldn't see their house from the road. But there was a mailbox out at the road that said Dodson on it. And the only time I was at the Dodson place, there was a stray dog came in and my cousin and I trained it to be a pretty good cattle dog. But it would always run away at night and so one night we chased it and we ended up at the Dodson place. And the dog was the Dodson's dog, and when they found out we were training him for a cattle dog they tied him up so he couldn't come back! But Kenneth Dodson was out trying to get their cows in and he was kind of mad cause the dog wasn't there. And we'd been herding cows with his dog all afternoon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, their place is over the hill here, and then up on the left, going over these Christmas trees next to some younger fir, maybe 20-25 years old, to the east there, that's the old road through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And the house that was in front of the Dodson place was right up on this knob here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the name of this house, who lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I think it belonged to the Dodson's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But were people living in it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. McCoys, the first people I knew that lived in there were the McCoys. And you're gonna see pictures of the McCoys, and the McCoys they had about. . . well they had a kid every year, I mean Mrs. McCoy was nursing one and carrying another one in her belly all the time we knew her and I think they had twelve kids.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we got to the point where the kids were in school.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay. There was one thing about the McCoy kids. All their names started with M. So we had Myrtle, Marvin, Melvin, Mary Jane, Max, Mabel . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's about as many as I can remember just off the top of my head! They were getting down young enough then that I couldn't remember them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They must have been having a hard time finding names, too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was kind of interesting, I was talking to my sister telling her about this tape that was gonna be made, and she says "Be sure and tell about when I went over to the house when they were eating breakfast," that was when they lived in the Smith house over across the street from us, and their little girl about three years old was eating breakfast and the fried egg was a little rubbery and it slid off her plate and so she climbed down off her chair and chased the chickens off the egg and picked it up and put it back on her plate and ate it! My sister, when she came home, wasn't hungry.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: G. The Mulkey Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: some cherry thicket in here, still they had a nice cherry tree in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, you can remember the cherry tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's still here, we marked it as a landmark. Can you remember anything about it in particular?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I picked cherries off of it one year. It sat right by the house, I don't know where the cherry tree is but it sat probably 25 feet towards the road and south of the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was a big tree back then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was a good sized tree back then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any other trees, an old orchard or anything through this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think there's some pears and apples in there, but I'm not real sure. Do you have the tape on now?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I want to point out. . . this isn't much of a hill here. But when we moved here, it went down into the bottom of that draw and then went clear up to the top and that was one steep hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This hilt up ahead here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That hill right there was one steep hill to get over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have a name for it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we didn't. It was always just the Mulkey-Vanderburg Hill, was what we called it. But you can see, if you look down where the field is down there, and dig the dirt out there where that field is down there, and then put the dirt up on the top, how steep that hill was. It was steep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, the Ennis' s lived here when you first moved in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and then the Mulkeys moved in. Men Mulkey.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then their son moved in next door.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who lived there before he lived there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and then Men Mulkey moved into this house afterwards. So, can you remember anybody talking about where Brinkley lived?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't recognize Brinkley at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. But you can remember this hill here. Trying to get up this hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet. This is the way we moved in. And we were loaded.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so, even this hill, the first trip across it you can remember.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet. Because we had a 1923 Dodge with a four-cylinder engine in it and three- speed transmission and we didn't know whether we were going to get up it or not!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you remember anything else about this place here, or the house that used to be here, anything in particular about the Mulkeys?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the house, I believe, was a two-story house, I don't think there was any basement in it. My sisters used to clean house for Mrs. Mulkey and the youngest boy, Guyland, was born here, and when my sisters would come to clean the house, that was Shirley and Wilma, they would have to change Guyland's pants and they didn't think he'd been changed for a week. They said she wasn't a very good housekeeper and she wasn't a very good mother. She was a school teacher.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Mrs. Mulkey was a school teacher?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And, she didn't care much about doing anything else.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, all these Christmas trees out here. Who's land was this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was Mulkeys. This was the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So what would be out there when you were a kid? What kind of crops?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oats, wheat sometimes, oats and vetch, hay, they had a barn on this side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's on the east side.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, on the east side of the road they had a barn and they milked probably 20 head of cattle in here. And we used to trade bulls with them for breeding our cows and so forth. But it was more of a dairy than it was a farm. They had an old McCormick Deering, 110 McCormick Deering with lugs on it that they farmed with. And between the boys and the old man, well they kept that thing going 24 hours a day, so in farming time, well they, we could hear that old tractor running night and day. And there is one thing I can also tell you, when Men got through thrashing he stepped off the tractor after he got through, we bound then, and thrashed with a thrashing machine. But when we got through, got Out of the field he'd strike a match on the seat of his pants and set the field on fire and it'd go "WHOOSH" and didn't hardly make any smoke at all because anytime you leave straw lay on the ground even over night it's drawing moisture from the ground. I believe there was as much burning then as there is now, but not near as much smoke. Because they burned their wheat straw, they burned all their straw, whereas now they just burn grass straw. But it went up so fast it went clear up into the atmosphere, and it was dry. And I don't know if you ever sat on a tile and got your pants wet sitting on a tile, well that's just the same thing you're doing letting your grass lay on the ground. As far as I'm concerned.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just drawing the moisture out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You're drawing the moisture right up out of the ground. And so that's my thoughts on this field burning, is the DEQ is making it worse instead of better as far as telling people when they can burn. Because I know that when the combine pulls out of the field that's the driest that straw's ever gonna get. And I saw one year, it was like this year only worse, and they let people burn after the straw was so wet that it would take three days for a field to burn. You never saw so much smoke in this valley. So, anyway I'm an old timer but that's my observations.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: H. The 000 Road

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Took off that direction.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so we're right at the 000 Road now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this is where the road used to go to the Dickey's, from here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but it went right straight back this way. See where the small trees are? That's where their road went, right through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this group of trees on the left.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were on our place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those trees date back to when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They were smaller trees, of course. And there was a lot of brush in there. We used to pasture our cows in there. Good spot for the cows to scratch to their backs and so forth. Now, I want you to look at how this road went on up this way and dropped down into our place. And figure out how you'd stop a truck with two wheel brakes with all your life's possessions!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so you can remember coming in when you were first moving?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, when we lived here, most of the time we lived here this road hadn't been cut through.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you came all the way up from the desert in California and you can remember this hill from that whole trip.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you bet. You bet. Because we had to come clear up to the top of this hill, and then "ZHOOMP", right down into our place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kind of an exciting entry, then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. We were kind of wondering. . . we had an emergency brake on that truck that came clear up to the windshield. Daddy says, "Grab the emergency brake Neil!" and so I planted both feet, I was pulling on the emergency brake and he was pushing on the foot brake.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had he ever seen the place before?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you knew when you got here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we bought the place from a realtor by the name of Dollarheide in Albany. And we stopped in Albany when we came up and he gave us directions in here. Well, daddy had directions before because he had a second cousin or something that lived over by Jefferson, and he came out and appraised the place for my dad, and he was an engineer and he drew maps and showed where all the fences were and all the buildings, and everything. So my dad had a pretty good picture of what he was buying.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, one thing while we're sitting here, we've got a good view of what you call Folks Hill. Does that look like . . . what did it look like back then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I called it Smith's Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, you called it Smith's Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I called it Smith's Hill. I always thought it belonged to Smith, but Folk lived on the other side of it, but I don't know that Folk ever owned it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. Now, what did that hill look like then? Was it covered with young fir like it is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, quite a bit younger. You could see sheep in quite a few areas out there. There was quite a few bare spots.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about this off to the right where we're looking up above where Coote's Mill was? Can you recall what that looked like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Coote logged it off. Or Wienert did. This right here was a grass hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The hill we're on?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, right here ahead of us. That's where that cemetery was I was talking about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And we can't see that right now because of the trees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, basically we need to go a little further ahead in order to be where we could see the cemetery because it was just over the break of the hill and you see we're not up to the top of the hill yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: I. Brinkley's Hill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're on Tampico Road, coming down to Smith's place on the right, just past the crest of the hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you tell me where the cemetery was and what it looked like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The cemetery would have been about 50 feet off the road here. If the old telephone line was there, it was the old telephone line went right over the cemetery, and the cemetery had 1 by 8 fir markers on it painted white. And by the time I came here most of the markers had been rotted off. But the people were still coming and putting flowers on the cemetery on Memorial Day. But I never knew who they were and the names weren't legible on the headstones. They were too weathered. It didn't appear that they were really that old at that time, but as I say the headstones weren't something that was made to last. And it seems to me like there was one baby's grave that had a fence around it. But we're talking 55 years ago, but it just, I remember it that way. But I do remember that this was a grass hill here, no trees on it whatsoever. We used to pick wild strawberries on this hill. Around that cemetery and so forth. It was all grown up to wild strawberries, and of course wild strawberries are pretty small, but the interesting thing, as I look at this place is how big the trees have got that weren't even here. I had my daughter Mary and grandchildren Peter and Anna Stone, and I asked them as we drove through this area, I says, "What do you see here that would be different than what it was when I lived here?" We were over on the other side of the valley here, and they said, well I don't know. And I says, well, these were all grass hills here. Now they've got trees on them big enough to log.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you say across the valley, that's the Berry Creek Valley, on the south side.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's gonna be, some of these things we've gotta put in here, otherwise it won't come across on the transcript.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Would you like for me to give you the names of the people that I wrote down for you and show you from here where they approximately where they lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sure, yeah, this is a good vantage point.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're looking from what Jim Hanish called Brinkley's Hill, and we're looking due south down Berry Creek Road. With Berry Creek maybe a quarter of a mile in front of us here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just this side of Berry Creek there was a road went back about a half a mile that went back to Forest Tandy's farm. His farm sat in an 't" in our place and he never did put any gravel on that road so it was always almost impossible for him to get out in the wintertime. But he was a good driver and he'd spin his way out and finally get out of there. He built a house for himself and one for his father-in-law, Mr. White, I don't know his first name. He had a son Charlie; we'll come back to him later. And, of course, his daughter was Mabel Tandy. And Forest Tandy was on the school board, as well as my dad. My dad always made me help Forest if there was anything to do with the school, so I got to be pretty good friends with Forest Tandy, as well as the fact that he had a daughter Edith Tandy and I was pretty sweet on her. But they lived right back, east of the road here, probably a half a mile. And then looking right down here to the bottom of the hill you can see the driveway going in to our house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now was that road beyond your driveway or this side of the driveway?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Our house. . . that driveway is right where our driveway was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but then, the road to the Tandys, is that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it was clear on down past our driveway. It was right down next to the creek. In fact he had a bridge across the creek over here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anyway, if you look at the road again, or the bank, you'll see that there is a rise right there again, so the road went down, went up and then went down to Berry Creek. Where you see those maple trees that's where our house was behind those maple trees. The house now is over here way this side of where the maple trees are. Those maple trees were planted in front of our house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you plant those maples?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were there. They were big trees then. And that's where we lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall who lived in the house before you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Rafiers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, the Rafters. And then the Vanderburgs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But the Rafiers, I doubt if you'll find any records of them because they were renters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who they were renting from, who owned the house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. I think you gave a name. . . Anyway, but at that time, you see, our house was on the level with the road. But now they've made a cut about four feet deep there, so we were up above the road when they made that cut. All the mail boxes were on the right hand side here. Right in front of our house. And .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be about where that mail box is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A little this side of that, and up on that hill. See, the road went up over the hill. Well then when the County came through and redid this road, it made it a nice deal for us, because of course in those days you don't have any fork lift or anything. We bought our gasoline in 50-gallon barrels. And so we could just back right up to our bank in front of our house, roll the gasoline off, and get the truck out of the road and then roll the 50 gallon barrel onto a sled and take it onto the field.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year was that that they improved that road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say that was about 1938. And then of course the Coote's lived in the house that's still here on the right hand side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you called that even the Smith house at that time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. He rented it from Smith. And Bill Coote lived there and his mother-in-law

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: lived there, and she was an invalid, she never got out of bed. I think she just wanted to be waited on. She had money, and that's where the money came for the Coote's Mills and the Cornutt Mills, because she was the mother and mother-in-law of those two boys. I know that they really catered to her. And I used to go in and see her with Clifford Cornutt, we'd go in there and we were ordered to go in and say "Hi" to her. But she never got out of bed and so I don't know what was supposed to be wrong with her, but she didn't appear to have anything wrong with her except she just liked to be waited on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Her name was Cornutt?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, she was a Cornutt. Now do you want to go ahead from here or do you want to move on down to look at where other people lived?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, from here is fine.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there is a lot of trees there now. From here I could have seen the school house when I lived here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, why don't we go down to where we can see things then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: J. The Vanderburg Place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're right in front of your old homestead and we're looking at an apple tree due south behind the maples.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That gravenstein apple was just on the south side of our house and east a little bit behind our wood shed. That had the best gravenstein apples you ever tasted on it, and I see they're ripe right now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You want to go get one and see if they still taste so good?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think we better go get one!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, let's go do it. ***

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the mail boxes were just about where they are now. Yeah, they were, beside Coote's driveway. And I don't think it'd be the same and this long back, but you see

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, all these maples were here, it wasn't just a couple, it was a whole row of them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this whole row was here. But you see the number of people lived in this valley. That's how many mail boxes were there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so you've got two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen. . . eighteen or twenty names. So you had 18 or 20 mailboxes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Those are last names.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And each one of those represented a different house in this Beri'y Creek Valley here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Doesn't seem possible when you look at it now, to think there was that many people there that long ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, supposed to be just be the urban fringe now, and it used to be an urban neighborhood.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, only we had a school house, and we had Sunday school, and I mean, you didn't drive to town.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was a regular little community in itself.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was a community itself. We didn't go to town to church. It was too far, too expensive. And the cars weren't that reliable that you wanted to take off on a Sunday.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you don't remember a name for that Peak up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm looking at what Jim Hanish calls Forest Peak.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Could be Forest Peak, I never even noticed it when I lived here, to be right honest with you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kind of a dominant land mark.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it is. We went this way and we went that way. And Jim Hanish's dad logged back in there, the Chaffin place was back in there Bennett's was back behind Dickey's. So I never realized it stood that high. I mean, I knew there was a hill there, but I didn't realize it came to a peak like that 'dl you pointed it out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But those trees out in the foreground, that was all logged off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any large trees, like I see a couple of old trees up there now. Can you recall any trees like that along the skyline or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that they left seed trees. They left all their slashing and stuff, you know, I mean, they didn't burn and they didn't clean up after themselves. And... but you see old Bill Coote, he horse logged and moved his mills to the logs. See, that's why he's got two mills down here only half a mile apart and another one up there only a mile and a half away. Because he could horse log and he would log down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was easier to move the mill than it was to move all those logs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet. You didn't have all that automated equipment. You fall those logs and hook onto them with a horse and drag them out and you wanted to drag them down hill as much as you could, basically on the side hill so the logs didn't go over the top of your horses. And after they logged for a while, they'd get a groove wore in the dirt so the log wouldn't roll down the hill. You always drove your teams from the top side so if it did roll you weren't underneath it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there ever an orchard over on the right side? We're looking at, I can't tell, maybe that's a pear tree there off to the west?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To my knowledge, there was never anybody interested in that type of thing here. They were renters and I don't remember any fruit off that place. The only thing I remember is there used to be a barn down below the house here by the creek, there was an old oak tree down there, and it had black bees in it, honey bees. My dad and I went down there and felled that bee tree and got about 10 gallons of honey out of it. And we got stung royal. Those old black bees were mean. We had a big old tree over here about where that maple tree is. And that was a big old tree and it was a honey tree. And we felled that and we pulled about 40 gallons of honey out of that tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the whole reason for falling the tree, was for honey?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So now we do it for board foot, but back then you did it for honey.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we made wood out of it. But we felled it because it had bees in it. We wanted the honey. Back in the Depression it was pretty nice to have something sweet. Sugar was pretty expensive.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, we're looking at a snag there to the southeast, and can you recall very many snags along the creeks or through this country?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That wasn't a snag, that was a big old fir tree in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any snags in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I'm pretty sure that was a big old fir tree, and that was right on the right of the bridge that the forest built across the creek here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall blue birds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't recall blue jays either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. What kind of birds do you recall around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't really recall many birds. I mean, it was just about like it is today, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not too many birds around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Starlings haven't moved in and I don't think birds were that common.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about pheasants. Did you get pheasants in the fields?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very rarely. Very rarely. Once in a while we'd see a pheasant, but it was rare. Once in a while when you were out mowing or something you'd kick one out, but they were pretty well hid. You know, I forgot about those buns on the bottom of those maple trees. Those things had burls on them when we lived here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So those burls are fifty years old at least.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or older than fifiy years.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But the strange thing is those maple trees are smaller now than they were when I lived here. You know how things are when you are a kid! Those were big maple trees!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And fifty-five years of growing haven't added much.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they really haven't. They're just kind of sitting there in place. You can see, that maple tree, or with that apple tree, you can see where our house laid and our . . . see that fence going along there, that fence is

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Down along the creek there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: our line there. And right down there where that. . . looks to me like they put a well down there. See where those electric wires are going right down to where our old pump was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it looks they're using the same well.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Looks like they may have dug that old well out. Maybe they had some problems and decided to go with the old well. Because that electric wire's going right down there to where we used to pump. But there used to be a row of blackberries, himalaya blackberries right here, just a ways below that apple tree. But it was still a straight row; it had been planted there. Now they took over the whole world.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that started off. . . when you were a kid those himalayas were just in a row.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were planted in a row.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we're seeing a hedge over here that looks like its been chopped down and grown up, and seeing a rose bush that's up around the edge of the house there that looks like it'd be pretty old. Do you remember anything about people growing old roses, or hedges through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Are we still being recorded?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We. . . when the Coote's lived here Archie Cornutt was, had the mentality of a 12- year-old or so. And he kept this place looking pretty nice. And there was a hedge here in this honeysuckle or whatever it is?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's St. Johns Wort, the yellow flower there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and this rose bush was here and the rose bush was growing up on the front porch and right on the corner of the house there was a tree that was about as high as

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the house, and it was always a joke between Clifford Cornutt and I, I asked him what kind of a tree that was on the corner of the house and he says, "Don't ask me." So after that we always called it the Don't Ask Me tree. So there was a Don't Ask Me tree there. But it's gone now, so I can't point that out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that rose on the corner there and the one in the front of yard was there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the one by the oil tank. Bill Coote burned wood, however, he didn't have an oil tank there. And right there on that little lean-to there, just the other side of the oil tank, that's where Mrs. Cornutt laid in bed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was her bedroom.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was her bedroom, yeah. We came in the back door and would just turn in there to her bedroom, and I went in there a lot of times because that was one of the things I had to do if I was gonna be a friend of Clifford, was see grandma every once in a while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: *** We're standing by, right back by the old shed that's probably from Camp Adair, and we're looking again towards Smith Hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We're actually looking over the tree that we used to hang our beef from when we butchered our beef.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That big leaf there? [Maple]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And right on, just about straight past that's the old community swimming pooi. Everybody swam in that spot over there. And I'd like to see you get in there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Haven't been swimming for a couple years. With those berries I think it might have been a couple of years more.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The only way you can look at the old swimming hole now is by getting in a helicopter and looking down at it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But everybody, all these families out through here and from the school and everything, that was it, that's where they all swam?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's where we all swam.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was on your property?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was on our property. In fact, they had a baptismal service there when a group came in here with some preachers, preached at the little Berry Creek School, and they had some conversions here and they had a baptismal service down there. They didn't have to wade through blackberries to get to the baptismal services, even. That was all lawn out there. Are we ready?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, we're facing down towards the old well site there now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When we lived here we had a hand-dug well, it was about 4 feet across, and it was 14 feet to water, and the well, they dug it down to 30 feet, and we had a old Fairbanks Morris one cylinder motor, ran a pump jack, and we had a big.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: paid dearly for that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hold on.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, this pump that we had, a what they called a pump jack, which was a thing with leathers on it, just went up and down and probably had a 3-inch leather on it, and we would start that up on Saturday morning, and we would fill up this 2,000 or 3,000 gallon tank, about 30 feet in the air, and then meanwhile we would irrigate our garden here which probably consisted of at least a half an acre. And in the summer time we would do both of those every Saturday, and then we'd have enough water to last us to

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the next Saturday. But now they're drilling down 250 feet for water and still not getting enough to take a bath. So I think maybe they, all these people that say witching doesn't mean anything, I think maybe they ought to let me come in here and witch around a little and see if I could find some water for them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now who witched your well here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mr. White, who lived in back of us with the Tandys.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so Tandy's father-in-law.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was an older man. Yeah, he was an older man, he had grandchildren that were in high school at the time. So, he was getting up close to a great grandfather.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This whole area in here, you were mentioning how you couldn't get to the swimming hole now. It's all covered with blackberry and weeds; mostly blackberries. Can you describe how the creek looked in the 30's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the way I remember it, the creek bed has washed down quite a bit, you know, this has got gravel base in it, but there's been quite a bit of erosion of dirt out from underneath that creek bed because that creek bed is down quite a bit lower than when I lived here. They put this bridge in right in front of us when we lived here, of course they put this road in also, and so they had to make a bridge that had a little more holding power and so forth. And there was a little lumber and stuff coming out through here. So they built this new bridge and I have a kind of interesting story to tell about that, that when they filled in at the end of the bridge they brought in some pretty big rocks because they had about a four-foot hole on each side of the bridge. And the dump truck was a three-yard dump truck and they were dumping these rocks, and one of the rocks was too big to go through the tail gate and so when that rock hit the end of the tail gate well it just picked the front end of the truck up and it was sitting there about straight up and down, and it took about four or five people to get the front end down. It was the first time I'd ever seen that, that was pretty exciting for a 14 year old boy!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that bridge in the same place as the old bridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. I've got another question too about the big leaf back there where you used to hang your beef. Did you have a particular name for that tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was just where we hung our beef!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so you'd just say, back on the maple or something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that maple was in the barnyard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you describe how you got the beef up in the tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we had a ladder and we put the ladder up in the limb up there that was about, probably 12, 13 feet high. And we'd put a pulley up there and run a rope through it and then we'd hook one of the horses up to the rope and pull the beef up as far as we wanted it and tie it off and let the horse stand there and graze grass while we skinned out the rear quarters and so forth, then we pulled it on up to where we could gut it out and skinned the rest of it off, and then we pulled it on up high enough so that animals couldn't get to it and left it there for a few days. Of course, in those days with no refrigeration or anything, well my mother always liked to have fresh beef liver when we butchered, and it tasted just like the inside of that cow smelled and to this day I can't eat liver because of that, but anyway we always had fresh beef liver when we butchered, and then after it'd hung for about 3 days then my mother would can all the beef and we had a fruit cupboard, and she'd put the canned beef in the fruit cupboard

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and that's some of the best eating beef you ever tasted is that canned beef because it's sure nice and tender. Made awful good beef pot pies and stews and stuff like that. Man, that was good!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever smoke any of it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Some, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you have fresh steaks after it aged?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we'd have a few fresh steaks, but most of it was canned. Yeah, we had the smokehouse but we usually used that for pork rather than beef. We had the pig pen right down there next to the creek and polluted poor Berry Creek something terrible, but anyway, we would smoke our pork, we did have the smokehouse on the other side of that apple tree that we were just at. And we smoked fish and pork in the smokehouse, mainly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those trees you say are smaller than you remember when you were a kid. Were those apple trees about the same as you remember when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well the apple tree is up a lot higher than it was when I was a kid, because nobody ever pastured under it when we lived here, so

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was talking about the flavor, though.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, they tasted good. My mother used to make fried apples and apple pie and applesauce and the first bite that I took out of that apple, I thought man I'd like some of those fried with a little bacon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One more thing on the creek there. All the weeds that are in next to it. What kind of vegetation was along the creek when you were a kid there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, on the left hand side here there was just trees and very little undergrowth in there. Mr. Archie Cornutt used to pasture his cows in there, or a cow. And she kept pretty much all the vegetation out from under the trees there. And I'll tell you a little story about Archie Cornutt. One day he went down there to milk his cow and his cow was in heat and she rode him. And boy I'll tell you, he wasn't very intelligent but his eyes sure got big and he sure ran. He got scared. He thought he was gonna get bred! But then there was sheep run on this side, so

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, on the side of, on the Smith house here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, clear back to the Dickey place. And they ran sheep clear on up across the creek on . . . they had a fence on up above there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. You said after Coote moved out, is that when the Cornutts moved in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Moved in, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And did they live here pretty much then until Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'm not sure but I think they lived here until Adair. I think they were still here when we left.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who lived here before Coote?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. I thought Coote owned it when he left here. But they called it the Smith place, but I just thought they called it the Smith place because of some previous owner. But I found out later that Bill Coote didn't own it. But I know that Smith had his sheep; he ran his sheep up here clear up past the school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So these were all Smith's sheep in here. These were Coote's sheep?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, Coote just had the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you have a rough idea how many sheep Smith used to have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Man, I would think up in the thousands. That was his income. As far as I know, he didn't do any farming. Never put a plow in the ground. And these old fields there

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: they'd get full of dry grass, but the sheep and the grasshoppers ate it. You asked me about the flowers and stuff, well there was lots of grasshoppers here. I used to catch them. I used to get 60 cents a dozen for catching them. And Donald Dickey showed me how to catch them. And you don't just try and sneak up behind them, always reach where they're gonna be, not where they are now. So you came in in front of them. And I could catch grasshoppers like that!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you'd sell them to people for bait?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For fishing, yeah. But down below the Cootes' house here, there was a grass patch that was just alive with grasshoppers. And also up here around the cemetery. And 1 could just catch all the grasshoppers I wanted in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything else right this area? It's your old home here, so we're getting quite a.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, except I don't know if I said on the tape that the mail boxes were here and so in the summertime all the girls came down here to get the mail because I was 15 and so were they so they got a big thrill with Neil.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One thing we didn't put on the tape either, you said you kind of shy then, though.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was very shy, and I'll say right now that Leslie Gardner and Betty White, when I was in the 8th grade they got the teacher to set them across from each other and me up in front of them. And in those days pants had buttons not zippers. So everytime I'd go back to the teacher's desk, well, when I'd walk back they'd each have a hold of the side of my pants and pull my pants unbuttoned, and they got the biggest kick out of my embarrassment, having to button up my pants right in front of them. And I think the teacher was in on it too, because it seemed like she got me back to her desk more than necessary!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were those a couple of girls that would wait by the mail box here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah. Yeah.
