Fact one time shortly after we moved here the two girls got in a big fight because they were jealous of one another because they thought I liked one of them better than the other. And they tore clothes off of each other, including their bras. Teacher made them go home and get dressed again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. And that was 8th grade?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I was thoroughly embarrassed!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of anything else here? Was that kind of the community gathering place then, the mail boxes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was on weekday mornings, they would sit under our maple trees, course this fence wasn't in here, and the road actually was level there, and they'd sit under our maple trees on the lawn there and wait for the mail man. And I don't think it was really necessary for them to get there an hour before the mail man but they seemed to do it. And this was during the summer time. And then sometimes they'd bring their bathing suits with them and go down and go swimming after the mail came, and so it was. In the summertime it was the gathering place where everybody came and even the Gardners had to walk clear down here after their mail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said you were the only boy in school above the 4th grade?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: 3rd grade, above the 3rd grade.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So is that one reason all the girls were paying attention to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah there was four girls and only me! So I was, and man I was handsome, too. You know, you can tell by looking at me now how handsome I am! [Laughs]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, it doesn't sound like you had a whole lot of competition.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I. . . how do I want to put this anyway. I was the most handsome boy above the 3rd grade.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Best looking guy in town, anyhow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. You bet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you think of anything else through this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I think that pretty well covers it until we get across the creek and we can get up there and we can kind of point out some other things to you when we get up there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: K. White's Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a house right in here,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we're going east towards the barn that' still there, just on the south side of Berry C reek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and that was where the Cornutts lived when we first moved here. And then Forest Tandy's brother Elmer moved into the house. And then one of the Bennett Brothers that had the mill up here lived in it for a short while. And then old man White that did the witching moved in here and apparently he bought some acreage because he built that barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that barn was built by White.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That barn was built by White. Probably in 1939 or so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so about every year there for a while, somebody else was moving into that house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But anyway, he built that barn there and he had a horse. And I don't know what the situation was because this was Smith's property and Smith pastured sheep in here, but the year Mr. White moved in here he planted that and took hay off of it and we, I helped in baling the hay, of course, we didn't have balers that would feed themselves, we had to bring the hay to the balers and pitch it in, and we had buck rakes, and we would go along and pick up all the shocks and push up to the baler and then a couple of fellows would stand there and pitch it into the baler. But it was a couple weeks work to bale all the hay that he took off of there. He got a lot of hay off of that field. So I don't know if he rented that from Smith or just what was done but they baled that hay and sold it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Prior to that time there wasn't. . . this was just only pasturage. There wasn't any

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was pasture. And of course the school Sat right there at the other end of that. There's a base marker up here on the left hand side of the road. Survey marker. And if I remember right, that marker was on the west or the northwest corner of the school. It was there then, of course, they had those there for years. But that's, that's where the school sat, was right in there just this side of the hill there. But then, it was this side of the fill actually. This road here is a road that went back to Hanish's and went back to Bennett's Mill. And you went right along Hanish's fence line, and then up a real steep hill, like maybe that one there. With that old Dodge that I had when I first started hauling slab wood, it was in the low hole and give her all you had to get up that hill, empty. And when I came down the hill, put it in low gear and put on all the brakes you had and come down. And I stacked the wood right here, just inside where the fence is now, and I stacked over 100 cord of wood in there. And one morning I came down that hill and there was a bridge about half way down, had quite a bit of slope to it. And I had it in low gear, and that was after I got the '33 Chevrolet, and I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: had it in low gear and putting on the brakes pretty good, and all at once my motor quit turning and away I went, and I got to the other end and then my motor started turning and I realized that bridge was frosty and I just slid across it. And I was scared!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's when you were about 15.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this road here, back to Hanish's and went up the hill, and then the other road went back up Savage Creek up there, did those connect back there anywhere?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or did this road here connect with the road that went over to Dickey's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was no connection between Hanish's and Dickey's road. Can't think. . . I believe that you could get across there someplace, because Mr. Hanish went up on this side to his timber, and I went up Savage Creek to his timber. But I don't know if the roads joined or just how I got across there. I know that there was a pretty big canyon that we across, and my dad took the team up there one time. King and Prince, like Donald said, you never forget the horses names, you might forget your wife's name. But anyway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: King and Prince was your family's horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: King and Prince were our horses, and they were a great big team of horses, and we took them across that bridge and Prince got pretty scared and he doggone near pushed King over the side and it was about 30 feet to the bottom. So we were pretty antsy. 1 don't remember why we went across that bridge, but I think we were trying to get up to the Chaffm place. I think we had some stuff at the Chaffin place. We were going to come in from the back side of the Chaffin place to get in. Going across that bridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this the, on the left here, was this the driveway that went into the house here, or was that just a farm driveway there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there wasn't any gutters beside the road then. And I'm sure the house set right in these trees. These trees were smaller, but you could just drive off the road and right in to the house, you know, I mean. I can't remember for sure, there might have been a garage there where that tile goes across.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But then between here and the base of the hill, was only the school. And from the school all the way down to the hill there where the Folks lived there wasn't any houses or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no houses at all except for the White's and the Tandy's back this way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, back behind the school there, there are some fruit trees in through there. Were those there then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, how about over on the mill side. Were there fruit trees there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't say as I remember that either. But I was gonna tell you, up there where it looks like there's a car or something up there, you may know what it is. That's where the old barn used to set that belonged on the Smith place that was all put together with wooden pegs. It didn't have a nail in it anyplace and that was the only protection that Smith's sheep had in this whole area whenever the weather got bad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that main barn there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it was a big barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And now you said that weathered the '37 snow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It weathered the '37 snowstorm and then a windstorm came along later and blew it

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: over. I have an idea the snow storm weakened it and then when the wind came along it just tipped it over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the wind was just within a year or two of that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Anti the whole thing.. . was that an old barn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I would think so. I thought the Indians built it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was built without nails.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no nails in it, and I didn't realize that until after it blew over and then I was Over there looking at it, I saw all these broken pegs, and then I realized it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would the mill have been in relation to the barn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would have been on around the corner, up the canyon there a little ways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, how about the mill shacks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The mill shacks were right on the creek. I think I told you that the mill shacks they built the out houses right over the creek and that way they didn't have to dig a hole for the out houses. And I remember one time we had a kind of a field trip from the school to pick flowers for May baskets, and we were over there by Savage Creek and Leslie Gardner drank out of it and she said if water has flowed over 250 feet of gravel it's just as pure as if it'd been distilled. And she went ahead and drank it. And all these out houses right about where she'd been drinking. She never got sick, but I think a lot of the reasons for that was that we didn't know any better. I drank out the creek all of the time. Both Savage Creek, and . . . but I didn't drink water that close to the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, there wasn't any mill shacks where you could see along this side then, those were up around the corner there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's say this, the trees are growing out here quite a ways from where they were. From the school, you could see the mill shacks. But I don't think that you could see them from here. You see, they were right on Savage Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, we should make it clear that you only started calling this Savage Creek since you heard that from Don the other day.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah. As far as I was concerned it was just Berry creek, and I never thought about it having a Y in here, I . . . I knew they did, but I just never gave it that much thought.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. You want to maybe try to find the Chaffin place right now and then come back and finish off this last little segment here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, if you know pretty much where this Chaffin place is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think so. Why don't we give that a shot.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When I used to go to the Chaffin place I went up the other road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we don't have that option any more.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: L. The 100 Road

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now, we're right at the first stop with the Road 100 intersection and we're looking just about due east towards John Smith's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's just a little bit north of east.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And then right back in here where these oak trees are is where Forest Tandy lived. Those oak trees were there when he lived there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That'd be about northeast about a mile? A half mile?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, three-quarters of a mile, something like that. By the way, the school teachers lived with Forest Tandy, because they had to, because he was chairman of the school board, and they had to walk through that mud to get to school every morning. But this is approximately the same place that the road was when I was here, only I remember it going more of a right angle than it's going here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's about it, that's about where a bridge would have been.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so the 150 going up, you think that might have gone up to where Hanish's old place was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I'm saying that's the road 1 got the slab down from Bennett's mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think this road over here goes up to Bennett's Mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that has the same contour. Maybe there's another one over here like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, let's try the 190 first. But we're right at the corner of the 150 here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I told you about that bridge there, you know, and I came down the hill and I hit that bridge, "YEEUMP" then I hit the dirt again. Now, I'm going this way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, that's the 170 there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: M. Cooper's Sawmill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're at the mill site on the 190 - 100 intersection shown by Rowley. And Neil and I are here next to a V that looks like a skid trail that's probably 8 or 9 feet high on the high bank and 3 to 5 feet on the kit bank, but we're not finding any evidence of a mill pond or anything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: One thing about this skid trail, it's a horse skid trail. A cat couldn't go down through there. So that's proof of logging back 50 years ago. I was up to Cooper's Mill one time, came in from Airlie, and this is about the proper location for Cooper's Mill as near as I can find. Donald Dickey said it was behind their house, and I know their whistle from our house was just about straight west, and this is not the Bennett Mill site i'm sure because the terrain is not right. So 1 would make a pretty educated guess that this is the old Cooper mill site. Like I say, it was a logging show. We haven't really located enough water to run a steam engine around here. And all of the mills except Bennett's mill were run with steam engines. And so that's the only thing that I'm not seeing that would make it the Cooper Mill site.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think another thing is we're seeing a lot of skid trails and road systems coming off the series of small benches here, and in this skid trail we're seeing trees that we're both estimating to be about 40 or 50 years of age, up to 24 or so inches in diameter are the largest ones.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This skid trail looks like it's going right into a mill pond. I mean you see several skid trails coming into this skid trail, but this one here looks like it's dropping into a mill pond.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of anything else in this particular area here? We've got the road system going into Airlie, we've got the location by the whistle, and we've got Don Dickey's word. When did Coopers move out of this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About 1939.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know when they moved in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were here when we came here in '35.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And do you know if they had more than one location up in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't. I do know that Red Fir Lumber Co. in Independence is the old Cooper Mill if you. . . there might be a possibility of finding out something from their history. They may have some history on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mean like legal description or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, something of that sort. Because it was the old Coopers Mill when it was here and they renamed it Red Fir Lumber Co. when they moved to Independence. And that mill is still operating and it's hard to say what they might have, but they might be able to help you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and then Don Dickey said there was no mills here when they moved here in '29.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And as far as the two of you could remember Coopers, Bennetts and the three Coote's mill sites were it for this drainage through here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And like I say, I came into Coopers Mill one time. And I never got down into the mill site, I was up by the maintenance department when it was on the upper side of the road. But that doesn't have much meaning because I .. . maintenance section was apparently back a ways from the mill. And I was in there on Sunday afternoon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, if we're not at a mill site, we're definitely on a site where a lot of logging has taken place. There's a lot of logs come up this skid trail.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, also if you look up we got quite a bit of sky showing through here, which would indicate possibly a mill pond and room for a mill in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or sawdust pile?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's a possibility.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Why don't. . if you want to head up towards the road there, I'll head down this way

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: and we'll see if we can find any more evidence here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: N. Bennett's Sawmill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I just took some photographs here we come up maybe a quarter mile up the 150 spur, and I took a picture of you walking up the ridge here. You want to kind of describe the way you remember this as compared to the way that you remember the Bennett's Mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, as we came up that first road there off the main road, we had a real steep climb, then a level spot then another climb and then very shortly after we got up the second climb we, Bennett's Mill was on the right hand side, and this terrain is about what it was. They had their mill up above the road. They logged with a cat. They pulled in their logs with a cable and a drum into the mill. The mill sat above the area where I used to haul slabs out of, so that they had room for the sawdust and slabs without having to use a conveyor system or anything. And they only logged for a couple of years and I don't think that they ever got where the sawdust was too bad. If they did they'd taken their Allis Chalmers bulldozer and dozed it down. But it was my job to keep the slab wood away from the mill because it would build up much faster than the sawdust. And they didn't want the slab wood built up so they. . . I don't remember

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: whether they sold me that slab wood for 50 cents a cord or 75 cents, but I remember I sold it for $1.25. And I was able to buy a '33 Chevrolet truck that was my pride and joy when I was only 15 years old. My dad always had to drive it down the county road because I wasn't licensed to drive it down the county road, or else he had to come with me. I had a learner's permit so I could drive on my learner's permit if he was with me. Some of the time we didn't even have the truck licensed, so

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're at what Neil thinks is probably the Bennett site. I was told to look for a road to the right. We're standing on a rOad to the right, we don't know how old it is, it could go back to the Columbus day storm, but a little bit lower down the hill, in similar terrain, there's evidence of another road to the right. So, would you think on this 150 spur somewhere between that first road to the right and this road to the right would be the mill site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would prefer to think that it was the other road to the right that we saw, because the way I remember it when I got to the top of the hill it was almost immediate that I made a righthand turn and went up the road up towards the mill and then back in below the mill to pick up the slab.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you mentioned that they used an Allis Chalmers cat, one of the first ones that you'd ever seen

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And, can you tell me the problem they were having with that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the Allis Chalmers cat they put a spring crossways across underneath the front of the frame to make it easier riding, but I think, I can't remember Bennett's name, but he seemed to think it was about like a slingshot sitting on the back of that seat with that spring, and they were constantly breaking that front spring, and when they'd break the front spring then they'd have to shut down the whole mill, because it was quite a chore to put that spring in because it was down in there between the tracks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, where would the sawdust pile have been from here? Just to get oriented.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would have been right under the brink of the hill, like right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, it would have been along this road here but to the right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To the right, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it would be on the east side of the spur road to the mill and it would have been visible from the main road, right along the edge of the slabs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I don't think we got it on the tape, hut you said they put out about 4 cords of slabs a day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A day, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you had over 100.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I had over 100 cords of slabs there by the time school started in the fall. I think I had 125 cords out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right there at the intersection of the 100 road and Tampico Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of anything else in this area? Any hunting or any animals you saw up in here? Or any . . how about these madrone? Were the madrone a common tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then, not real common, I always, for some reason I always thought a madrone was pretty. And whenever I saw a madrone I looked for it, and we had one on our farm, and I always enjoyed that machone. And we had a small one on our farm and

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: somebody stole it, they dug it up and took it home. They thought it looked better on their place than ours!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you call it anything other than madrone?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know what to call them. I thought that it was a possibility that it was myrtle wood. That was my guess on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear them called laurel?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But there. wasn't that many of them around. The only one I knew was there on our farm. And I've seen quite a few of them on this trip.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So you think there might be more of them now, or you think we're just going to places that

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think there's more of them. I mean, after all, I went up and down this road three times, or six times a day all summer long that one year, and maybe my memory isn't as good as it oughta be because I was more anxious to get up there and get loaded and get back down again than I was about the scenery, but I'm sure that's the road I came up to Bennett's Mill, I'm absolutely positive of that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about oak? Do you remember more oak in the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember any oak up in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, it looks pretty much the same then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty much the same. Of course, these trees were a little smaller. And we found quite a number of rotted off stumps that were in the 20" range, and that was . . . I told you before, I don't know if I told you on the tape or not, but most of these little mills were cutting for railroad ties. The railroad during the Depression had enough money to buy ties, and ties had to have the heart in it and you got more money if you could put the heart in the center of the tie. So these little trees 20" in diameter or so they could peel off some 2 x 4's and one-inch stuff. In those days there was a lot of barns built with I x 12's in a vertical position. There was a pretty good demand for I x 12's and 1 x 6's. We built -- our fence on the farm was all built out of oak posts that we cut ourselves and I x 6 boards going lengthways with it, rather than wire fences. One of the reasons for that was that Bill Coote lived right across the road from us and my dad had 2 24-inch pipe wrenches. Bill Coote wanted them and he said "I'll give you 2,000 board feet of 1 x 6's for fencing material for those two pipe wrenches." So my dad says, "Okay, if you'll let me borrow them if I need them," and Bill Coote says "That's a deal!" And so the next day a truck came and dumped 2,000 board feet of 1 x 6's and that's what we built fences out of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we're looking at an old stump over there that's 35 or 40 inches, and we've seen afew of those scattered around. Would they have logged those for fuel for the boilers, maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they didn't use a boiler on this site. They used Allis Chalmers diesel motors to run this mill. My guess would be that they probably cut those off short as a tie, with a little bit of trim, and were able to log them in that short of a log. But they defmitely didn't have the power to pull a long, big tree. But you'll find that most of these trees are in the 16-22 inch bracket that I'm talking about, and that's what Bennett and Bill Coote were both looking for when they were logging, was anything they could be sure to get a tie out of. You could almost get a tie out of that 10" tree there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would the larger trees, were those the ones that were left pretty much as seed trees then?.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, when you come to an area that had been logged off like this it would be back to just a few scattered larger trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right. And of course in those days they didn't clean up their mess so there was a lot of brush on the ground. And we see a little bit of evidence of tops and stuff as we walk around here, that are pretty well rotted down. And I wouldn't be surprised if they go back to that era.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of anything else in this particular spot here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's about all I can. . . Like I say if a guy took the time, I think a guy could run up and down this draw here and maybe find more evidence of the mill. Or it might have been right here. But you might find the evidence of the sawdust pile down here. We're standing within 300 feet of the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I think we've found a new mill site on the forest here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay!

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: O. The Chaffin Place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're at Rowley compartment 14 [compartments are a system of mapping and management developed by Man' Rowley for OSU Research ForestsJ, we've been looking at Rowley compartment 6, and we just came from Rowley compartments I and 9 in South Berry, and we found an orchard up by I and 9, and blackberries, and no sign of the chimney. And we're looking now where we're showing a building site, we've found a bunch of moist moss and an old road on the upper side of the road, but it's not matching up to the Chaffin place. So, Neil can you tell me what between these two sites looks most like the Chaffin place and what we're missing most?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, did you tell them this was the first site we looked at?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, well, that site, the terrain

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Compartment I and 9 was the first site.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay. Well, the terrain looks good there. This one, down here at the 14 is too flat and the Chaffin place was built on a sloping hill with a pasture down behind the house and then a large pasture Out say 60 or 80 acres down in front of the house. Of course, that's all in trees now, and so for pasture that's pretty hard for cows to eat those trees, and it's a little hard for me to digest them, too, but I think we're pretty close. So, we want to look at some aerial photos of that back in the '30's and I think I can pick it Out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now, let's say the upper place is the Chaffin place. You don't remember anything here by compartment 14?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I remember nothing there. It's a possibility that we came down right past there, because the terrain looks familiar as a road coming out of the Chaffin place, but if there was a cabin in there in 1936 and '37 I walked right by it and didn't see it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the first place, can you remember any orchard in there at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'd have to get my bearings a little more. If there was an orchard, I don't think it would have been as far from the building sites as we're looking. We did see two building sites on that upper place there that I had already called the Chaffin place. We saw two building sites and there was a barn, a pretty good sized barn, and a house

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: there. And I think the barn was probably closest to the road and the house was down below, so I think probably the terrain is about right. But it's a little confusing with as much change has been there, so if we can look at an aerial map I think maybe it would help quite a bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you think of anything else about these two sites here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'll say this. Like I said to Bob, when we got up to Bennett's Mill, I was positive where I am. Was. But right here, the road system, all the trees that are growing and stuff, leave me a little bit wondering. But I'm sure it can't be the lower place so I'm virtually positive it has to be the upper.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Daryll and Wilfred Ray, their mother died and their dad was raising them, and my mother got in touch with them through the McKibbons. And Mrs. McKibbon was looking for somebody to take care of these two boys, so my mother took Daryll and the Tandys took Wilfred. Daryll was a big thorn in my brother Bill's side, because they were both the same age and my brother was jealous of Daryll because he was kind of getting some attention that Bill thought he should get. So there was quite a bit of conflict there. And even today you mention Daryll Ray to my brother and he's fightin' mad. Wilfred went into Tandys, and the Tandys really fell in love with him. They only had an only daughter, and she was at that time about 14 or 15. And so they adopted Wilfred. And Wilfred lives next door to Edith Tandy down at. . . I had it in my mind...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yoncalla?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yoncalla. They live side by side at Yoncalla and still are just like brother and sister. But that's the Ray story. Daryll Ray lives in . . . I don't know. No, Daryll Ray lives down by Toledo now, and Wilfred at Yoncalla.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Does he have anything to do with Ray Realty there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, maybe his kids do. Daryll was diesel truck mechanic, I understand. Their dad lived in Summit when he brought the kids to us. And that's all I know, but when I saw Edith and Wilfred here about 10 years ago they told me that Daryll was right there at the Siletz junction and worked in a diesel truck shop there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, how did their dad happen to bring the kids over to Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he couldn't take care of them. Their mother died, and so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But I mean, how did he happen to know people in the Berry Creek area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He knew the McKibbons. And the McKibbons talked at Bible study or some place and found out that my mother and Mrs. Tandy would be willing to take care of them. The Tandys were fairly well fixed because Forest Tandy logged with a team of horses and so forth. All my dad was doing was farming, so we needed the money, but the Tandys took him just out of the kindness of their heart. But then when the old man got laid off, well he came and got Daryll but since the Tandys were willing to adopt Wilfred then he left Wilfred with the Tandys.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so Daryll was only with you like for maybe a year or two?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Or less.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: P. The Gardner Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Top of this hill here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, we're right by Gardner's right here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had to come in here after they made this cut, because when they made the cut they left Gardner's high and dry! Like I told the kids, there was no trees in here, this was all grass.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's that oak tree right there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But you don't count oak trees on a farm. But there was none of this fir, and all of this fir was logged off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Looks like a lot of work.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, all this up here was logged of, and then from...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was all grass here except for a few spots, you know an oak tree here and there. This was grass like that over there is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, the road from the second mill, you said they had to come in from down here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there's a road went in just somewhere in here, right straight in. And then I think it's probably a little further here, but not,very far from here. Of course, see all these cuts have been put in here since this was done so you can turn off anyplace. But I would guess that the road went off right about there. And went back in there and then might have been that one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I could tell more from coming the other way. I doubt if it was that far north. The road came off to Coote's Mill right at the top of the hill there by Sheppards, and came back paralleling this road, for half a mile or so, and then you went down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. How far over from this road do you think it was parallel, the old road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The mill was probably less than half a mile off of this road. See, that was all just bare grass, there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, was the whole area from Sheppard's to Coote's second mill bare grass pretty much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this on this side was trees and this was grass. We had trees starting in about here. Sheppards logged his place, or we cut wood off of his place, my dad and I Cut wood off of his place. But the old Coote's Mill road would have gone in here. It would have gone back that way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then all the way back to the mill there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But then it would have been going through the timber then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But you see might be right there. I bet that's the road right there. Because this road was graveled up to the top of the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This road here was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And so Coote could go in that road, and get to his mill. Sheppard lived right here at the bottom of the hill, and he had a house fairly close to the road here. His house isn't there anymore. It was real funny, I was hunting in here, that time I found Donald. This gets pretty steep back up in there. Goes back up in here further. Dobrinins lived just about where this spot here is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they live right along the edge of the road here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they had a barn and they had some of prettiest Indian paint horses you ever

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: saw. Pintos. But they would have lived right in here somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you recall anybody living on the other side of the road over there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, you asked me that the other day. And I don't remember anything. Anyway, there was a logging road went up this way, when Don and I met each other.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That' d be this road right here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so. Anyway, I had a four-wheeled drive and a guy got a deer right up on top there. Well there was a cat road, a landing up there and then a cat road went back up on top. This guy shot a deer right up there on top. He was going down to get some help get that deer down. And I said, "Well I've got a four-wheeled drive, I could probably go up and get it." And, "Oh, you couldn't possibly get up there with a four- wheeled drive." So anyway I went on up the road, got up the landing, went up the cat road, got up on top, parked right by his deer and went hunting. He came back to get his deer and my pickup was parked about 10 feet from it. He didn't know where four-wheeled drives would go!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any name for that road going up in there, or for that ridge or anything back up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, far as I know that road was put in after the college owned it. We were hunting out there on permits from the college. But they weren't stopping four-wheeled drives from going in there then, now they do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, we're on 99 next to, what's the name of that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: South, or north gate, Mary's River Lumber Company.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And your question was, whether we're getting all disoriented today because of the same reason Jim Hanish did. All those field and meadows and marshes have all grown up into trees, and I was just wondering which is the more pleasing to you, which you think is the better environment?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I thought it was a very pretty setting for those meadows up there, with the trees surrounding them, was a very beautiful setting. Also, the moss under the trees and ladyslippers and stuff were very beautiful. But I'm quite adaptable, I like down in the desert, I like, I think mostly my main interest is farms. I enjoy seeing what farmers are raising and what they're doing. So basically I can't necessarily say that I like one better than the other. But I like to go from one to the other.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you see those trees up there? Is this kind of like tree fanning, type of a fanning?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm seeing quite a bit of moss growing under them, which is a good place for such things as ladyslippers and some of these other flowers that grow in that kind of environment. And that's all coming back in the area that was logged off when I was younger. And so I'm not seeing too much destruction by logging, myself. I mean, I realize that a person 18 years old thinks that 50 years down the road is forever, but when you get up there and look back you have a different view of it. And I'm seeing that it's pretty nice up there again where all that area has been logged off once in my lifetime, some of it twice in my lifetime.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think the management with the mills and the old farms and everything else, overall it's been pretty reasonable?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I think so. I think it was kind of nice that farmers could homestead up in the timber like that. And clear out a spot. But I think most of that's probably in the past now, we have modem transportation, electricity, and that sort of thing, and I don't think there's very many people would be willing to do without. You know, I mean, back there when the pioneers were here well if they wanted to get away from

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: everybody they could and get back up there and make a living. But that's something I don't think we can ever see again. In the first place, like I say, it's not the high cost of living, it's the cost of high living in lots of things, and we're kind of used to the high living. We wouldn't be willing to go back to driving a buggy up a hill like that and doing all the work it takes to eek Out your living out of it and go without a lot of things and so forth. So I think it's some of these old homesteads are not ever gonna be able to happen again, and I don't think anybody'd want to do it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think it'd be worth it, or do you think it'd be worth it for the forest in particular, the Research Forest, to tiy to recreate one or two of those old homesteads to show people what it was like in those days? Keep some of those fields open? Or keep some of those houses built up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think you'd find anybody to live in them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, how about as a demonstration, kind of like they do with some of these historical recreations on old forts or something. Do you think a farmer thing like that, or do you think that would be too expensive?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think he could make his living anymore because, let's face it, it was a pretty meager living when we were young. And we didn't have any electricity bill, no telephone bill, we bought a little gas we went to town once every two weeks. Our cost of living wasn't all that much. We had milk, we separated the milk and kept the skim milk for ourselves and sold the cream. And now there isn't any demand for cream because they found out now it's got cholesterol in it. So you wouldn't have anything to sell, really, and you can't sell milk to a creamery or anything, there's no demand for it, because you've gotta be grade A. So you get up there, what would you have to sell. I mean, basically, you might be able to get some beef out, but how would you get them out? Milk was the thing that most of us raised 50 years ago, on the farms, to get the milk check, and chickens, sell eggs, and that's where we got our money from. Well, our milk check is a thing of the past, the competition with eggs where they have these egg farms that produce thousands of eggs, your little dozen hens wouldn't make you much money. You couldn't pay for the feed. Mass production, that's what you have to have now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you think about, f the School Forest has a loss, or that type of situation to make money was to charge people admission, the type of thing where it was kept as a living museum. That type of concept. Do you think it would be educational for kids, or worth it for older people to go back to old fields and subsistence farms off in the hills, one or two like that, just for educational value?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it would be interesting. If you had something like that and made them walk up there, like I had to. You know, rather than to have virtually a freeway going right past the front door.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hike into it like they do now at a wilderness area, but hike up to an old farm the way they used to have to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. A mile or two off the road and let them hike through the trees and enjoy the timber the way it is. You've got timber up there that you could do that with. You know. And, that would be a possibility, but it would be quite a chore to clear off and make something like that. Big as the trees are there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, you think that that might be a reasonable attraction, but not a. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know how many people you'd get to go up there. It would take quite a few people.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about people in the future, one or two generations from now. Maybe only five or ten people a year, but that want to report back to other people, or recreate that type of environment. Would it be worth it for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well economically it wouldn't. It might be for the benefit that the people would get out of it. But I don't think you could ever make it pay financially. Hey, your boy's up there. [Returning to NW 15th street in Corvallis. Notices Paul Gorow and Alistar Zybach working on roof] He's been waiting for you to come home for a long time, he didn't want to work that late. He's got two of them up there. One of the boys own a car?
bracketed_corrections: Returning to NW 15th street in Corvallis. Notices Paul Gorow and Alistar Zybach working on roof

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, one's got that [Fordj Mustang.

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Map of the tour of Berry Creek and Oak Creek with Neil Vanderburg on January 26, 1991.  Notice that many of the stops on this tour are included on the previous tour map on page 26.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part III. January 26, 1991 Interview

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Neil Vanderburg on the road to the Coote and Weinert's sawmill, January 26, 1991.

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Interview conducted by Bob Zybach.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Q. The Mill Pond Creek

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've just come up and out of Sheppard's, and we're moving towards the Coote's and Cornutt Mill to the north of us on Tampico Road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm going to make a correction. Cornutt had dropped out of the Coote's/Cornutt deal when he built this mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was strictly Coote's mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was strictly Coote' s mill. But he did move the steam engine and a lot of the stuff from the Cornutt mill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When Bill Coote built this mill up here above Sheppard's, the road didn't go through from Berry Creek, however, he did live at Berry Creek, so he built a road from Sheppard's house, or from where the road ended at Sheppards. Came right up to the top of the hill, and then he took off at an angle and went back probably close to a . oh, between a quarter and half a mile to his mill site. Then they put this road

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: through, and then right where we're sitting there's a little rise in the road, and about in there was where he went right straight back in to his mill. So he didn't have to maintain as much tram road, is what we called it. It was a plank road, was what he was going in on, and actually when he built the road straight in, I think that he gravelled that. Right here at the top of the hill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You're talking about the top to the south of us?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To the south of us, yeah, right above Sheppard's place, they hauled the slab wood out of Bill Coote's mill and stacked it right there, and at one time there was probably 200 cords of slab wood stacked right there at the brink of the hill there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was real visible as you were driving up the road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Of course this road wasn't here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and when you said his road angled off, you mean to the west of this road here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, his road took off. And it was a fairly straight road. It went back a little ways and then made a curve and there was a small creek that came down there, that he ran his mill pond with, and I don't know how that came through here anymore. I can't recall where that creek crossed over or how it got down into Soap Creek. It must have ended up in Soap Creek. And I don't know whether we'll find that creek any more or not because I'm finding that a lot of this area doesn't have as much moisture in it as it used to when I was a kid. There was a lot of these small tributaries that just all I find is a ditch there anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're about halfway between Sheppard's and the top of the rise here towards Smith Peak. Can you describe, from where we're sitting now, to the west of us, about where Coote's tram road went through?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say from here it probably wasn't more than oh, maybe 200, 250 feet from this road, but of course this road wasn't here, so it's kind of hard to get your bearings.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If we go up to this next road here on the left, and walk in, can we maybe find the old track?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's where I would guess it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, why don't we do that then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're just past. . we've got a puddle of water on our right, flowing to the east

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: toward Smith Peak, and a little ditch on our left. On school property.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say that that is probably where the little creek came through that Bill Coote made his mill pond on. And maybe an easier way to find the old mill Site would just be to try and follow that ditch up to there, or we can go on up here and hit that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did the plank road cross this creek here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't think it did. I think this creek is going to veer off to the north, and his mill was on the west side of the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Feel like taking a short hike here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sure!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: *** Did this creek have a name here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I sure wouldn't know it if it did. But it does have running water here, it is in January, like Bob said, but it's about the size of the creek that I'm talking about. And also we've had freezing weather for quite a while so it wouldn't be flowing as hard as it might have been when it was raining hard. I think most of what we've got running here is probably coming out of the ground. Probably out of the trees. I'll have to come back here in the summertime and see if it's running.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it run all through the summer before?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you call it any name like Coote's Creek, or Steele Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We're standing on a road here, it's not quite where I pictured the old Coote's mill on, but I did say just a few minutes ago that I thought that Bill Coote had graveled the road, the second road he built in, and we're standing on a gravel road just within 500 feet of where I thought the road was. And I am quite sure that this is probably the old road that went up to Bill Coote' s last mill. The one that John Weinert ultimately took over because Bill Coote had gotten so far in debt to him because when he first got this mill built, he'd hardly got into production and it burned up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The one up here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It burned up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it burned up. And so Bill Coote didn't have enough money to pay his employees, so John Weinert owned a grocery store in Airlie, and he made arrangements with John Weinert to furnish food for his employees until he could get back up and running again. And so that was what was done, and then just about the time Bill Coote got running again, maybe a year or so, well then John Weinert felt that Bill Coote was not the manager to ever pay him back apparently, so he foreclosed on him and then John Weinert ran the mill until pretty close to when the government took this over for Camp Adair.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that Weinert' s first mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Weinert was just. . . he owned a grocery store, service station, post office and anything else you wanted in Airlie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the same Weinert that owned W.O.W. [Weinert, Oudeuiru & WienertJ in Eddyville?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know for sure. I know that his son is down there now. His son, I think they call Jack Weinert.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he the one that owned Yaquina Head?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what he owned after he left here. But I know they did move down into the coastal area someplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Weinert that had the store in Airlie, do you know where that family came from? Was that their first business in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. He had two daughters and his son Jack.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what year it was that they took this mill over then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it would have been probably about 1939.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many years did they run it? Up until Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up until '41 when Adair took it over. '42, whatever it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, before we go any further here, we've got a bunch of windfall in front of us. Can you remember what this road looked like back in 1939 and 1940?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I thought it was quite a straight road, and we're standing here looking at a fairly straight road. Of course, at the time that they were running the mill here, they had cut all the trees down around here, so we were . . . I mean, it looks different now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, on the aerial photos from 1937 they show this being logged off. But they show a lot of standing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are those old snags, or just. . . what did they leave standing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can't honestly say.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And it looked like maybe a fire had gone through here. Was that possible?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not that I would have any recollection of. Now, the aerial photo that you are talking about. There was nothing on the other side of the road was there'?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No. Just a little patch of trees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Because that was all farmed in the '30s.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But this was logged, but there was quite a bit of material that was still standing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And actually, these trees that we're in now, the bigger trees are the size that we were logging. I can't tell on the tape, but you see there's one, probably 20 inches on the stump. And that one there, that's

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that one over there might be 30 or 32 inches.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And that's an old growth from my recollection, what we've always called old growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's got rippled bark.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's got rippled bark and broken off limbs and stuff, and that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That might have been an understory tree when they logged here before. It looks . . . they would have logged this 52 or 53 years ago, and that looks like it might be, what, 60 or 70 years old?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, something like that. But that is, from what my memory is, the old growth was more of a grade of tree than it was the size of a tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jim Hanish pointed to that age group, and up on Forest Peak they'll get quite a bit larger than that. And he called them old growth, and they're about 70 years old.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But you see that tree there is possibly 70 years old, but it was probably a pretty small tree when I lived in this area, but that's interesting that we . . . now you see these little saplings here? Those are old growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just because the way the bark is forming?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: See the bark on it? Give those 30 years and they'll be old growth. See what I'm talking about, those two right there'? Why don't you take a picture of those?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. [Phtographs on file with OSU Research Forests]
bracketed_corrections: Phtographs on file with OSU Research Forests

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: R. Possible Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're now at the old mill site, or what we think is the mill site.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What we can look for to find the site for sure would be an area of possibly a flat area where there was a lot of bark chips and stuff off the logs that settled to the bottom of the pond, and in all likelihood there should be some evidence of that old mill pond here. My brother and I were up here in 1956 deer hunting and we found parts of the old dam. Of course, that's another 35 years ago, and that wood is probably completely demolished now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the dam was made out of wood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The dam was made out of wood with dirt on the sides like we found up there at Cooper's mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they logs or cants, or . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were lumber. Probably 3-inch lumber, 3 by 12's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were built into a framework or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were built into a framework and then they were slid, these boards were slid into the framework and then when the pond got full of bark and stuff they could slide these boards out and drain it and refill it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the boards were put in vertically?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Vertically, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they tongue and groove, or just regular boards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think they were just regular boards. I think there was some leakage through the dam. Now this is a fairly big flat spot in here, and Bill had the sawmill and he also had a planer mill. And he had a resaw for taking his 2-inch or 3-inch or 4-inch lumber and making it into 4-inch, 6-inch, or 12-inch planks. And so it was a fairly big operation, and I think right here is just about the only place it could be, don't you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It looks like we're at the headwaters of the creek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: lJh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've got a hill coming down off the west there, and we're in a big flat, and we're in an area that's held pond water here just recently. This winter.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They did drag logs in from the north with horses, so we may be able to find some skid marks from the logs over there where they skidded them up to the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, why don't we try to do that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So we've got a couple of things here that we might be able to look for.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I just took a couple pictures of you, Neil, with the sprouts in the background and the old mill site, and we're standing here along what looks like an old skid trail.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They brought some of the logs around the head of the mill, the mill pond. We've got a skid road here and we've got a skid road right there. And I remember those skid roads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, those are coming in from the northwest on a flat that's covered with hardwoods now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Alder, or something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When this was a skid road through here, was this all muddy, or covered with bark? Or did they deck logs here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, of course all the logs that were brought in here were brought in by teams of horses and it got muddy in the winter. But not as bad as you would think, nothing like what cats do. But basically they were pulling the logs in from this area right in to the west and the north of us. And I never went up in the woods where they were getting them from, but I did work in the mill for a week or so when I was about 13. I got paid cash because even then I wasn't supposed to be working.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you were working in this mill right here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was working on the planer. I was grading off the planer down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that when Coote owned it, or Weinert?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was when Coote owned it. My dad worked here when Weinert owned it. But I worked for Bill Coote. Bill Coote felt kind of sorry for us, we were farmers and so forth, and so he gave my dad a job and let me work once in a while when he could get away with it. But this is definitely the old mill site. I'll betcha that if you'd go down on the other side of the creek in there with a metal detector, you'd pick up some nails or something of that sort.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now they logged with horses on this side. How about from the south there? That was all logged out by the time they set up the mills?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was just a natural clearing in there pretty much. We actually. . . this whole

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: area down here was a plank dock. The planer sat on a plank dock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big was that dock? About.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, gosh. Probably about 100 feet square. 100 on each side. Maybe not quite as wide as long. But it went down there just about to the trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of power did they have here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had a steam tractor. Clifford Cornutt was telling me when they brought that steam tractor over from Berry Creek over here how by the time they got up to the top of the hill over here above Berry Creek it was getting dark, and he says, "Boy that old steam tractor sure did glow!" Because they were throwing 4-foot slab wood into the fire box, and the old smoke and sparks were just coming Out of that thing coming up the hill!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they used a steam tractor from the old mill to yard itself up the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would they do that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it had wheels on it. It was an old farm tractor, an old steam farm tractor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was the only power for the mill here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's what ran the mill, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So did this kind of look like kind of a "Smoky Stover" kind of operation, or did they put it together pretty nice?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I thought it was a pretty good deal. And of course they had a steam whistle on this that you could hear all over the valleys here and so forth. And I think I mentioned before that my dad used to tell me when Bill Coote would blow his 5 o'clock whistle, he'd say, "Well, that's one thing about being a farmer. You don't have to quit when the whistle blows." I think I mentioned that before.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was one of those whistles he was talking about.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was one of the whistles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What dimension lumber were they turning out here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, most all of these mills were tie mills, railroad ties. And you had trees that were, oh, somewhere between 16 and 20 inches on the stump. So you could maybe get 2 by 12's, maybe even as much as 14 under the slabs, then you would get almost the heart, then you would turn your log and start cutting the other way. And of course, the ties I think were 6 by 6, so you ultimately ended up with 2 by 6's or 2 by 8's when you got down to the tie size.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how many thousand board feet they'd turn out in a day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't the vaguest idea because I didn't know that much about lumber. But I know they had two lumber trucks that were very modern. What they did, they had rollers on the back of them with a flatbed on them, and Bill Coote built some stands out of tie wood material that were just the right height, so when they would back under and roll that load on, well that tie stand would fall down and he could push against the mill and push that load of lumber clear onto his truck and then tie her down and away he went. And boy that was really modern!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were vertical stands, were kind of just made to be knocked over?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, just made to be knocked over so that he could back on under it. Sometimes he'd have to jump out of the truck and kick the stands out of the road, and he'd back on in and when he left, well then they'd stand the stands back up and stack their lumber on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he own the trucks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many people worked here in the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it would take me a while to figure it. There was the pond monkey, and the sawyer, and the ratchet setter, and the off bearer, and the resaw man, and the cutoff saw man, and about 2 or 3 off bearers off the green chains.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So with truck drivers there were about 10 or 15 people here keeping things going?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, then we also had the engineer that kept the steam engine running, and he was a millwright, I suppose you'd call him now. Of course in those days you had babbitt bearings and he went around every two hours or so and oiled all the babbitt bearings and stoked the boiler, and then of course if a bearing went out well he'd pull it at night, so he was there too. And then of course we still had the planer over there -- that probably entailed at least four people involved in the planer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they sent finished lumber out of here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it air dried?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they'd cut cants and air dry them. Would they have a drying area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Actually, they didn't air dry them. They just sanded them green! Because we didn't have room in here to air dry them. As you can see, there was just room for the mill pond, the sawmill and the planer mill in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then where would the lumber be trucked to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. The truck drivers. . . he put that set up with the rollers on just before John Weinert took over, and the truck drivers lived at our place. Because they, well they were close to the road here. And when John Weinert took over, I don't know what he used for trucking or anything, but Bill Coote had the truck drivers board at our place. They were single guys and they owned their own trucks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What size of trucks were they driving?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, Chevrolets and Fords.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Flatbeds

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, 85 horsepower, whether you needed it all or not! With 30 speeds ahead or so. [Laughs]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was it, a big 6, maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: V-8. Fords had the V-i's in those times, and Chevrolets had the 6.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they just have a single dual wcle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, just a single axle, duals. I doubt if they hauled more than about 2,000 feet per load.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you don't know where they hauled those loads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many teams were logging up in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Three.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Three teams?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Donald Dickey told you the Burbanks, and Forest Tandy, and who did he say the other one was? I can't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Burbanks, Tandy -- oh, McAlpine. Did McAlpine die by this point?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I didn't know McAlpine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. But we can look at Dickey's transcript. He named. . . now was this a year round operation or seasonal?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, it went year round. And basically, I believe that they put that road through because of Bill Coote's mill there I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tampico Road, there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. That and the fact that we had a whole bunch of high school kids down there at Berry Creek all at once which we were having to transport almost to Airlie and up to Suver and around that way. So I think that was. . I think about '38 that they went

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: ahead and punched this road on through and made it a year round road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So at that time the kids in Berry Creek took the school bus.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Soon as they built this road to Corvallis High School? We all went to Corvallis High School.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why don't you tell that story now about your family history in Corvallis High School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know exactly what you want to know, but I have 1936 annual from Corvallis High School showing that Corvallis High School was way out in the country when I was in high school. The Future Farmers farmed the 60 acres just north of the high school there, and there was no houses. I mean Corvallis High School was sitting out there all by itself. You could see it for miles when you come into town on 99. And anyway, I take it you want me to also tell at our 40th class reunion, I graduated in '41, and when the '41 class had their 40th reunion, well they asked who had the most kids. Well, I had six children and Keith Robison had six, and so they asked us what our kids had done that was noteworthy, and I said well all six of mine graduated from Corvallis High School. And so Keith gave up, so I got the prize, and now I've got a granddaughter going to Corvallis High School.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When does she graduate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Four more years I believe. She just started this year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But this year you'll have your 50th reunion.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we'll have our 50th reunion. I got a letter from the people that are putting the reunion together, I got it from Aloha, Oregon, and of course the woman was married and so I didn't recognize the name and didn't know what it was all about. But I got it yesterday, inviting me to the 50th reunion, and we're going to have two-day reunion. We are going to have a dinner in the evening, we'll take pictures and make kind of an annual for those of us who are still alive. And then on Sunday they're gonna have a tour of the Corvallis area. I don't know whether it'll be a walking tour or what, and then those of them that want to play golf, they'll play golf across the [Wilamette] river from Corvallis there, on that golf course. But anyway, when I make my reservations I'm going to tell them that I financed the rebuilding of Madison Square in Corvallis, and if you go in there -- we put in an elevator -- and if you go in there you will see a plaque above the elevator to Mr. Kleinschmidt and Carl Werner. Well Carl Werner was my wife's father, and we dedicated it to him because he had just died at that time. Anyway, I'm going to write, when I make my reservations, and tell them that, because when we were in high school that was Whiteside's Hardware Store. It took that whole corner there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any other kids from Berry Creek or Soap Creek that you can remember that might be going to this reunion?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Possibly Edith Tandy, maybe Betty White. They were the only two that graduated with me. You saw the pictures of our graduating class.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they're still alive?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, all of them but Leslie Gardner. Leslie Gardner died of cancer ten years or so ago. But I talked to Edith Tandy, and Betty White is her aunt, but Edith Tandy is a year older than Betty is. And I wouldn't be surprised to see Edith Tandy there. She lives down at Yoncalla.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We just took a couple pictures next to this old stump here, and could you describe why this about five or six foot [tallJ stump is here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is what we used to call long butt. Donald spoke of it in his book, Donald Dickey, and we had a little trouble understanding what he was saying. But it sounded like he meant that they were 16 feet long. But my guess was always six to eight feet long. We've got one laying here that's about five feet long, and the contour of it shows that there was some, either some pitch or damage on the butt here. Maybe something had hit it, maybe another tree fell against it or something. So they long- butted it to where the good wood was, and that's what Don was talking about in his book.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You can see where this injury is that caused the butt to flare, so somebody looking at the butt there might think they've got a 28 or 30 inch tree, but where they cut the log five feet up it's only about /8 or 20 inches.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: How would you like to know how big it is? [Laughs and pulls out measuring tape.]
bracketed_corrections: Laughs and pulls out measuring tape.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, well let's find out. Let's see how good my eye is here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: How about 24 inches counting the bark.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well you can't Count that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, then we'll go for 22 inches. Twenty-one inches, whatever!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The stumps we're looking at are mostly about a foot to 20 inches, and how much product could you get out of one of these trees here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Some of these, just slabs and ties. Some of them, of course, we got some lumber out of. But we can see evidence here of some of the old stumps that are still here that you'd just get maybe one tie and maybe a 2 by 4 off of one side of it, and they had to have, in those days they had to have the heart right in the middle of the tie, so these small trees made awful good ties. Because you take a tree like the one we just took pictures of here, the heart could be way off to one side from the injury and so forth and make it awful hard to get the heart in the middle of the tie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So would you just not cut a tie on that, or would you actually set up and still cut a tie?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They'd still saw up to three inches of the heart on one side. Unless the heart was crooked. Of course, in this case here it was probably crooked in this area, but it might have centered once you got up past the long butt.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would the trees be yarded in tree length to the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they'd be around 16 feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that'd make two ties then, each log that would come into the mill would make two ties.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And actually they cut them an extra six or eight inches long for trim. Because the loggers with the old swede fiddle, they couldn't cut square and the ends of those ties had to be square so they gave them trim on it. And that's what you cut off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, out here the trees would be. . they were using chainsaws at that time, weren't they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They were still using hand saws and horses until /941?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I hadn't heard of a chainsaw until 1946 or '47. And I tell you, my sister wrote to me and told me my brother-in-law, he worked in the woods for Werner Timber

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Company down there on what do you call the name of that creek?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Euchre Creek. Over in Lincoln County.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Eucher Creek. And he was. . when Werner Timber Company bought their first

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: chainsaw -- they didn't really buy it, they just gave it to him to try out to see if they wanted one or not. And they were kind of skeptical about it being as good as what they said. And of course in those days the chainsaw was a two-man saw, and the motor unit probably weighed 80 or 90 pounds for the simple reason they didn't use aluminum in those days on a motor. So it was all cast-iron motor. And so you had to they also hadn't learned the technique of being able to go around the tree with it. So the saw had to be as long as the tree was thick. But anyway, going back to my story, my sister wrote me a letter and told me that they had given Orval [Cummings] the first chainsaw to try out and they didn't know how it would work out. And being down in California, I didn't see how they could Cut with a dog chain, or a logging chain, any kind, a bicycle chain, or any kind of a chain I ever saw, and so I couldn't hardly wait to get back to Oregon to see what a chainsaw looked like!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, do you remember the brand name of the saw he was using?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He used a Mahl and he used one made up in Canada.
