entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that a Timber Beast?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Timber Hog.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Timber Hog.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But anyway, that was at least in '46, '47, in there was the first time I ever heard of a chainsaw.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: My great uncle JBen Robbins] used one on the Lewis River in 1936 or '37. They blew up two of them in the first two days. But, didn't they have handle bars, and one guy had the handle bars? You couldn't tip the motor even sideways, could you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, you twist it. . . you had a round thing on the drive, and if you wanted to fall, then you just released it and turned it on edge, whichever way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was 90 degrees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah . . . to whichever way you wanted to turn, or if you . . . actually, if you wanted to undercut, you could turn it 160 degrees and come from underneath.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the person operating at the other end, he operated what was called the stinger, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the stinger was the other end. It just has one handle, and that was called the stinger.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that was the second guy operated the stinger.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the second guy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he have a name? Was he called the bucker, and the guy that operated the saw called the faller or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the guy on the one end was the stinger operator, and the other end was the power saw operator, is all I ever heard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's what they called them, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But you see in those days they had carburetors on, and if you tipped them too much, well you'd poor the gas out of the carburetor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well they still had to limb with axes, didn't they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they used axes to limb, and then they used the swede fiddle to buck.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, back when I was working in the woods. I never worked in the woods with a

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: power saw. I've used a power saw a lot since then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would they fall these smaller trees here? Would they use a saw for them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They didn't use power saws for them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But they used a cross-cut saw and then an ax to

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And contrary to what a lot of people would think, when we cut an undercut, we chopped the whole undercut. We didn't even saw on the bottom. Most of them saw it on the bottom. But of course the undercuts in those days were flat on the bottom and sioped on the top, now of course they

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: More like a beaver cut or something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Well, actually it was flat on the bottom, V-shape. Like I told you this morning about my brother-in-law when he was falling those spruce down on the Alsea, they laid in the undercut, so it was flat on the bottom.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we cut like that even some in the 70's. But then they started putting in what they called Humboldt corner, where it's flat on the top and then you cut up to it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Reason for that was, you take on a 6-foot tree, your undercut was at least a foot of whole log lost. If you cut up from underneath, you didn't lose that much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or you take 150 20-inch trees in an acre, there's all your largest diameter ends right there. So, on the back cut, would the back cut come in level with the top?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sloped just a little bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sloped a little bit down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. That was to keep it from going over backwards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you aiming kind of to the base of your undercut, down to the flat part on your undercut?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We usually tried to come in about two inches above the undercut.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you'd still have your first buck then, you'd have to cut away your stump? So you'd have not only the waste on the stump but your first cut there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm talking about hand tools. I don't know anything about power saws.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But then your bucking was done with hand saws, and not with axes or anything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What they now call two-man saws, but we only had one man on 'em.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, you only had 20-inch trees though, too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, when I worked down there on the coast we cut a lot of stuff there that ran well, I bucked on tree that had 14,000 feet in it, so

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: With a two man saw by yourself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the ax, was that called a faller's ax?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Called a logging ax?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we just called it a double bit ax. And one side of it was sharp for cutting undercuts and the other side was sharpened more of an angle for knocking limbs off. If you ever took your side that you cut the undercuts with and hit a limb with it you just pulled it over because it tapered out so high on that end that you didn't cut anything but good wood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you knocked the limbs out of there you were able to get. . . you weren't actually cutting through the limbs, you were actually knocking them out of place and getting them flesh with the bark that way.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We weren't chopping the limbs actually, we. . . I mean the ax was sharp enough you could chop them. But most of them that you're knocking off, a lot of them are dead

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: limbs anyhow. And they're hard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you kick those off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beat them with an ax. We always get the right side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: WOuld anybody ever cut into their foot or anything while they were limbing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I suppose.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wasn't real common though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we were pretty careful. There was a funny thing happened while I was working the woods down on the coast. We were eating lunch, and we always sharpened our axes after we finished lunch. And one time my brother-in-law, that's Orval, wanted to borrow another guy's file, and so the guy tossed it with the sharp point first, and it went into my brother-in-law's ankle. And the guy says, "Watch out!" And my brother-in-law says, "Why, you gonna throw another one?" By the time he said "Watch out!" my brother-in-law was pulling the file out! But as far as . . . I heard of a lot more of fingers and toes getting chopped splitting wood than I ever did in the woods.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of hats would you wear out here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: None.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No hats? Not even a felt hat to keep the sweat out of your eyes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we wore those old red hunters' hats. You remember those old felt? Okay, well by the time spring came the brim had shrunk down to about 3/4 of an inch and draped over your ears and it had enough sweat and oil off your hands and stuff so that it was pretty stiff and so every fall in hunting season we all bought a new hat, and then by the next fall it was pretty well used!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those were the "Red Hat Days"? When hunting season would come around.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was red hats in the fall but by the next fall when you bought a new one they were getting pretty black.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What. . . as long as we're on the topic, what kind of shirts would you wear, and pants, while you were logging?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In the wintertime it was what they called tin pants. They were made out of canvas and I don't know if they were waxed a little bit or what, but when they got cold and wet they got so stiff you couldn't bend your knees, you just kinda walked along like this! I'm showing you, I can't tell it on the recording, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kind of like goosestepping or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. It was. . . they became very stiff. But they didn't leak, and they didn't. you didn't sweat in them near as bad as you do in the plastic coats that they wear today because they did breathe. But they would be. . . the coat would, by the middle the back, it was six inches off your back. And so you had a lot of air circulation from underneath. They would just get stiff and they would just kind of fit you as you were going like this, well pretty soon the coat was way out in back of you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they get limber during the day while you were working?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We took them off, when they were limber. We never had one on when they were limber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would you wear in the summer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a regular shirt.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would it be like flannel or wool, or. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, usually.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wasn't like now, where everybody wears the same kind of shirt?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about suspenders or belts?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We all wore snagged off pants; our pants were all cut off almost halfway to the knees to keep the limbs and stuff from getting caught in the pants. And of course our boots came up higher than where they were cut off, and most everybody wore suspenders. To let air circulate, and also the suspenders were good for hanging things on when we were moving from one tree to the other. It was just the way you did things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you call them "snagged" trousers. And I've heard them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "Snagged off", yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: i've heard them called "stagged trousers", too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But we always called them snagged off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of caulk boots would you wear? What brands?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there were some Currins made up in Washington, up by Centralia. But I wore Wescos. And they were sold by Western Auto Supply. And they were. . . 1 could buy these Wescos for about $13, which was like a week's pay at that time. But my brother-in-law Orval, he always had to have the Currins. They were more expensive, they were more pliable, and they were easier to . . and they were also more

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: waterproof. That was pretty important when you're wearing a pair of leather boots all day. Once or twice a week we would always hang our boots over the old wood cook stove that the wife worked on and get them good and warm, and then we'd take some deer tallow and mix it with linseed oil, one thing and another, and grease our boots so that we could keep our feet dry. And we greased them summer and winter because if you didn't grease them in the summer time they wouldn't hold water next winter. So it wasn't a case of just keeping your feet dry, but to keep them soft also.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of gloves would you wear?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never wore any gloves.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did very many people wear gloves?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They did after they started using power saws, but I don't think. . . I think it would be dangerous with axes and stuff to use a glove. But I . . . one thing my brother-in-law was always jealous of me, when we'd work in the woods and both of us would be bucking, I was ambidextrous, and he says I got to rest half the time! He had to stand there and saw all day with his right arm, and I'd saw for a while this way and then I'd get over here and saw with my left arm and my right could rest! He was always jealous of me for that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of anything else in this particular area? I think we've covered.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think we've pretty well covered it. And I'm real tickled to find it so obvious because I haven't been out here in over 30 years, and we just walked right into it by walking up the creek here. I knew that's what we could do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But if you didn't know a mill was there, you'd think it was some natural meadow or anything else. You'd have a totally djfferent idea.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It very likely was a natural meadow when he cleared out and put his mill in there. You know, I don't think we ever did go down there in that bottom.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Fifty years later and there's hardly a trace.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, except for some old skid roads, and the creek that he made the mill pond with and stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If you didn't know better, though, that could be a little bit of a sluff, and some seasonal drainage ditches there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, if you didn't know there was a mill, if you didn't know it when you came up here you'd never find it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But we found quite a bit of evidence of it. I wonder if these logs had been cut 50 years ago?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'd say that these shorter stumps and these ones hollowed out have to be. Because this area was all logged off then, and they didn't have any more logs until 10 or 15 years ago. And then we're seeing some newer stumps that look like they were thinned out of this area, probably letting this poison oak and grand fir understory start to sprout here. But I. . . it looks to me like this is logging that you took part in here. These old skid trails and these older stumps have to date from that time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I found those trees that we called old growths, you know, because people today, an old growth is a big old tree, and actually an old growth has never been to me necessarily an old tree!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well at least we can say for people in the Berry Creek and Soap Creek area, everybody I've talked to, it's the condition of the bark, and it's a rivuleted bark, and it seems to come on when an tree is 60, or 70 or 80 years old. And that's what they're calling old growth, rather than necessarily a larger tree that's younger with smoother bark.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But also, any old growth they were a slow growing tree. The railroad used to, back in World War II times, require 18 grains to the inch. And that was old growth. I mean, there was no second growth that had grown that slow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So those smaller trees that we were looking at, took the photographs of, those definitely would have 18 rings to the inch. That would determine them as old growth. By railroad standards.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would think so. Except possibly when they are young they may grow faster. But as they, you know, I mean maybe along close to the bark.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think the reason those are so small, though, is that they were suppressed and probably the logging 50 years ago released them. So even when they were young, they were probably like these understory trees we're seeing here, which are 20 or 30 years old and three inches in diameter. That'd be my guess as to why they're so small.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But you see that's an old growth right behind you there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, and it could have some larger rings in the middle.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You can see looking at that tree right there . . . we had what we called a Spud that we peeled the white firs with, and then they took them out as buckskins, and took them down to the paper mill. Then they chopped them up and made paper out of them, and it was good, pure white paper because the white fir itself was fairly light wood inside. Plus the fact that there was no bark or anything on it. And boy after you got through peeling one of those, you didn't want to try and step on it, because it was slick! That old slimy sap in it!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now these were sent to a pulp mill, so the white fir would be separated out and sent to Salem, and then the Doug-fir would be hauled down to the local tie mill and cut into ties.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the slabs would be taken off the tie mill and sold for firewood.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Slabs were sold for firewood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any other products coming out of here? How about madrone or oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. No, basically there wasn't much. . . actually most of your white fir wasn't intermingled with your red fir or old growth. Because your white fir seemed to grow down pretty close to creek bottoms. See you probably won't see any back this way, but we're getting down towards the creek bottom. See there's one you can see down through there, just to the right of my pickup, quite a bit bigger than this one. And you can look at the bark, now that I've pointed it out to you, and see that that's different than the Doug-firs here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I got to tell you though, I already knew the dWerence! I Laughs]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I know, but I didn't think you called them white fir! I thought you had another name for them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Piss fir.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is that right!'? Well, I don't think they made lumber out of white fir in those days. But most of it they could clearcut and not be bothered with white fir, because I suppose you know they grew on the creek bottoms. Pretty much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we did a lot offalling of white fir and Doug-fir just on the other side of the hill. This was six or eight years ago, but yeah, and they come up in the shade here, and they grow, we can see they're growing faster f anything than the Doug-fir, they probably put in more volume in these wetter areas.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course, you have less grains to the inch, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was Hanish. . . now he logged off a lot of white fir and sold it into pulp?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But did he sell any logs that came over to the mill here at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So he was almost strictly a pulpwood logger.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Old Hanish was kind of a hermit. He. .. I mean if he could have made more money I don't think he'd have sold logs to the mill. He was just. . . of course, there is one thing. When they loaded the logs in those days, when they did put them on trucks, they had rollers, which was two or three logs running lengthways and built up on a stack of logs, and then they had to roll them onto the truck with a Peavy. So they didn't build high loads like they do now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would the lengths be, would they be 4-foot, or 8-foot lengths?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh no. No, 16.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they'd run them the same. . . and then they'd haul them on flatbeds with stakes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the log trucks had trailers. They didn't have any brakes on their trailers, they were single axle trailers and single axle

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But Hanish would haul out of here by log truck?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He didn't haul. There was a contractor that came in. He sold them on the ground. And then they came in and logged them out. And, I don't know, there used to be a paper mill in Salem and I think that's where they went. I don't know whether that mill is still there or not. I doubt it, because paper mills stink.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're now about 150 feet west of the road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right up to that knob of the hill I was talking about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nearly on top of the Smith Peak crossing here. We're standing on what looks like a really old road bed, crossing over Smith Peak from Soap Creek to Berry Creek. Can you describe this here, Neil, or what you remember about this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, just that probably what we came in on was probably the old tram road, and they probably put some rock base in for the tram road. And then this is the road that he put in later after the county road was put in. I'm having a little trouble here seeing where this road could have gone from here, but I guess it went on down around those stumps and then right there. Yeah, that's about the way it would have come in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It looks to me like it curves down, and curves uphill around the creek, and maybe connects into the mill up there, and that would have been the crossing. That there was an old loop in the road here maybe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. This road would have to end up down below the mill. That's where they came out, down below the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this road, even after the county road went in, this road here was being used to get to and from the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We put this in after the county road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this road is actually younger than the county road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Yeah, the county road of course was a summer road a number of years before this road was used. I have an idea that probably the old steam engine came in on this road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This road here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is essentially just the logging, milling, millworkers road. And would they use this road to get to and from work, or was it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, after they put this other road through. But I think what we came in on, if you remember how I talked about that other road there, coming off of Sheppard's, that that was mostly plank road. But this one here was an all-year road without any planking on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was rocked?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Apparently. It seemed to me like he rocked it. But of course we've got so much moss and leaves and stuff on it we couldn't see if it was rocked or not here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the cutbank has washed down quite a ways in most spots. How wide were the planks that were put on those plank roads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Four by 12's. Two wide. You always, you had to be careful your front wheels that you didn't get in the crack, because they'd do the splits, and then you'd fall down through and then you had to jack yourself back up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were running out in the direction of the tires?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so there were just two tracks, basically?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so each track was 12 and then the cross ties were underneath?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How often would they run the cross ties?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably every four feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the actual railings themselves were maybe 8 foot long?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, probably 16.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sixteen?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The ones going lengthways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those would be four foot thick and twelve inches wide, and so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, four inches thick.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, four inches thick, and twelve inches wide, and just the width of the tires.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you had 24 inches altogether. You had two side by side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. For each tire.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For each tire. So you had 24 inches. Might have been 20 inches; might have been ten-inch planks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you called that a tram road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We called that a tram road, yeah. And then, when you went around the curves, then they would put the lumber crossways of the road because your front wheels and your back wheels wouldn't all track together, so whenever you went around a curve then you would have a section there that was the boards were going crossways, solid.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would you call a corduroy road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, all the corduroy roads I knew were gravel roads that had gotten the bumps in them from use and hadn't been graded. I never heard of a corduroy road in the plank roads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear of anybody making a corduroy road on purpose? To get up and over a hill, say, or something like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So that was just something that got into a road by wear.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Actually you start bumps and pretty soon the bumps get longer and deeper. See this is right up on top of that ridge. I told you right where it was. But this other road, 1 think probably when we came into that other road, probably is a different road where those feathers were. [At the starting point of this stop we had discovered a recent site with a large number of wild bird feathers and empty beer cans.] I think it went on down further before it came into this road. it's possible, where those feathers were is where the slab wood was stacked, though.
bracketed_corrections: At the starting point of this stop we had discovered a recent site with a large number of wild bird feathers and empty beer cans.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then all this across the road on the east side there, that was all field?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: With some oak trees, scattered oak trees. Actually, it was sheep pasture.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who pastured up over there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. The Gardner place came up almost this far. I understand you found evidence of a house up in there, and Donald [Dickey] remembered some woman living up there, but he didn't know who she was. And there was nobody living there when I lived here. And I don't know how she got up there, whether she came up through Sheppard's, or whether she came up the hill. But it would have had to have been a buggy road, it couldn't have been a car road. Of course, Donald thought they improved this road a long time before they actually did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember a pond over there at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: S. The Coote—Cornutt Sawmill #2

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're just coming down the hill, 300 or 400 feet to the west of Tampico Road, and we're sitting at the site of the second Coote's mill here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You could not quite see Bill Coote's mill from the county road over there, so probably back of us a little bit, but his housing for his mill crew was over here on Savage

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Creek. And there wasn't all these trees in here then. And the reason why he put the mill shacks on Savage Creek was so he didn't have to dig a hole for their outhouses. They just did it into the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they have platforms built up over the creek, or have to go out in the weather?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had outhouses, sitting over the creek, but they just had some legs down to the creek and washed on down the creek, and no problem at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did any of the neighbors mind?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I remember one time we went looking for Mayflowers for Mayflower baskets when I was going to grade school here, and Leslie Gardner took a drink out of the creek, and she says, 'Dh, it's all right, as long as water has flowed over 300 feet of gravel it's all purified." And we were standing there looking right at the outhouses over the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there wasn't near the concern in that day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but of course at that time there was quite a number of mill shacks in here. Some of them were back on the side of the hill here, and actually. . . I mentioned Harvey Tandy. He lived over back next to the hill here. And there was, well, there was still probably four or five families lived right here in this mill shack area here. But the sawmill was, like I say, probably back another 100, 150 feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now where. . . on this road that we're on, was this road here at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the road came across the county road, just probably 400 or 500 feet before the road started the steep incline there. And came up at an angle.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About where it does now, pretty much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm not seeing any road over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, about where those cows are is where the road cuts in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, right in there, and it came on up here, and it went on past the old mill and then went on past the first mill that Coote and Cornutt had, and ultimately ended up at the Chaffin house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this road we came in on, is this the old road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So if. .where this road used to go, not where it goes now, but where it used to go, up to

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: the Chaffin place, where we're now sitting.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. See they. . . it wasn't a year round road, it was. . . Chaffins used horse and buggies to go up there, and they could get the horse and buggies up it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. But that was this road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was this road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I understand from talking with you and Jim Hanish earlier that the other road went up Savage Creek there and crossed over and went into Chaffins .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: From the other side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From the other side. So this is a big circular road system here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Basically, yeah. But at the time I lived here, until I herded sheep with old McKibbon, Gerald McKibbon, I didn't know that that road went through over to where the Hanish place was. I always thought that the road pretty much ended right there at Chaffin place. And then when I was herding sheep up there, well we pastured sheep over there on the other side of the mountain there, and then we'd bring them around to Chaffins, count them, and pen them up for the night. So that was the first time I knew that it went on around. But this was the road that Chaffins came in on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The one to the mill here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. Now this mill here had the same steam tractor as the...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And how about the first mill, did it have the same steam tractor?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did this mill site here have a pond to it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this mill here, they yarded trees downhill by horse to this mill site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know. This mill was closed probably six months before we moved here. When I went to school, of course the school [Berry Creeki was right over there by that wagon. And when I went to school, well Clifford [Cornutt] and I used to come up here and play in the old mill site, and all the timbers and the floors and the roof and everything was still on it. And we'd play hide and seek and climb in the rafters and all things that 16 year old kids do. And this was a good place to play. And of course, I told you about the old big barn that sat right down there. That was all put together with wooden pegs.
bracketed_corrections: Berry Creeki was right over there by that wagon. And when I went to school, well Clifford [Comutt

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay now, where was that barn located from where we're sitting?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just about right straight ahead of us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where that hay is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, quite a bit further. These trees weren't all in here. You could see the barn from the mill site. And it was on down, oh probably 500 feet and back a little closer to the creek than what you can see here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that barn fell over during that snow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it withstood the snow and then I think we had a windstorm or something a couple of years later and it went down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the windstorm would have been '39 or '40?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that barn was built out of old wooden pegs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there were no nails in it whatsoever.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the people that lived in these mill shacks continue living here when they continued working at the Coote and Weinert mill site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember an old cabin or anything right around where we're sitting here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. There was several of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1 don't mean mill cabins, I mean like a log cabin or an old homestead?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there were just mill shacks up here. And this. . . when you look down there where that old barn is that's still standing that old Mr. White built.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that's the barn that's still standing, next to Berry Creek there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. White was the last person on this road till you got clear up to Gardners. Except for these mill shacks. And the rest of them were all clustered around Berry Creek there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were these mill shacks. . . did you get the idea they were built here at the same time as the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn hmm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they were just built out of mill lumber?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Rough lumber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About how many families lived in this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would guess maybe six.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did people look at these people that lived here any different than those of you that lived on the farms there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not really. Parkers were looked at a little bit. They were wood cutters. And wood cutters were looked down on, but loggers and mill workers were not looked down on. In fact, if anybody had a job working for a sawmill, had what was considered a good job. The best job you could have during the Depression was in the paper mill, and the next was in the sawmill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So even the little sawmills like this were. . you were a mill worker whether you worked in a little sawmill or a big sawmill in the city?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, if you worked for a farmer you got 15 cents an hour, and if you went to work in a sawmill you got 35. So that was quite a step up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were some of the older families that had been here for a while, say like the Mulkeys and that, did they see a lot of you moving in during the Depression, working in the mills on the farms, as

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Actually, we lived here before the Mulkeys did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. So this part of the Mulkey family moved in later.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Ennis's lived on the Mulkey place when we first came here. And the old man Ennis, he got ulcers and died of a bleeding ulcer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So really the only old time family around here may have been the Smiths? Everybody else kind of moved in in the '20s and '30s.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. The Smiths and then the Dickeys.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well the Dickeys didn't move in until '27.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but they were old timers when we moved here. And the Hanishes were not very far ahead of us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Early '30s.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the Tandys, he moved in probably early '30s or late '20s.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So these mill workers would have been pretty much like the localfarmers. You all moved in here in the late '20s, early '30s, first part of the Depression pretty much.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I don't think that this ground was farmed all that much. As a big farm. More pasture type farm. This soil down here on the creek, that's Chehalis, and that is very good soil, but very hard to work with a team of horses. I mean it just really makes hard clods that you just can't hardly break down. And the hill ground was also covered with fern and Canadian thistle that. . . it wasn't a real good place to farm. I really believe that a guy could make money nowadays with the herbicides and the big tractors and stuff, I think I mentioned that before in our conversation. But this ground right straight ahead of us, I saw that farmed one year while I was here. Otherwise it was pastured by sheep. And this was all pastured by sheep on this side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were these Folk's sheep through here? Or Smiths'?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think they were Smith's. I never knew that Folk had any sheep. I thought he was more of a cattle farmer than a sheep farmer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So people were living here in mill shacks, and there was an old tumble down mill and an old barn here and sheep wandering around through the area too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Basically that's about the size of it. However, I didn't see that many sheep on this side of the road. At that time they were pasturing on the other side of the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this pretty pleasant in here? Playing with the kids through these houses through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. It was nice in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: People keep lawns or grow flowers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. No they were poor people.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did most of them have cars?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Old cars.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Model T's, that type of thing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, really Model T's weren't that. . there was Model A's, and there was old Nashes and Studebakers, and Chevrolets, and there was quite a few Chevrolets went back to 1923. The Model T's went out in '28 and we're looking at a Model T at that time was almost 8 years old, you see, when I moved in here. And they were a cheap car to buy and all that, but they weren't all that popular.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they kind of look like a Yugo or something like that now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, one thing, they didn't have a transmission in them, as such. They had what you call a planetary transmission, is what hydromatic is now. Only the hydromatic shift, with those you had three pedals under your feet with a Model T Ford, and one of them was the brake and the other two were gear shifts. And you just pressed on them, and you pressed the middle one and partway down it went into low, and then if you pushed harder on it you engaged another band and that put you in reverse. And the one on the right was considered a clutch but it didn't completely release. And the Model T's had magnetos on them for ignition and they had to be turned, the motor had to be turned over probably 30 or 40 revolutions per minute before those mags would put out enough spark for it to run. So you had to really wind its tail to get it started, unless you had a battery stuck on there on the side to get it started with. A few of the later ones had starters on them, but they

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have a hand crank?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Most of the Model T's were hand cranked to start them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They all had a crank hanging on the front of them all the time. You didn't take the crank out, you just, when it started you just let it hang and it swung in the breeze while you went down the road. And so it. . . they were popular early on, but Ford was slow to change.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It just seemed old fashioned or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was other cars that were much better. They started putting in gearshifts in them. You take the Model T going up this hill here, if you didn't have a full tank of gas you had to back up it because the gas tank sat right up here in front of the windshield and if you didn't have enough gravity for it to flow into the carburetor well you had to back up the hill so you had gravity to put gas in the carburetor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it uncommon to see Model T's backing up hills?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not at all! Not at all!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sounds like a pretty common way to get up the hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If you were low on gas you backed up the hill. You had to know before you started up the hill whether you had enough gas to get up the hill or not. And also the bands on a planetary transmission. . . I don't know if you know what a planetary transmission is or not, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, Tm just learning about it right now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But anyway, you have a drum and you have a bunch of little gears that run a gear underneath. And as long as there is no pressure applied to that drum the power goes right straight through on it. But if you want a reduction gear on it, you got a band on

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the outside of it and you tighten that band and that makes those gears turn inside and then you get a lower gear. And you picked up the reverse the same way. Well, you start up a hill and it wasn't too uncommon at all that if your bands weren't tight enough, the bands would start slipping and they'd burn out and you didn't get up the hill and then it was a case of turning around and backing up -- use your reverse bands to get up. But Ford was very slow to . . . they wouldn't pay any patents. You see, Chrysler came out with hydraulic brakes in 1927. Ford waited until 1940 before they put hydraulic brakes on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just to keep from paying the patent on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And there was a lot of people killed because Ford was not willing to spend the patent money to put good brakes on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that any kind of national news at that time, that people were getting killed because of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, people knew it, but they didn't have lawsuits like they do now, you know. But the thing is, clear up until 1937, when the Fords put brakes on all four wheels, you had brake rods going to each wheel. They were 3/8 steel rods, and if you made a real hard stop those rods would stretch, and they all stretched different, so the next time you stopped you didn't know which wheel was going to take hold and which one wasn't. So you had to have a pretty good hold on the steering wheel to keep yourself on the road until you adjusted the brakes again, and many people weren't mechanically minded enough to ever adjust the brakes. So they virtually drove without brakes. By the time they got up to '36 and had the V-8's, well those V-8's would go 85 miles an hour and you couldn't stop them! Till the next county!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The same old kind of braking system with the steel rods and stuff?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And in '38 Ford came out with what they call a steel-draulic brake, which was cable brakes, with a self-energizing brake. Now a self-energizing brake is a brake that when the shoe comes out against the drum, the arms that the shoe is hooked to are made so that they feed into the drum at an angle, so when the shoe comes into the drum then these rods come out and give you much more braking power. And that's what Ford called their steel-draulic brake. And they ran that until '40 when the patents ran out on the hydraulics, and then they went to hydraulics.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. They didn't change their policy, they just waited until the patent ran out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They waited until the patent ran out and then they put on hydraulic brakes. So that was one of the things against Ford. So you didn't see that many Model T's in the . Model A's weren't too bad, Model A had a top speed of about 55 and generally stopped all right. But, boy when they got into those V-8's, they were dangerous. They were light and they were dangerous.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Model A's were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the V-8's. Before they put the hydraulic brakes in. In the '40s and '41s Ford really made a complete change, streamlined them and all that stuff. And then he sold a lot of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Got the American public's confidence.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But this area here then, we could guess that most of these guys might be driving older Chevrolets, and. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: An old Nash, or a Star, or that type of thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But probably wouldn't be seeing Model T's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not too many.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did any of the farmers use Model T's in their field or anything out here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Most of them used Dodges.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dodges?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dodges had a real slow speed motor with a big piston. They had a lot of power at low speeds and there was a lot of those that they made tractors out of. Oh, about 1940 or so, we're talking about a 1927, '28 model Dodge. There was a lot of those that were.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any farms around here still using steam?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They were all using gas powered tractors and horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mostly horses. When we moved here my dad borrowed money from the FHA and they would not finance a tractor. They said tractors were not the way to farm. So they financed our horses and we farmed with horses. My dad's brother had a Fordson tractor in Fullerton, California, and my dad took the old '23 Dodge truck and brought that Fordson tractor back up and we used it. And they were very dangerous because they had a worm gear in the rear end that drove the thing, and so when you got on a hard pull the front end came up off the ground and it'd come right on over if you weren't on your toes. Especially if you were going up a hill and the front end was already light and you would hook a rock or a stump, you could get killed. But we did farm that place. And that old worm drive had a lot of friction in it. My brother-in- law Orval Cummings came into the family along about then, and my dad had gone to work for Bill Coote by then, and so my brother-in-law and I, we were plowing the place there, and we were driving it 24 hours a day, and at night you could see the rear end was red hot. . . I mean there was that much friction on the rear end!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it just down a foot or two below you, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You were sitting virtually on it! It was hot! I mean it could be a cold night but it was hot sitting up on that tractor! Yeah, at night the exhaust system would all glow and everything, everything was hot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would anybody use International or John Deere?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah. Yeah. Same kind of a deal, they ran 24 hours a day around here. And the old Johnny poppers, they were of course noisy. You could hear them from 2 or 3 miles away all night long. And there was a lot of 1020 McCormick-Deerings around; that's what Mulkey farmed with, was 10-20 McCormick-Deering at that time. And they. . . the front ends on them stayed down a lot better than they did on the Fordson for some reason. I don't know why.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You say "Fordson." Is that common name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a Ford tractor, yeah. It was made by Ford, but they called it "Ford Son."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said that when they were building this road through here, Tampico Road, coming down from Smith Peak on the Berry Creek side where they've got that cutbank, that they used dynamite there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they used dynamite, and then they had a 60 Cat in here. And they called it a 60 Cat because it had 60 horsepower whether you needed it or not. And it was a diesel. They had a starting motor on it; they'd start the starting motor and get the Cat started. The blade was on the back so the guy running it was sitting with his feet one direction and his head the other one all day, and probably had a horrible kink in his neck, but that's the way they did it. And one interesting thing about this road going

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: up the hill here from the Berry Creek side, he ran into a spring about half way up, and it was always a pothole and they could never do anything about it, and they've still got that spring there; they've still got the pothole I've noticed since we've been working on this deal!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still now, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it's still there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that spring have a name or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. It just. . . it wasn't a spring until they dug it out with the bulldozer. Well they dug it out and it's been leaking ever since.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they just have the one bulldozer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know. It think there was just one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the county built that road through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The county, yeah, Benton County built the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But then, this road that we're sitting on here, the one that goes to the Chaffin place, this was here from.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Bill Coote probably developed this road, and when it got past his other road then it was just a buggy trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did they haul the logs down to this mill? Did they haul down to this road here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. This mill, of course, was closed before I came here, and apparently there wasn't any log pond here. The reason why I know is I've talked to Clifford Cornutt on the phone since we've been working on this. I was curious and I asked him. He says no there was no pond here. And I didn't remember any.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: T. Coote—Cornutt Sawmill #1

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've traveled south from the second Coote's mill site, and we've passed the first intersection, the one coming in from the gate on Tampico, and we're right at a little hill here on the east, maybe a quarter mile or half a mile from the second mill site, and we're looking west here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. That's where that mill was, was a quarter to a half a mile up the creek, the way I remember it. And then there should be a real steep mountain on the other side that we spoke about that Mr. Gardner's relation got killed trying to ride a log down the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that hill there to our west, somewhere down there they just. . . they had a log slide.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Log slide from up on top of the hill, because the hill was too steep to bring the logs down with horses on because the logs catch up to the horses, so they just turned them loose up there and slid them down into the bottom here. Now I thought I remembered that there was a mill pond that they slid into, but Clifford Cornutt can't remember it. But Clifford Cornutt, you have to realize, was only in 3rd grade when he left this country. So he may not remember as good as he might.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember a mill pond for sure, or is it just one of those things you're not sure?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just one of those things that I think I remember and he doesn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the log slide, then that would have been just right over mud, or right over dirt?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They actually laid some logs down and the logs slid in the logs. The logs guided them down, kept them lengthways so they didn't turn crossways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was just log guided, and then it was dirt. They didn't float in water or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, 1 remembered that they slid into a mill pond here at the bottom. Otherwise, I don't know how in the world you could get them into the mill, because you sure wouldn't want to be down there with a team of horses. You sure wouldn't want to get in there with a team of horses and pull those logs into a mill when they were sliding logs down at you! And to me a mill pond would be the only way to float the logs away from the stuff that was coming down the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could they have just yarded to a spot on top of the hill and then moved them down, ran them down the trough there for a while, and then stopped, and then yarded them out of there by horse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's kind of what Clifford Cornutt said, but I just, seems like I remember a pond slide there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would have been right where . . the hill had to be steep, and then Savage Creek was

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: down along the base of it, and that would be the site of the first Coote's mill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the site of the first Coote/Cornutt mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any old buildings or anything from that mill when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was nothing there except that log slide when I was there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And maybe a pond.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. The remains of a pond. But that mill had probably been closed five, or six, seven years by the time I got here, and all the timbers and everything . . . if Bill Coote didn't take all the timbers, well probably the farmers did. So there was virtually nothing there except kind of what we're finding, an old mill site, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Vine maple.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did this area in through here, had this all been logged off by that time, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I'm sure it had. We didn't go up very far before we were in virgin timber above that mill. I think they logged more off over here, to what I'm thinking is north, when they had that mill in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it go up and their logging kind of butt into Bennett Brothers logging?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well of course Bennett Brothers was a lot later and in my mind the Bennett Brothers was quite a bit west of where we are here. You know, when you're talking about logging with horses, a half a mile is a long ways!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And Bennetts is maybe two or three miles west of here, so their logging could have been totally separate.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'm sure it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and then this road here, the Chaffin Road, that came in off of where we were just sitting, it kind of goes up the ridge of that hill there? We're not on it anymore.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it went up the creek for quite a ways and then it veered off and went up on top of the ridge right there just below Chaffin's house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So it came from his house fairly quickly and came down to this creek. In pretty close order then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So where we were walking back there in that old road bed may have been the old Chaffin road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It could have very well been. But like I say, the Chaffin road was not a developed road, it was a buggy road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And then. . . so where we've been driving the truck along we haven't actually

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: probably been on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, I'm sure it wasn't this far from the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you remember anything else about that first mill site? Well, we haven't got it on tape, the story of how Gardner died.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, all I know is what the Cornutts told me, was that at quitting time one night, well I didn't know until I talked to Clifford who it was, but I'd heard that somebody got killed on that slide where they slid the logs down. What Clifford tells me is that they cut a log loose up there at quitting time and this Gardner he decided, "Well, I'm not going to climb down that hill," and he stepped up on the log with his caulk boots on and the log rolled and killed him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, was that Gardner, was it his brother or his son that had the place up here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Clifford didn't know. I asked him and he said it was a relative that was living with the Gardners up there. But probably, maybe living in the other house. There were two houses up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the Gardners have both houses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the Gardners ended up with both of them. Actually, there was some preachers. We always called them Two by Twos, I don't know what their religion was, but they believed that they were sent out, like Jesus sent out the disciples, two by two, and they were supposed to go out and knock on a door and ask if they could stay there. And they were supposed to be supported by the people and they were . . . if the people turned them down they were supposed to shake dirt off their feet and leave, and in the scriptures they were more or less condemned if they didn't welcome the disciples, and that's where this group started. Anyway, they lived in the Gardner's second house when I was here. For two or three months.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the name of the Two by Twos?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's all we ever called them, was Two by Twos. But they.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And there was two of them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was two guys. There was a Mr. Plum and a Mr. Larson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, Mr. Plum and Mr. Larson were the Two by Twos.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they only lived here for three or four months?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Three or four months. And they had a baptismal service down here and Mabel Tandy was one of them that was baptized. And also Edith Tandy was baptized at that time by these Two by Twos, and then after we moved over to Oak Creek, well one day somebody knocked on the door and here was Mr. Plum and Mr. Larson. They were starting to have meetings in the school house up there on Oak Creek. We didn't go the second time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have them come in and stay?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, they shook the dust off their feet at our house, because we felt that they were not scriptural. We . . . all of our family has pretty well studied the Bible and they were, as far as we were concerned, a cult. There's quite a bunch of those Two by Twos, I think that's the name they go by, up in Kings Valley today.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. The Burbanks. That's their religion.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they the ones that invited Mr. Plum and Mr. Larson here, or did they get baptized at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the Burbanks, I don't know whether they were later or earlier or what. But I met

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: a couple of Burbank boys at the Brand-S Plywood mill, they worked at the plywood mill for a number of years, and they lived over in Kings Valley, and of course that's quite a ways from here. So I didn't know the Burbanks at that time. However, one of the Burbanks was doing the logging for Bill Coote, I found from Donald Dickey, but there's a whole raft of them over there in Kings Valley. And I hunted with the B urbanks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you say a Burbank owned Bamm Hardware over there in Philomath?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's what I was told. No, a Bennett.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, from the Bennett Brothers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know whether it was from Bennett Brothers or not, but that's what I wanted to find out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, just a Bennett owned it, and you wanted to find out if he was related.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Somebody, I don't know whether it was Donald Dickey, or somebody told me that they thought that it was the same Uibe. But apparently they moved to eastern Oregon, now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So those Two by Twos only lived here for just a few months.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were just missionaries. They would preach in an area and then they'd go on. It's quite interesting, just a little side line, when we moved up here my sister was going with a guy by the name of Harold Jones, down in Los Angeles. And when we moved up here the school bus driver lived at our house, Al Fennell, and he was going to OSU. He lived at 9ur place and drove the school bus. So anyway, one day a guy came and knocked on the door and it turned out that his name was Harold Jones and he was a friend of Al Fennell's. And what had happened was that my sister wrote a letter to her friend Harold Jones in Los Angeles, and she put our address on it, Monmouth Route 2, and the mailman knew this Harold Jones and so they sent it him. So he thought he was invited over to our house because my sister had written and told him that he was foolish for coming up here because she wasn't interested and all that sort of thing. But at the end he said she was a glutton for punishment, if he came up. And then she says, "P.S. I got a haircut." Well, this Jones that didn't even know her got the letter. So he went upstairs with Al Fennell and showed him the letter and Al got a big kick out of it and came down on the landing and read the letter to my sister. She about died. Anyway, so we invited this Harold Jones to stay awhile, as long as he slept with Al, and so anyway this Harold Jones from California came so we had two Harold Joneses with us for a while! But anyway, what brought the subject up was later when I was hunting with the Burbanks, I found out that this Harold Jones had married one of the Burbank girls. And so I met him again after about 40 years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had he become a Two by Two?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, his wife was. I don't know whether he was or not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We talked about the Mennonites before. And the Two by Twos. But wasn't there a local man that went out preaching at times, too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of. The American Sunday School Union, most of the time I was here, had a Sunday School in Berry Creek School. But it was, for the most part, it was a case . . . now Donald Dickey's mother was my Sunday School teacher. And it was just a local deal, my mother taught, and my dad taught, you know. And it was mostly kids with adults teaching, was basically what it was. And every quarter or so we would have a missionary from American Sunday School Union, would preach a sermon and see how we were doing, and so forth. That was all the religion actually

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: that I know of in this area. We went to Airlie once in a while, there was an Evangelical church in Airlie. The Phelps preached there. And I got quite a bit of my Christian foundation from Mrs. Phelps. She led a class on Acts that was very informative to me, which of course is how the church started after Jesus died and so forth. And Saul meeting the Lord on the Jericho Road, and so forth, and so I got quite a bit of foundation from her. She was a one-legged woman. She was diabetic and they had cut her leg off clear to the hip.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you say "Evangelical," what do you mean by that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the name of the church, the denomination.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have anything unusual? They were like Presbyterian, or Baptist or just.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, probably closer to Presbyterian than what we have normally been. They believed in sprinkling, which we don't, and that sort of thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sprinkling as opposed to full submersion [Baptism]?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the Two by Twos?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They immersed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they use Berry Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They gave their baptism right there in our old swimming hole on our place in Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's what, 100 feet down from the bridge or so, somewhere in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, more like 300 feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Back of those blackberries.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah. You see the creek turns and then goes, went under Tandy's bridge and then came out into our place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody from your family get baptized there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Not at that place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just let them use the swimming hole.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And actually we let them use our house for a dressing room, changing room and so forth. I remember my mother saying that there was a woman that came to the baptismal service, and she was from the head office or something, and she must have drank 10 cups of coffee in an hour and my mother says, you know a lot of Christians talk about people that smoke, and she says, "All that coffee that woman drinks would be much worse for her than a little smoke!" You know, once in a while there's something when you're small or younger that just sticks with you and that always stuck with me. That woman drinking so much coffee, and my mother thought, "Boy that's terrible!"

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the woman from the Two by Two office and Mr. Plum and Mr. Larson, they'd lead the baptism?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there anything unusual about the preachings they gave or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think most of it was fairly fundamental except for their. . . I don't find anyplace in the scriptures that says we're supposed to carry on what the disciples did, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. So they took it pretty literally that they had to go out and do like the disciples did.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. There's a lot of religions that carry on. Like foot washing is fine, but we don't feel that it's necessary. Jesus washed the disciples' feet. But basically I think that's probably as much as I know about them. I sat and listened to their sermon, but there was nothing that was that. . . basically, in our religion, for the most part, unless it's in

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the scriptures twice we don't feel that it's something that we have to carry on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But if it's in there a couple of times then you do.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, then quite often. See, it only mentions that Jesus washed the disciples' feet once, and basically what it's saying is that humility, it's a lesson in humility, not in washing feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the Two by Twos, they took all that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They took all that stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have frimilies?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever know what happened to them after you moved to Oak Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. No, see, they were just like the disciples, no wives or anything. They were just two men traveling around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything about them personally, what they looked, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mr. Plum was short and fat and, who did I say the other one was?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Mr. Larson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, Mr. Larson was the short fat one and Mr. Plum was the tall skinny one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they dress all in black or anything, or just dress normal?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but I think they did wear stovepipe hats, if I'm not mistaken. But that may have just been their own choice, not necessarily a uniform of the religion.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're looking.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's possible we've got a pretty good hill right back this way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think we do, 1 think there's a steep hill right through there. And it looks like these berms that are in here just don't look natural, do they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not really. There is one thing you have to realize, this Savage Creek gets pretty savage. When we had a lot of rain right up . . . it's a short creek, and when it rains, it drains fast. And so these creeks get, Berry Creek and this can get pretty wild. And so you may be looking at, like that wash across there, you couldn't have crossed that in the high water. So that could be causing some of our unnatural landscapes here. Did you want to walk over and see if you can find that steep hill? I can probably get across the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, 1 just took a couple pictures of the berms down there. We're just upstream along Savage Creek from the berm, and right at the base of a steep hilt here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that's probably the hill that they slid the logs down. I called it a flume. I thought they actually had water running down between the logs and kind of halfway floated them down. And I had a picture of them landing in the pond when they got to the bottom. And where were standing here now, they could come off that hill and actually slow down before they hit the pond, and it's possible maybe we can find some evidence of where the logs might have slid on in, but more than likely that log chute would have kept them from making a trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've got a trail right where we're sitting here. And a high point up above us here. And this would be the headwaters of the pond. We can see some settling right there. It looks to me that there's some possibility we're right in the chute.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And we've got a nice level spot over on the other side for a sawmill. I have an idea that if we would climb this hill that we could find evidence of logging that they did

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: up on top. I know when I climbed this. . . I just climbed this hill once. And I was about, oh, 13 and I know I got Out of breath going up that hill. So it was a pretty steep hill, but I think possibly we've got a hill here that would qualify for that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this might be the first site here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. This is about the distance I remembered it. From the second mill site. Or from the school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you say you came up a road on the east side.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Came up a road on the east side, or I may be turned a little bit, I want to call it the south side. Southeast, I guess. But the road hung fairly close to the creek but not on the creek. And that was the road that went on up to Chaffins. From this point on it was just the Chaffin road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but we can say it's on the Smith Peak side. And then the Chaffin road went up the Smith Peak side and hadn't crossed over this creek yet.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember that it ever did. I guess it must have, huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe it went up above the headwaters and followed the ridge. It might not have.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Might be. See we went on . . . I think the creek stayed on the righthand side of us. And then we went up on the ridge and I think we went on the ridge maybe a half a mile, something like that. To get to the Chaffin place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now, over there on that side where you said would be a good place for a mill, it looks like there's some evidence of a depression right through there, like maybe

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, possibly where a log slip was going back up this way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they have hauled them out of the pond by horse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they would have a winch run by the steam engine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If that berm were there, we're on a fiat here, if that berm had been built out where we thought, then this would be about the extent of the pond right through here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Yeah. The mills quite often sat beside the pond, but more likely below the pond. You dumped your logs up at the head end of the pond and then you had. what they tried to do was turn the mill so that the back end of the mill was like this and the pond was in here. And then they just pull them off the side of the pond.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think we can jump across there pretty easy. [Crossing creek]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, let's walk up on the head end of there and see if we can spot anything else here. *** We're about 100 feet up the ridge in that one little grove. We can see some stumps off to the right here where there

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, this is all old logging in here. I'm trying to get a look. . . where I can see.. it's possible they put that chute down this ridge here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, that lines up with what we were seeing below.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So darn much viney maple here that you can't really get a picture. Those trees are getting higher and higher across here. That's the bank right there. And that's darn steep. He might have slid those logs down to this point, and hooked on to the trees down here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we've got plenty of slope here, they could still be going down hill, if they're pointing the right direction, right down that groove we've been walking up.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he shot them right down through here. Right down in through here. See that would have been pretty.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would come right here, and see where we've got the cut right down there? And line right up

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: with the pond site.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Because you see this is pretty steep to horse log, because those logs would come over the top of them. They were pretty touchy about logging down hill. 'Cause when that old ground gets wet in the wintertime it gets slick. We've gained quite a bit of altitude from the creek here already.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you spell viney maple with a "y" or an "c"?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, but I just say viney maple. I never did have to spell it. I would have called it "ie" if you hadn't asked me. Just to be different. Well, I'm pretty sure we're pretty well in to the. . . this is a pretty steep walk down through here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I think f we haven't located all three Coote's mill sites, we've come as close as anybody has. At least 50 years later.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I think so. I think we're . . . we can't actually pinpoint it, but I think we're awful close.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything else about this site? I think we got the names of all the mill families, and.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I just came up to this mill once, actually. And all there was was a log chute there then. And we went by it when we went up to Chaffin's place. But Clifford Cornutt and I, one day after school, climbed up to the top of that log chute.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that when he told you somebody had died on the chute?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now see right where we're coming through here, it would be the type of thing where logs could have been getting skewered, or thrashing back and forth, and it lines right up with where it looks like there might be a pond.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not only a pond, but also a level spot for a mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, and a mill spot, both.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course you can see on that number three mill how Bill Coote was trying to find a fairly level spot for his mill, so he didn't have to do the leveling himself.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now from up here, too, you can see that little basin in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and that's just the way we're coming down here.

entries.speaker: Q
