entries.text: We had to have at least six cars around before we had enough batteries to use it. It was just kind of a fun deal for the men to do while they were sitting around waiting for dinner or something.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your place was right here, and how about out in that direction there, looking east?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, this road coming up here, right there where it corners that was as far east as we went. Then we went over that way quite a ways.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who owned the land south of you, on Bald Hill there?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Knights.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It wasn't Knightson, it was Knights?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just Knights.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then down at the base were the Tortoras. Did their land go out that way, then?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Out toward Oak Creek.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: See our . . . we turned just about on the property line between Tortoras and us. And their property went back as far as ours did. And we had adjoining fences there, and one time I tried to ride down this hill on a bicycle and I sure got scratched up by the rosebushes. That wheel just slid all the way till I fell down.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now on Tortoras, from then towards town then, what was the next family out this way?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Knights came clear to the road here, and went clear back up on Bald Hill. And there was nothing at all on the other side of the road until you cross the creek. Then on one side of the road was.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The old homesteads there are Withams and Mulkeys. This is Johnson Mulkey's homestead is what you called Knight's place. In fact, Mulkeys formed a solid string here all the way out to Walnut Avenue.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is that right. Well there were some Bartons lived on the north side of the road just over the creek there, and he ultimately ended up having some mental problems, and he got pretty violent. He had 12 kids. And they just mostly raised horses and just kind of liked horses and I don't know how in the world they made a living. But Bartons lived over where Gilbert Ennis later lived. And they moved over here before we did. And Hubbards lived on the right hand side, just after you cross the bridge, in that big house there. And I believe they raised turkeys. Yeah, I know they raised turkeys, because we could hear them gobbling clear up here. And that's the only job I ever just flat out quit. He asked me to work for him one time and they were thrashing his wheat and he wanted me to get in the barn and mow the straw back. They were blowing the straw in off the old-time thrashing machine. And I got in there and I worked for about five hours and his straw was practically all . . . never thought I'd forget the darn stuff. . . dog fennel. And my eyes were about to fall out of my head and the pollen had got in my cheeks and stuff, and man I was just swelled up like a pup. And I climbed out of there and I says, "It's time you put somebody else in there and let me do something else." And he says, "If you can't do the job I give you, you
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: don't have a job." So I says, "Okay, I don't have a job. Pay me off, I'm going home."
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was dog fennel?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Do you know what dog fennel is?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nope.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh boy. It's a little short plant about this high usually. It's
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About six or eight inches high.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and it's got yellow flowers on it. And it's got. . . well, the plant is very much like a russian thistle, if you were ever in the country that has russian thistle, when they're green and small, they're similar to that. They're kind of almost like a fern, really, but they've got these yellow flowers, or white flowers with the yellow center in them.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do they look kind of like daisies?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they've got kind of a stinking smell to them.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why was he thrashing that up?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he was getting the wheat out of it, and then of course the dog fennel was blowing in the barn, he was going to feed it or use it for bedding or whatever in the winter time.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1 see. That was just li/ce a weed.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But all this country had dog fennel in it before we had herbicides. In the spring you'd see acres and acres of the stuff.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so that was just getting in there, it wasn't supposed to be there.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But I was sure hurting when I got through! Anyway, I'll tell you another little story about this barn if you've got a little bit of time. My dad didn't go for any foul language or anything. And he broke his leg, he was on crutches, and I climbed these cotton-pickin' hills and brought the cows down. And just as I got them down to the barn, it was in the spring, and the grass was good and they didn't want to go into the barn. They turned on me and ran up this cotton-pickin' hill. And I was working for another dairy, I got up at 2:00 in the morning, and went and milked cows for another dairy over there by Philomath, and I came home and I climbed the hill and got these cows. And it was probably close to 8:00 and when they turned on me I said, "You SOB's!" Only I said the words, with emphasis. And my dad says, "All right. You go on to the house, I'll take care of things." That was the only way he'd punish me was like this. And so he climbed that hill on his crutches, got the cows in, milked them by himself, and I sat in the house. And I felt just an inch high. I mean there was no way he could have punished me more. I never said that again. But that's the way my dad dealt with me. And I had a lot of respect for him and everything, but he never. . . his punishment was what, some people would say, "Oh boy, I don't have to milk the cows!" but that wasn't the way that it affected me at all.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that upset you towards him, or did you kind of admire him for going at it that way?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I admired him for it. It upset me to me, not to him. It was good punishment. For me to have to sit there and watch him climb this hill on crutches and get those cows back down and put them in the barn and milk them all by himself.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So how did you punish your children when you raised them, then?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I tried it but I wasn't as good at it as he was! No, I raised all my children, and I'm
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: very proud of them, my wife and I. And my method of raising my children was consistency. And my children, if I told them to do something and they didn't do it, I told them again, the third time I says, OK, come here and pull your pants down. They knew that third time was. . that was it. And they learned real quick and they never.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: after the first two or three of them got whipped the rest of them got told by the older ones and I never had to do it anymore. My youngest daughter, I never spanked her. Because the older ones told them. But if I was raising kids now they'd probably throw me in jail for it, because when I whipped the kids, I had a friend, who was a girl, who had her spine injured by her dad spanking her. And I weigh 250 pounds, and I was afraid I would do that. So I always spanked my kids with my belt. I doubled my belt and when it would hit them it would really pop. And it would raise welts, but it couldn't hurt them. But it worked. And it didn't hurt anybody. I mean, there was no chance of me hurting any spines or anything else with that belt doubled. But it did raise welts. Today, they'd throw me in jail for that.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think you're probably right. Times have changed.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And my kids, I'm proud of every one of them. All but one of them went through Bible School, two of them graduated from Bible School, and I'm proud of every one of them.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How do they raise their kids, more like your dad raised you?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they're sliding down the hill a little bit more. And their kids bother me to be around because I want to discipline their kids and I have to bite my tongue. But it's just one of those things, I think, that people get more lenient each generation and so forth. No, it's kind of interesting that with me. . . I did pretty well financially as I lived, and my kids never knew I had any money. I raised them.. . I didn't want them spoiled and I didn't buy all this stuff for them and all that. And they bought their own stuff, they bought their own cars and the whole works. I furnished cars for them when they went to college, but it was still my car. They could take it to college and stuff, but most everybody was quite astounded when I retired at age 56. Even my plant manager out there at the plywood mill, when I quit the plant manager said, "Well, what are you gonna do?" I said, "Travel." He says, "Well, how are you gonna do that?" I says, "Oh, I'll get by." And he says, "What, did somebody die and leave you some money or something?" I says, "No, I've been saving it for the last 35 years." But I didn't want my kids having the idea that dad's rich or anything and so what they got was pretty slim pickin's. The only thing was they got a lot of steaks and that sort of thing, because I always had them on the farm and butchered my own meat. And my son he didn't care all that much for steaks until he went to Western Baptist Bible School up here in Salem and got all the spaghetti and all that stuff, and rice and so forth, and so he told the kids, "Well, I'll go home and have some steaks for a change." They said, "You get steaks at home?!" We always had steaks! That's about the story of me raising my kids, I guess. Of course you know my daughter Mary, and they're all about the same caliber.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay what about the rifle range?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, when we get on down here darn near the. . . first I'll tell you this is our driveway and there were these trees here. That's where I was telling you the college kids made out all the time. Underneath the trees.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that have any name to it or anything, like Lovers Lane, or. .
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think it did to the college kids. We didn't call it anything. It was also, the
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: old road went over the top of this hill, and this road was clear out here. They used to get up on top of that hill there and make love.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Over here?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that little knob where the cut is. This was Knight's driveway here.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he have a bridge there?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. So anyway, I'd figure that pistol range goes right up here.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right across from Knight's drive.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And that's the old Barton barn there.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Which one? The one to the right?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The old barn there. The other barn wasn't there. And then that big house was big enough for their twelve kids.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did the Barton's live there?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. They lived there. . I believe that the Bartons owned that up until
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: about 10 years or so ago.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then this white house here, that was the Hubbards?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the Hubbards, yeah. And that's where I got all the dog fennel in my face.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was just very few farms up in this area at all?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was all. Then the college dairy barn.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the county fairgrounds still here at that time?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so. The fairgrounds was closer to town, I believe. I entered cows and chickens and stuff in the fair and I don't think it was this far out of town. I don't know where it was.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you don't recall anything else being built up around in here?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is the road I used to go milk those cows. I went out 54th and over on the old Philomath Road about a mile or so. South of what is now the Phiomath Road. And milked cows. It was a grade A dairy. And we had to be through milking by about 6:00 so he could get his milk into town to go on the milk truck to be delivered all over town. In the morning. You see in those days milk would last two days and that was about it because you didn't have refrigeration, you didn't have the bacteria killing abilities and all that stuff. And I imagine our bacteria counts were probably up in the millions, you know. And so they delivered the milk the same day they milked it. And we would milk, and we would put the milk cans in water, and we would strain the milk into the 10 gallon milk cans and cool it with water, and we would do the night's milking and the morning's milking and then they would take it to town and bottle it and get it to the customer before evening. Milk trucks all had ice, they iced the milk down in the milk trucks.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did . . . after you moved from this house here, where did you move to?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then we moved to LaComb.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now who moved into this place after you left, do you have any idea?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What did I tell you was the name of the people that we rented it from?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm not recalling their name right now.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not either.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But they moved back into it?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did they move while you were living there?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea. In order for us to rent that place we had to buy all their cows and some farm machinery and a whole bunch of stuff, and the Farm Home Administration,
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: that he had the loan with, they were the ones that found the place for us to rent. And so I think it was about February. So we moved in there and we bought their old cows and they were so skinny they'd have to stand twice to make a shadow. That's another one of my dad's sayings. And we just paid a whole bunch of stuff for nothing, you might say, my dad took their cattle and stuff to the auction and so forth. And we didn't have an airtight lease on it, so when we went to work and plowed the whole thing in the spring, and finally got it ready to plant it was too late, so we figured we got the ground all ready to plant this fall. Cranes was their name. And so in the fall they came in and said we had to be out of there by the middle of October. So we paid a whole bunch of money for absolutely nothing.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And did a lot of work.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. My dad really got shafted on that. But it was . . the administrator of the
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Farm Home Administration that. . . they were the ones that got us into it and responsible for it, but still we had to pay for it.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Cranes, did you ever see them again?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. There was only one thing that we got for nothing there. They had two high school girls and the mother and they were all redheads. And they had a whole big closet all full of, well what you'd call pornographic magazines.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mean the mom and the daughters did?
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And they left them there and I got to read them for a while till my mother realized what was going on. She got rid of them then. I still remember one of the jokes, something about a...
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I got the tape recorder going here.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you do! I won't tell you then!
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just tell me what kind of pornography they had in those days.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well actually it was more jokes and stuff than it was actually pornography. You know, I mean, like my brother says, the biggest thrill he could get was to look in Sears and Roebuck Catalog as far as pornography was concerned. And see the models with the bras on.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: More than any kind of material they were writing fbr people then.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they weren't writing. They were making jokes that were. . . had two answers to them, you know, and one of them would be dirty and the other one wouldn't be.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was kind of curious, I was thinking what's happened in my lifetime with pornography in the last 20 years, I couldn't imagine what they had in the '30s!
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But they had, I don't even remember, but I know my mother didn't want me reading It.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't know if want to end this actually talking about pornography or not. If th4-zt's the last thing we want in there.
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've told you everything I know!
entries.chapter_ref: Z. The Tortora House and Raising Kids

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part IV. October 11, 1991 Interview

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [interview with Neil Vanderburg, conducted at his home in Independence, Oregon, on

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: October 11, 1991 by George Wisner.]

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. Coote and Weinert's Sawmill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Neil when did you first go to work for them [Bill Coote and Cljfford CornuttJ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, let's put it this way, I went to work for them when I was about 14 which would have been 1937.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What mill did you go to work for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was up at the last mill [Coote and Weinert. Stop # ..].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would be on the east [south] side of the [Smith] hill there as opposed to Berry Creek- Savage Creek, whatever.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. The first mill was actually on Savage Creek, the first two were.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The first two were there and you worked on the other.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I worked up on top of the hill there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That is the one I am in reference to. Now you went to work there in 1932?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, 1937 or '38, right in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, what did you do for them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Actually I fed the planer. I don't even know if they had a planer when Weinert took it over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The mill was still owned by who at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I worked for Bill Coote.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bill Coote. What was Bill Coote like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Bill Coote lived right across the street from us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you say he lived across the street from us, what do you mean?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You mean where did we live?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ok, we lived coming down into Berry Creek from the north right at the bottom of the hill there. There is still a house there. Across the street, is the old Joe Smith house and he rented the Joe Smith house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, he lived out across the street from you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. The Joe Smith house is still there. Our house was moved by the government when Camp Adair came in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ok, what was your house like, was it a single story?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a wood frame, it was a five-bedroom home, 2-story, we had a full width front porch and back porch. Bob Zybach has got a picture of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He does, ok. Was the color white?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I am not sure what color it was. You know that was about fifty years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1 can believe that. How did you come to go to work for Bill Coote?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Because he was my neighbor across the street. Actually I was way below legal age to go to work. But one day somebody didn't show up for work, so he came down and asked me if I would go to work for him. I didn't ever have a real permanent job. He

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: would come and get me when he needed extra help cuz I was a pretty husky boy then, I probably weighed about 170 pounds then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was Bill like, can you kind of tell me a little bit about him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bill was a machinist really, and a mechanic. For my part, I think he was a pretty smart man along those lines.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he operate the mill by himself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well he started out, now we are starting out in the middle of the story actually. But he started out with his brother-in-law, his last name was Cornutt, and the first two mills were Coote-Cornutt mills. They were brother-in-laws and his mother-in-law apparently had the money that set them up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he have any brothers or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not as far as I know. He was always pretty poor. I remember one time ... the policeman came out there to their house to pick him up because he wrote a rubber check for a license for his car. [He had a brother, Alfred; sister, Gertrude.]
bracketed_corrections: He had a brother, Alfred; sister, Gertrude.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So many a time I knew him he wasn't all that wealthy. When he paid you he told you to hold it 'til Tuesday or whatever and that is kind of the way it went.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so cash flow wasn't all that great then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. But he was always happy. My dad had a couple of 24 inch pipe wrenches and he traded him 2,000 board feet of I x 6's for fence for those two pipe wrenches. My dad traded him on the basis of he could you use them any time he wanted to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Bill Coote own that land that he was logging on?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would doubt it, but I wouldn't know. You have to realize that I was just a young teenager then and basically I did more playing around than anything than I did working around the mill. See when I first came into the country I was still in grade school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did you work for him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Basically over a period of a couple of years but probably not over fifteen days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did they cut at that mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Railroad ties. We call all those mills in there tie mills. They would peel a fairly thick slab off of each side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this strictly railroad ties?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I'm just starting to say they were peeler, fairly heavy slab off. They sold the slab for slab wood and most of them were hauled into Salem for furnace wood and stuff like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Slab wood was used for furnace wood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was used for heat, yes. Banks used it and homes used it and so forth. Then after they took the slabs off of it then they would get one or two inch boards off the sides. At that time the railroad required a heart in a tie so this was ideal for what they call the tie mill because you take small log and you take a few 2 inch Cuts off it and then you have your tie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they log it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Teams of horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many teams of horses did they have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think there was three teams. They only used two teams, or two horses to pull a log.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was three teams of two horses roughly?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did those horses come from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Farmers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All over the area or one particular farmer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty much all over as far as I know. I know Forrest Tandy had a team up there. I think the Dickeys had a team up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Mr. [Tom] Stephenson said something about a guy who had horses at the mill who would go to a firm up on the hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: 1 never worked in the logging.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they cut the timber?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: With a Swede fiddle [crosscut saw].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Two-man buck saw?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. You were falling with a two-man buck saw but you didn't cut them up with a two-man buck saw. It was the same saw, it was a quicker saw, the same length, but only one man ran it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many men worked at that site out there as you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In the mill where I worked there would be. There was a pond monkey, and he pulled the logs up into the mill. You had your sawyer who was the guy that decided how the log was going to cut. Then you had your ratchet setter that set the depth of the cuts. The 2 inch stuff dropped into an edger, which made 2x4's, 2x6's or whatever out of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The edger operator, was he a special person, a separate edger operator?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have anybody there to fire the boiler?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, that's what Stephenson said he did. He was a boiler firer he said.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He would know more about that than I would. But when they built that mill up there at first we had an old steam tractor that they ran it with.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are we talking the same site or are you over on the Savage Creek sites?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The same site.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Same site. Can you tell me a little bit about how that operated, type of machinery they had there like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, now I wasn't there when they moved that steam tractor from down on the bottom of the hill up. But Clifford Cornutt was my best friend, and he told me about them guiding that tractor up there, up the hill. They did it just in the late evening and that was before that road went through that you can now drive on. There was no road up there at that time. He said that when they ran that tractor up there at it was dark. He says you could see fire from that thing all over, fire and steam, going up that hill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What time of year did they move it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, they moved it before I moved in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I played in two old mill sites as a kid. 1 was in grammar school when I moved there and we used to go and play in the old mill sites. But that mill was there just before we moved there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the mill was there before you moved there. Was there one to move the tractor to, in otherwords the one you worked at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The one they moved the tractor to was the last mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. They used that steam tractor at the other mills as well?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Now you spoke of some concrete deal there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was a couple of arched fire boxes. There were two fire boxes in the mill and the old arch and brick and sitting on top of that sat the boiler.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Shortly after that mill was put up there, it burned down. And that was how Weinert got involved with it. It sounds to me like you had a different fire box then what the mill had before it burned down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this would have been a fire box that came later?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Because the old steam engine, I mean it was a boiler and so forth on four wheels. You just drove it up there and actually they used the steam engine with a great big pulley on it and that's what run the mill. I mean the whole thing was all that tractor. Line it up with the pulley and put blocks under the wheels and fire her up and Start pouring the steam to it. That's the way they ran the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That ran what?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That ran the whole thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what was the whole thing, you had the edger, the planer and...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What we call the head rig. I don't know how much you know about saw mills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I know a little bit but not a whole lot.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: After the edger was the trim saw. They cut the length on the trim saw. That was my dad's job. It sounds to me like they put in a different boiler after it burned.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That may well be it, when did it burn, do you remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would guess about 1938. Bill hadn't got it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It burned shortly after you started working for them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anything about that fire?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't know anything about it 'til the next morning.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was there to burn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The whole mill was on a wood frame.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. What did the wood frame look like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: 6 x 6's, you could walk underneath it. The conveyor went underneath the whole unit, and after the sawdust burner and so forth, but I can't remember for sure. But I imagine down at the head rig, probably there was 10 foot of clearance up to the head rig, and the conveyor went uphill a little ways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The platform, was it an enclosed platform or did it just have pole sides and a shingle roof or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was enclosed the way I remember it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have a shingle roof?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it had a tin roof. I know that Bill Coote told me that if he would have had one more bucket of water he could have got the fire out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did they get water from up in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You see they dammed that and made a mill pond and all the logs were dumped into the mill pond. Then they were floated over to the mill and pulled into the mill. So you had a mill pond, so even though the creek was pretty small, over a period of time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You had plenty of water backed up there to use?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But I don't think Bill Coote had a pump or anything for pumping water for a fire.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was a bucket brigade?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he was the only one there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He was there when the fire started.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he was doing some welding or something of that sort.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there anything in the papers at the time on the millfIre out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We couldn't afford papers in the Depression, we didn't know what a newspaper looked like hardly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay you don't [knowI of any newspapers at all? What was wages like out there for you guys?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think probably around 35 cents.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: An hour?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Boy, Tom Stephenson gave me a figure of $2.50 a hour for his job. [That was actually his daily pay. J. W.J He said he was real well paid.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'd say he was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was a lot of money for the Depression.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he ... well if he was there when Weinert was running it and maybe they got up that high. I don't remember him and he may have come quite a while after I did. In 1940 1 was working for a shingle mill and I was getting 97 cents an hour and that was big pay. So I would say that he was in there at the start of the war if he got those kind of wages because that was big wages.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's a lot of money.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know anybody that made that much money at that time to be quite honest with you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Anybody live out at that mill site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a building there? Stephenson said something about a caretaker's shack was there, and the caretaker lived there off and on.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There may have been after the fire.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but before the fire there wasn't?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do they know how the fire got started?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah I think that Bill Coote was pouring a bearing or something like that and a spark got in some sawdust.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You say pouring a bearing, what do you mean?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well in those days we used babbit bearings. You took those hand molders, something of that sort, and you had your cast iron bearing then you poured the hot metal inside of it, you filed it down to fit the shaft and put the top on it. I never did pour a babbit bearing, I was a millwright all my life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So basically it was a result of a fire?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That would be my guess, I don't think Bill ever did any welding. He did a lot of forge work.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have a forge out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I am sure he did, but I can't remember where it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we found what I think is the top of the old forge, I think. You haven't been out to the site, have you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We didn't find it. We were down the creek a little ways from it, probably 200 feet from it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why I want to take you out and have you walk the ground.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That might bring some memories back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Take me through a day out at that mill when you were out there. What time did you go to work and what did you do?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the whistle blew at 8 o'clock in the morning. All the mills had steam, and we had steam whistles going all over that country. 8 o'clock in the morning, one would be a little ahead of the rest. In those days they had what we call the strattle bug that they moved your lumber with and you have probably seen them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Big straddle carriers. Well, actually they were used for carrying amunitions in the war.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were used before the war. What you had was a block about this long with some steps in it. You stacked your lumber on that and then you drove a scrattle bug. He [driverj had some levers up there that he swung an arm in underneath the loads to pick them [lumber] up. The later ones had the shoes on the side and they picked up the lumber.
bracketed_corrections: driverj had some levers up there that he swung an arm in underneath the loads to pick them [lumber

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Up from the side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but the original ones he also had, they stacked their ties and stuff. They came out with rollers on the flatbed trucks and they could back these flatbed trucks under the loads and not have to man handle them. There was no fork lifts or anything like that so they had to. The road came in underneath the loads. Then he just had a roller on the back of his truck, rolled the load onto his truck and bound it down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the road like to get in there? Was it a dirt gravel roads, plank or what?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course when we first moved there we were on the Berry Creek side but the road didn't go through over to Tampico and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did the road go at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The road came in from the Tampico side to the mill. That road when you are coming up the hill from the Tampico side. ..just before you got to the top, the road took off from the present road and went kind of west and stayed in the bottom of that draw. You can still see remains of that old road in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a plank road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, what did they use for planks?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of trucks came in to haul this stuff off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were all Chevrolets and Fords and of course in '37 the new one was a '37 and there was even Model A Fords came in there, 4 cylinder.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kinds of a dam, can you tell me a little bit about the dam structure they had there, is it an earthen dam?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was a lumber dam. It was built out of lumber and it did leak a little bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How do you build a lumber dam? Is that just kind like tongue and groove?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They just threw logs across the creek there and put boards vertical in it. When they swelled up, they were tight.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, about how much water did that hold?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't the vaguest idea. It seemed like a big mill pond to me but I doubt if it was any where near as big as I remember it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were around when the mill burned, in terms of being in the area that is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You went up there afterwards, what did you see?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't go up there afterwards not until they were rebuilding it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When they rebuilt it do you remember what they rebuilt up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not at all. My dad worked up there after they rebuilt it, but I never went up there after it was rebuilt.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did this thing come about with Weinert?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, Weinert owned the Airlie store. Bill had just got his first mill going good and it burned. So Bill kept some of the crew on that was good help and built the new mill. He got credit from old John Weinert at the store to feed these people. So what it amounted to was it was loaned to the individual men, but Bill Coote signed the voucher. So that went on for about three days and old John Weinert came up and said this is my mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He just took it over for payment on the bill and that was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well he had gone through legal channels and everything. What he did, he forced Bill Coote into bankruptcy, and then he was assigned, anyway, given the job to supposedly get Bill out of it. Where it ultimately ended up with was he said that Bill never paid, so Bill Coote was out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, what happened to Bill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well now Donald Dickey who was up there, did you see the book on Donald Dickey that Bob's [Zybach] got?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah I've seen that one.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've got a copy of that, my name is on that book also. But anyway we went and interviewed Donald Dickey and Donald Dickey stayed in touch with Bill Coote clear up until he died I guess. But to me he just disappeared. But he had a machine shop on the north side of Dallas and farm work and stuff you know, sharpening ground shears. He was good at it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did Weinert operate the mill? Did he go into the logging business then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, his son is still a big logger over in the Eddyville country.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That is John Weinert. John Weinert took the mill over and was it John Jr. that worked there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: John Jr. now has a helicopter and logs with a helicopter over somewhere around Eddyville [Weinert was part owner of a mill that operated in Eddyville after \VW II known as the W.O.W.Weinert Oudekirk, and Weinertmill. It had ceased operations by the early 1970s].
bracketed_corrections: Weinert was part owner of a mill that operated in Eddyville after \VW II known as the W.O.W.Weinert Oudekirk, and Weinertmill. It had ceased operations by the early 1970s

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The old man has retired.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The old man would be dead by now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I know he is, but John Jr. is now retired.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah I suppose.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He is living over in Hawaii, I talked to him afew weeks ago, he says he can't remember anything about the mill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is that tight!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Either he is not talking or not remembering.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was going to college during all that stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Weinert was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, John Jr.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so he came up and helped around the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Junior, I never saw him around there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So strictly John, Sr.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: John Sr. ran the mill and of course John Sr. was still around the grocery store there at Airlie for a number of years, and the mill both.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember how long that mill continued to operate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't tell you that, we left and moved over to LaComb in '42 and we actually left before the war took it over. There was some Sort of a deal. We had a loan with the Federal Land Bank and Federal Land Bank knew the government was taking over so they kicked us out before the government took it over so they could get the whole thing. Otherwise it would have had to divide what the government allowed for the farm. There were several of us in there put arrears on our payment and all. They just kicked us out so they got title.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you work with Weinert at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, my dad did but I didn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Back to the mill site itself when you were working there can you describe for me how that edger worked and what kind of machinery you had there with that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The edger was nothing but a machine about this wide with blowers in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That is about 2 1/2 feet wide.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And these rolls feed the wood. Then there was, I would say, probably 6 saws in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So rolls feed the wood. You mean just flat rolls like regular rollers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, then the edgerman just fed the wood into rolls and then it just took the wood through.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the saws were they set up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were set up side by side. Then they would slide on the shaft. The edgerman had numbers on a plate in front of him. For what he wanted to saw he would just slide these saws back and forth for whatever he wanted, 2 x 4's, 2 x 6's, 2 x 8's, 2 x 10's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then if he wasn't using all the saws he could shove them clear over to the left. If he just wanted to make 2 x 12's, he just used two saws. But if he wanted to split, make a whole bunch, maybe he wants to make 3-2 x 4's, well he is using four saws.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this a brand name edger of any kind or just a home built kind of thing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a brand name but I can't give you the name of it. My dad worked off-bearing the edger and trimming. So he worked with the edgerman quite a bit. If the edgerman had any problems, well my dad came around the edger and got these..

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any of the names of the fellows that worked there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can picture them, but I can't come up with

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Take me for a walk through the other machinery then, describe that tractor for me, was it a John Deere tractor or what was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You never saw a steam tractor?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, I have seen them. But I can't remember what kinds they had or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There is a whole bunch of them out there by Woodburn, you know. They were just the same as those were.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have a name to them, regular name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I am sure they did. There was a Waterloo or something like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They had large steel wheels on them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They were used, the old tractors. After the gasoline tractors came in and so forth, they were used in prune dryers and any place that you might want steam. This

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: was the situation. I worked in a shingle mill in the early 40's and we ran our shingle mill with an old steam tractor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they get water into that steam tractor, did they put it in by hand or did they pipe it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I worked with steam quite a bit myself in my millwright work. You have to have a pump to pump into a steam engine because you were putting water with virtually no pressure into a boiler with 120 pounds in it. So you have the steam pump. What it amounts to is a cylinder run by steam. It pushes a smaller cylinder, it pushes the water into the little series of valves so that it just goes one way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the water was then piped to that steam engine and it came from the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, gravity.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About the head rig, what did that consist of2

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well you had a saw on the top and a saw on the bottom that didn't quite match up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Circular saws?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Circular saws, yeah. For the most part those logs there didn't ever reach the top saw because they weren't big enough, just on the butt. Where you did, you had a step in your lumber because the saws couldn't match up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In other words, if a log was too big the top saw kicked in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The top saw kicked in and cut it off, usually it was just on the butt, swell butts.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You had the planer, what did that consist of?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You know I don't know much about the planer even though I ran it. Of course, they had planer knives in them. Basically it was a deal where it was a bit like the old lawnmowers only the blades came around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you describe one of those blades for me can you tell me a little bit about those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I might be able to find you a planer blade.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is it just a piece of steel that's cut blade shape, how long are they, about a foot and a half long?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were about 16 inches long something like that. They were considered real good metal for making butcher knives out of when they were wore out. Everybody wanted them for butcher knives.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there any other machinery on the site there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I can think of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Anybody doing any drinking out on the site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That part I wouldn't know. I was too young to drink at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I found some old Acme beer cans.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I have an idea there was some beer drank one thing or another. In fact I think I know one guy that probably threw those there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, what was his job out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he pulled the green chains.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's sort of what Stephenson said too. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That whole mill had to be up in the air quite a ways. Like the guy that took lumber from my dad, he flipped the lumber down just a sliding deal onto the green chains, he had a 6 foot drop from where my dad was down to the green chains. They had to pull the green chains. They stacked that lumber so the truck could get underneath it. So you are getting up fairly high there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there other men that weren't loggers and fallers that cut the timber up on the hill around there, hook it to your teams, drive one log at a time down put them in the ponds? Did you have a cable system or any series of dogs to bring the lumber up from the ponds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a cable system that brought the logs in. They would roll the logs into the pond with a peavy because they couldn't get the horses too close to the edge of the pond in the first place and they couldn't take a chance on the log pulling the horses in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Peavy, is that one with a hook?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They would roll them into the pond and then the pond monkey would line them up with the head rig and he would probably have four or five of them lined up ahead all the

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The sawyer? He operated the head rig entirely? Is that all he did?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he was the brains of the outfit, more so than the other man.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The guys, did they have to maintain their own machinery? Did you have a millwright out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bill Coote was the millwright pretty much when I was there, he did all the saw filing. See in those days you didn't have carbide tips so you filed the saws every two hours. What they did on the head rig, the teeth were removable. So at coffee break, we took a coffee break not because we needed the coffee but we needed the down time. They had a deal and they just roll these teeth out and roll new ones in and away we went again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did they do with the teeth, just leave them lay?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Resharpen them. He would sharpen them while the mill was running.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you did that how many times a day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Four times a day.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did the men get to work in that Site? Did they come from long distances or did most of them live in the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were all local farmers, most of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Stephenson said he lived in an old boarding house, there was a farm right down the road there a ways.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That would have been on the other side of the hill, that must have been on the Tampico side. My mother boarded two men for awhile but that was way before he was there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't know if he's talking day or hour but he's saying hour, that just sounds like a lot of money to me for that period of time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: See, 15 cents an hour was pretty common. That is what farm hands got. Getting $2.00 a day for 10 hour day. Its clear out of line, I don't think that mill ran long enough for him to get that kind of money is what I am sayin'. I think Camp Adair took it over before he got anywhere near what he said.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I guess the government took it over not long after that and shut everything down.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It got Weinert started in the timber industry, the government paid him enough. Of course, the government may have let him run it for awhile because they needed lots of money to build Camp Adair so I don't know when they shut it down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would that lumber go after you folks milled it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I am trying to remember just what the deal was but I worked for, I think I did work for Weinert for a little while, and he hauled the lumber to Suver and had a planer at Suver. I think he planed it over at Suver.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any kind of planer set down at Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never was in at Adair, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay that is where it was at that time, so you are talking the same planer probably. Stephenson mentioned one at Adair.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That would have been at Suver.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Suver was Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Suver was part of Camp Adair. Suver was a railroad siding for years and years and years. There was the church there. There was the Town Hall there, and they held dances in the top.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was a pretty big town then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah. They had a grocery store and they also had a couple service stations there but not where the ones are there now. Al Flickinger had one on the southwest corner of that intersection and he became the big gas dealer in this area and then Camp Adair made him move kittycorner across the street.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you recall how much wood a day they were planing there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't have the vaguest idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Five days a week?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Whenever Bill Coote had orders and whenever the mill wasn't broke down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any particular problems in the years, time you worked at that mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: in that mill also we were also shut down for dry weather because it was up in the timbers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now lets go to the other side of the hill over on the Savage Creek side over there. Bob fZybachJ and I went back in that mill yesterday, we found what appears to be part of the old platform and there is a whole lot of timbers and stuff over there. Did that mill have a plaorm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well it was up above the ground like the other one for sawdust removal. All that stuff and was probably 2 planking that the men worked on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was a similar type of set up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. You had the catwalk, or the walk where the guy worked from the head rig over to the edger, and then out past the edger and rolls out to the end. So you would probably have a 60' catwalk there of varying widths.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have substantially the same equipment down there as up on the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All the equipment that was there was up on the hill when I moved there. That was just a place for us kids to play when I moved there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It still pulled all the timber would have been pulled from right there in that immediate area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. That's why they moved the mills. You see in those days you built a mill and sawed the timber out around it that you would pull in with horses, and then you moved the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that is substantially what they did on all those mill sites?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 2. Bennett's, Cooper's, and Ford's Sawmills

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you work at any other mills out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bennett's mill. When I was fourteen, my dad had an old farm truck and I took a contract from them since I wasn't old enough to work. He sold me the slab wood for 50 cents a cord and I loaded it at their mill, brought it down to the county road and stacked it, and Jack Green paid me a $1.25 a cord for it down at the county road. So I made 75 cents a cord. You were asking how much lumber Weinert put out. They put out 4 cord a day at Bennett's mill in slab wood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh wow. Was Bennett's mill primarily a slab wood mill or what did it..?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a tie mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember how many railroad ties either Coote or the Bennett's cut?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't the vaguest idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How much dimensional lumber did they put out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well actually they put out more dimensional 2" lumber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know where those ties were going?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just the railroad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they took them wherever they took them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But they called it a tie mill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got that one [Zybach's earlier interviews with Vanderburg] and I am going to incorporate some of that plus some of what we are talking about here. Because I think I am getting into a little more detail on the mills then he did. When we go over the actual site and look at the mills, look at the site out there, I am probably going to go into a lot more detail with you and see the whole picture.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Will you have a key available to get in with a vehicle?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. I'll have a key to get in to two mill sites down on Savage Creek, I can get into there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course you can walk in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, once you get down there and then you can walk into the other one. The other one is not far off the road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah I know but Bennett's is a couple of miles from there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah that's a ways in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And Cooper's mill is quite close to Bennett's mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay we went up to those, I was up to those this week.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh were you, Bob take you up?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. There isn't a whole lot there. That upper mill at Coote has a lot of stuff, and I'd really like you to see that one.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah I want to see that. I am sorry I didn't keep walking. But we came to that flat spot, the ground there, and it was just about where I figured it was. We stopped and I shouldn't have. I told Bob right at the start, we were coming up from the Tampico side, and I told Bob that road took off to Coote's mill right at the top of the hill and went back. We went in the old road, the old slab road, tram road, and I found that spot. It had some characteristics of where the old mill was. So we looked around there and we found a little bit of evidence but not much. Then we came out. When we came out, we were still south of the top of that hill, where we came out so I was scratching my head. But we seemed to be coming out an old road there, but we didn't come out where I thought we should have.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you work at any other mills up there on the OSU Research Forests?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those were the two you worked at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the only thing you did for Bennett was haul the slab wood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What years did you do that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gosh I don't know, I don't think that Bennett Mill was in there more than about six months. But that would have been close to '40 because they were logging with an Allis Chalmers cat and they didn't have a mill pond. They were pulling three logs at

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: a time with the cat and then they were pushing them up pretty close to the head rig and then pulling them in with a cable, they weren't floating them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many people worked up at the Bennett Mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Three brothers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Three Bennett brothers. Do you remember their names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they own that land there or were they just millwrights?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No I think they just bought the timber. I think they probably went broke, I don't know because they didn't stay long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was a pretty risky business in those days.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why was that? Just because of the Depression?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well yeah. How would you like to sell lumber for $10.00 a thousand. That's what it sold for then $10.00 a thousand for 1 x 6's for $10.00 a thousand.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Couldn't make a whole lot of money that way.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, even though you weren't paying much for help, that's another reason why I don't see any possible way that they could have paid that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It seems way out of line to me but I wanted to come and check.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would guess it was more like 35 cents an hour. After we moved from there and went up, my dad worked for Ford's mill which is the Ford in Roseburg now. He started up at LaComb. And he was just as poor as old Bill Coote was. He had Ford logging trucks because Ford gave him credit for them. But anyway, my dad got 35 cents an hour when he was working at the Ford mill in 1942. That was pretty darn good pay by 1942, the war was already going by then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then they were paying a little better?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Because they had them? Do you remember any more about that Coote mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: .they put that..one thing that might be of interest, there was two reasons why they put the road through from Berry Creek over to Tampico. One of them was we moved in there and we had two high school kids all the time. The bus had to come around by Suver and come through Polk county and back into Benton county because we just barely lived in Benton county. So it was making a lot of extra busing to pick up my two sisters to take them to high school. By the time I went to high school they had that new road through. That and Bill Coote's mill were the two things that made the county put that road on through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How far away is Suver, about five miles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Six miles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That pretty much ought to do it for this.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't find the little piece of that first Coote mill but they had a, they logged their logs down a ridge and then they ran them down a shoot with water in it and that shoot was real steep and I did quite a bit of calling on this deal I did for Bob. I got ahold of one of the Cornutt boys and I asked him I says I heard that somebody got killed trying to ride a log down that shoot one time. He says, "yeah" he says that was. Mr. Gardner's brother.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I think I remember that in his report. in Bob's story, / think I remember you talking about that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But I have not found the hill steep enough. I climbed that log shoot when I was in

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: grammar school with old Clifford Cornutt.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there still a log shoot there then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah there was still a log shoot there then, we climbed up it and it was steep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That is the one now at the early mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the first mill. And I tried to find that in the pickup. I wasn't satisfied with the location Bob and I came to, and so I rented a plane and I flew over it and I couldn't find it flying.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still couldn't find it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but I am not satisfied with the terrain that I am finding there. I walked up to the old Chaffin homestead and Bob was completely amazed because I told him about how they had this big 60 acre meadow and all that stuff, and he knew about where it was. I was just going by the seat of my pants by the terrain, and we got up in the area there where I thought it was and there was all these trees this big around in that meadow, that grass meadow. Shoot, they are just about 3 feet in diameter and that was a grass meadow when I was there and naturally seeded with kind of adverse conditions.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That is kind of a big growth then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, people think that we are cutting these big trees and are gone forever. In my lifetime up there, there is a lot of stuff that we logged that has been logged again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Grown back over. There is a lot of big trees, lot of windfall on that upper Coote site and just a lot of big trees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bob asked me one time, he says he wanted to know what we did with the old growth. And I told him that an old growth as far as us oldtimers are concerned is a breed of tree. I showed him some there that weren't that big around, but they got real deep bark on them and that's where it gets the old growth is the growth of the bark. And I showed him some on that Bill Coote site there, some old growths that were like this. But see I have made lumber for the railroad for the inside of the box car and they required 18 grains to the inch. So you see these little trees with this heavy bark took them 18 years to grow an inch. So that's an old growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, that would be.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But now anything that's 3 feet is an old growth but that is not true.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ain't necessarily so?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So anyway that might be of interest to you.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 3. Suver

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Specifically where are we at right now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well this is the town of Suver. This is where the city was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is the center railroad tracks just east of Highway 99 and Richards Store, about a quarter ofa mile.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is Suver and there used to be a, right here on this corner, there used to be a kind of a City Hall, they had dances and stuff. It was two story, and where you see your siding right there, Willamette Seed and Grain has taken that over. Right in here was where the planer was on this side of that siding.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The planer was on the west side of the rail siting here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did the planer Consist of?

chapters.title: The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bill Coote just hauled his lumber out here, ran it through the planer and into the box cars and trains took it off wherever it was going, 2" dimensional lumber.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about the railroad ties?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well they went from here too from this siding.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did you work here?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh probably '38 or '39 right in there. I just worked here a couple of days. They transported me over here from the mill. I knew about the siding because I came down here. They had church meetings and stuff like that.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What all was here at this particular siding, there was the planer mill and what was around it?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was all that was here that I remember. There was a loading dock there and the planer. As far as the siding was concerned, they also shipped grain. Farmers used it. It was actually originally a farmers siding.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay we are now about a quarter of a mile north of the pre-existing road, the initial road into the Coote mill site. Neil, tell me about this road and what it was at one time?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I am pretty sure that this was a gravel road going in here, I think there is actually about enough gravel in the soil that we just graded it and there was gravel they got to airight.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this road was put in when roughly?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, let's see, we moved here in '35, I would say '31, 1938.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, it was put in when, when the Berry Creek road was put in?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When the Berry Creek road was put here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This leads directly to the mill site, right?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I'm pretty sure it was not a tram road.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We are now on the Coote Mill site and we are standing in front of a large cylindrical steel framed object. Neil, what is this as best as you can determine?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would call it the shell around the boiler that had the fire in to heat the boiler.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is not part of an old steam tractor then?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is it part of a steam donkey of some kind?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. It could be. But that is the fire box there.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is the fire box.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Here's the door where you stoke the wood in.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay he's pointing at a square opening on the top side of this metal object. How would you describe the plate? is it boiler plate, steel or what is it?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No that's just a burner. It is about as thick as it ever was. I would say that this has rolled over. That door would have been on the side probably not on top. If you had a good hot fire in your boiler, you'd open that door. It would singe your eyebrows with it on top.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This goes back to a point then, like a wigwam burner?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. It just collapsed, it would have been the same all the way back, a cylinder.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
