entries.text: Describe for me this platform here again, what do you think it is?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I'm sure that's where the old steam engine sat. Whether it was the old steam
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: tractor or whether it was a steam engine. But those stakes is what they could run over to the mill with it.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Three pipes in the ground at the end.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course they are all kind of loose now. This is all decomposed in here, but certainly it was very possible if you pull one of those stakes up. It has rusted off down there.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, you would believe a steam tractor engine was on top of there.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Originally Bill Coote ran this with a steam tractor. My dad worked here after the mill was rebuilt, but I didn't. It is possible that that steam tractor was ruined in the fire, or they still could have used it. But they do have a burner here for heat. It could be they ran some steam pipes in here to help the steam tractor along, I don't know. When I was here, the old steam tractor sat in here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How large a platform would that have been?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The steam tractor would probably have been pointed to the south rather than what you are thinking of with the north. It would have been backed in here. Then those pipes would have been behind it. This would have been the platform where they fired the boiler. Then they would have had their wood stacked back in here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Describe this babbitt bearing for me, would you? How it would have been used?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well what they did, I never did pour a babbitt bearing. I worked around them quite a bit. But what they did, they had a ladle and they would put, well it was basically kind of a lead. They would put it in the forge and they would heat it until it was liquid. This thing here, they would put ends on it and put a shaft in it and then they would pour the babbitt around it. But they would put something on the shaft so it wouldn't stick to the shaft. Then when they got it poured then they pulled the shaft. They had a tool, I can't remember what it was called, but it was kind of round a little bit like a round wood chisel. It was sharp on the sides, and they would fit that with that tool. It was no small job to pour a bearing. I mean by the time you poured it and then you cooled it and then you ... it was not a small job.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is kind of the mold for the babbitt bearing then, this is half of the mold?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, because the babbitt stayed in that, you put that on the, you held the babbitt bearing with that.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, how was this attached to the shaft?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a deal that fit over the top of it with four bolts. It came through it from the bottom and the half was pulled down.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mean they were just bolted down with nuts?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and long bolts. Probably the bolts went through the wood frame of the mill, those bolts were probably 10-15" long that held that bearing down and went through...The thing that they did, another thing they did when they poured these, they put shims in them, on the sides. When it started to wear, they could start taking these shims out and tighten it back up again. They could make that bearing run quite a little longer by taking shims out. Cars up until about 1930 had babbitt connecting rods, and they were poured the same way. Then they came with the inserts and they had babbitt on them, on the surface of them. Later, they came to the stainless bearings that we have today.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The babbitt was what kind of metal, just poured iron?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No it was lead, it was soft. That was the reason why they could work it. Also, if that bearing went out. Most of these shafts around these mills were at least 60' long. If
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: you had a steel bearing on there and that went. You would gaul [score] the heck out of that shaft. You would be replacing 60' shaft and taking all the bearings and everything off of it, and all the spools and everything. So they would rather have the babbitt go out than the shaft.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The babbitt bearing was then expendable?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Compared to the shaft?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, by far.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's move over to some other pieces of equipment over here, we are moving to the east. We ran across a wood supported piece of tin in a semicircle, what would you describe this as?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My guess, it is purely a guess, but I've used them and that would be the mold for fitting new bricks in the boiler. Now the ones I have always used, you worked from the inside and you had a convex. But this looks like the angle of the boiler. You take and lay your brick mortar and lay your bricks in here as far as it goes then move it and glob it up and put in another batch of them until on both sides you get to the top and you put in the key brick or the key stone. That's my guess.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now looking a conical topped metal piece to the north of the boiler, Neil how would you describe this, what's its purpose?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say it was a suction cone to pull the sawdust off the head rig. It is way out of place from where it belongs. It should be down there by the creek, because it should have been on the main mill. But the mill has been down for a long time and things have been moved around. I am sure that's what it is. I can show you a bunch of them in mills today almost identical to that.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why do you describe it as that, you mentioned the dogs on the side?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well those, actually there's some baling wire sticking out of this one and they hung that above the saw to, either the saw or the sander, or more likely probably the edger. You see that is just about as wide as that edger I explained to you. So I bet you that was the hood off the old edger.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that would take and funnel the sawdust away and then fuel the burner?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the shafts adjacent to it? There is two shafts there about 4' long, one is about 4' long and the other is about 3' long.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This shaft here is driven by something that was pinned. So it would probably pull a pretty good load for its size. The shorter shaft is a bigger shaft, and I believe that that bigger shaft would fit that babbitt bearing that we found down below there if the babbitt bearing had the babbitt in it. If you had to turn it off, it had a belt going down in below the mill where the main drive shaft was. This belt had some slack in it, then there was an idler with a weight on it. It held that belt tight. So if you wanted to shut your machine off, you would grab that belt, pull the idler off the belt and then the thing goes to a stop and the rest of the mill would continue running.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What are you describing here, how does that fit into that picture?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I kind of think maybe that this might have been some part of that metal that the rope hooked on to to pull the idler up. But you see it was very important that you had all these machines driven by idlers because even pulling the idler they were slow to stop. If somebody got caught in a machine, it took a long time for the whole mill to just stop.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What you are describing then is a piece offlat iron with two pieces offiat iron welded in a
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: "V" shape at the end of it?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's use the word forge welded. That is a forge weld on there.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How can you tell that is a forge weld?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You don't see any bead on there and what they did they twisted this piece, then they heated the whole thing quite hot and hammered them together. That's what they call a forge weld.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The holes in both ends would have been for what?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bolts. That is a forge weld and I haven't seen one of them in a long time. Probably the first one you ever saw.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Probably it is the first one I ever saw. We have moved over the east of the large boiler, we are now looking at one or two metal cylindrical objects, sort of wrapped in log cable with all kinds of metal pieces hanging off them, what do you think they might be?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I know what it is. It is a running board. It is an old truck body. These are the fenders.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, what kind of truck?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea but that's the clutch pedal sticking up there.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you suppose that would have been used for? Why is there a piece of log chain wrapped around it?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Log cable. I don't know. But they did use old truck motors and stuff like that, leaving the clutches on them to pull logs out of the mill ponds. It may have been cut down. On the back end of the motor a pulley was put on it to run something like that, leaving the clutch in it. Didn't you recognize that?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: fLaughterj
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You were standing on the running board.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We have moved about another 20 yards to the east of the old truck body, we are finding a large brick double enclosure with trees growing out of it and trees falling over it. How would you describe this?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well as I stood here and looked at it, there is another one beside it. I imagine after I left here and after Weinert took it over, that they put in a kiln drier and this is where they got the steam for their kiln drier, that would be my guess. That is not any part of any boiler that I ever saw.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would those work? What would be the purpose of this stuff here?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They used steam and built a building. They run steam pipes back and forth in the building and bring the heat up to 150 or so degrees and then when the steam is reheated, it could have even been for hot water.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would this be the firebox to something?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This would be a firebox here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The fireboxes, what would have been on top of it or around it?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I don't imagine you'd want to stand on top of it, probably pretty hot.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There wouldn't have been anything on top of it then?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This just would have been straight fire inside here?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fire inside with some pipes in there to carry it.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, you've got pipes coming out here on both sides.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, well I have an idea now. Back when I was a kid the old wood stoves had pipes coming out of the burner to heat the hot water tank and they were embedded in the bricks. The bricks get red hot and the pipes are embedded in the bricks to keep them
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: from burning up. I have an idea that is what they did here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would those pipes have gone?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They would have gone to the dryer.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would the dryer have been possibly in relation to all this?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh any flat spot. But that is not a boiler per se.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why would there have been log cables attached to this?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That held the cement together. That was like your building.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why would there have been two fire boxes?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well they probably built one, they didn't have enough heat, they got one to get bigger, so they put another one right beside it.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The pipes that you see in there would have been how the water was heated as it went through there?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would think so. There was probably more pipes than you see, I think there was one up here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they would have gone to the dryer, what would they have done at the dryer?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Heated it. Now you would have seen something else that you don't see anymore and that is thermal circulation. Your hot water goes in the top as it cools it goes down and the hot water keeps pushing the cold water back. So that's where you get your circulation from.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So inside the dryer, what would the dryer have looked like?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a wide open building that you could stack lumber in.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It just would have been hotter than normal inside?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would have been like maybe 150 degrees.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Because of the hot water flowing through the pipes?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I am not absolutely positive but you asked me for a guess and I'd say that is a guess. But I think it is an educated guess, because I have been around lumber dryers and veneer dryers, I could show you a lumber dryer if you want.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well tell me a little bit about this dam again, as you see it, it is diagonally across the creek and how would it have been built?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well they put the boards sloping probably 30 degrees so that the pressure was pushing down on the bottom of the boards. I think they had cables across the back of it, strung across between some trees to hold it from going on down, and the boards were vertical. I believe they were 2 x 8's in a vertical position. Then they had the timber across the top they leaned against. I think most of them were nailed in but right down there at the creek there were some of them they could pull out so they could clean out the pond because the pond would get full.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay what we are looking at is a diagonal slice of bermed-type land running across the creek and sloping downhill, at the moment it is rounded and humped and covered with ferns. There is an anchor bolt about midway down the bank. Does that bring anything to mind as to what that might be for?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say that that anchor bolt was below water level. The water level would have been clear up to this bank up here. Another proof that this is a old mill pond you look at the height of the ground here and over there. I mean there is still a lot of bark and stuff in this thing. That was a problem with these old mill ponds especially in these small mills. Debris that would build up in the bottom as the logs would slide down the hill and stuff.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would he have brought the logs in from and how would he have gotten down to the
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: mill pond?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They came brought in by horses right over on that bank over there, rolled them into the pond, pulled them across the pond.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Looking at the bank on the south side, northeast of the creek, they would have been brought down by horses?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They didn't have any tractors, they brought them down by horses.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They would have dumped them here and from here how would they have been moved up to the platforms?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They just had pike poles and pushed them across.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They pushed them across over to what over here, what have been on the south side?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a wood ramp right up here on the bank. They had a cable come down through it, and that's what I thought possibly the truck engine was hooked on to. If you look up there, probably that truck engine is right straight above us here and you see.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Before we go any farther, there is something else I want you to look at, just shortly a little ways away from here. Looking up stream from the dam about 25 yards we find an old barrel welded together with another barrel and two semi circular metal objects. Describe the metal barrel for me. What do you think that ought to be used for?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In my lifetime as a millwright we've done this to a lot of barrels. We even threw a 4 foot pieces of wood in them and keep warm. And we are not too far from the head rig here. You take the ramp that I was talking about that they pull the logs up is right here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You are pointing directly to the east?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I would say we are pointing south.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You are pointing south that way directly to the south of the metal barrels, there would have been this ramp?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have an idea, you take the sawyer, he didn't do any work basically except run the carriage through, but he did some paper work so in the winter time he probably needed some heat and these barrels were a heater.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was just a barrel stove.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a barrel stove, yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about these two other pieces of metal right directly to
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is half the pulley that drove the head rig. The head rig ran with a 12" belt. This would have been the pulley that probably that ran the edger or cutoff saw or something like that.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There were two halves so they could be dismantled?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. You have a shaft that is 60' long. You had to take the pully apart to put them on. You had deals similar to that bearing that you saw that fit in here and rocked on the shaft.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They were belt driven?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Large rubber belts or leather belts?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were rubber belts. They weren't endless like they are now, we had to lace them.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are these in approximately the position they would have been in had everything been here?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well basically I am saying this heater would have come from the head rig and I think the whole works was brought down from up there about 35 feet.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That is about 35 feet to the
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where the head rig was.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: to the northeast they would have been hauled.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You see we would have still been standing in the water in the pond right here. Somebody has moved these things, scavaging I think. What we should do is go over on the other side and find where they dumped the logs in then we could tell more how high the mill pond was. I think the mill pond would have been up about the height we are right here. They brought the logs in on the other side and I don't know how this creek runs but apparently it works its way that way so there was a lot of timber on that side of the creek.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We are standing by at this round, heavy metal cylinder back on the main mill complex. First Neil thought it might be a barrel arrangement of some kind. You have looked at it again and what do you think now?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think this is a storage tank for these steam engines. They didn't recapture any steam, it all blew into the air. And they need lots of water for those things. I think this was a thousand gallon tank that was evidentally pulled out of the creek here to supply water to the steam engine. It is right close to the steam engine here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay by right close you mean it is right close to that plalform that you think the steam engine could have been on?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where the stakes were driven. We have made a trip around the pond. Definitely we found the dam site and so forth and come back up. Found where the head rig was and everything, so I am quite sure that the boiler was taken out of here and this was just an old tank of 1,000-1,500 gallons and they used a lot of steam in those days. They didn't even waste much water out of a boiler in town to blow the whistle as what they ran here just starting it up. I think it blew steam. You could see the mill for 1/2 mile away from the steam. And you would hear the 8:00 and the noon and the 1:00 and the 5:00 whistles clear down where I live from this mill which is probably a good 2 miles, maybe 3, you could hear them all over. We could hear 5 miles just from our house every noon and start up time and quitting time.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Some time it used to be around 1,000 gallon tank, right now its an old dead fall of windthrown dougflasJ-fir laying on top of it.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't think about them having had storage for that boiler. If we would have followed that road straight in we would have come in just about right on this mill wouldn't we?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I would suspect so.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If we hadn't cut off and gone down the stream. The road came in just below the mill. I would say down here, maybe somewhere between 50-100 feet from where we are standing, is where the road came in. The lumber was taken Out of here.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They got it out by truck?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. A lot of it was rough lumber, most of the ties were rough.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From here it was taken down to Suver?
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.text: Maternal Ancestry
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following genealogy of Neil Vanderburg's maternal ancestry, compiled by his daughter, Mary Stone, traces the family's migration from Massachusetts to Oregon over a 200-year period. Neil's direct ancestors are given in italics in order to better clarify the family's history.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: THE WILSON FAMILY
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Thomas Wilson
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Thomas Wilson came to this country from Scotland in June, 1633 with his wife, Ann and three sons; Humphrey, Samuel and Joshua. He also had children born here: Deborah in August 1634 and Lydia in November 1636. His home was in Roxbury, Massachusetts, and he had the misfortune to lose his house and goods by fire. He left the Boston area on account of the Armenian controversy, and began a plantation at Squamset Falls in New Hampshire, which they later called Exeter. He occupied the island at the foot of the falls and some land on the eastern side of the Piscataqua River. There he built his house and the first mill in town for grinding grain. That part of the stream which runs in the channel on the eastern side of the island was known as Wilson's Creek. He died in the summer of 1643.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Humphrey Wilson
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Thomas Wilson's son, Humphrey, continued to operate the grist mill and was probably an inhabitant of Exeter the rest of his life. Humphrey married Judith Hersey 21 December 1663 in Exeter. They had children: Judith, Elizabeth, John, Hannah, Thomas, James, Ann, Martha, and Mary.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Thomas Wilson
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Thomas Wilson, son of Humphrey was born 30 May 1672 and married Mary Light on 16 October 1698. They had 14 children: Humphrey, Rebecca, Anna, twins John (probably died soon) and Thomas, a second John, Sarah (probably died soon), a second Sarah, Joshua, Mary, Jabez, Jonathan, Moses and Judith.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Humphrey Wilson
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Humphrey, son of Thomas, was born 9 December 1699. He married Mary Leavitt in 1727 in Brentwood, NI-I and had Captain Nathaniel and others. Humphrey was a first settler
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: of Gilmanton, New Hampshire.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Captain Nathaniel Wilson
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Captain Nathaniel, son of Humphrey, was born 24 June 1739 in Exeter. He married Elizabeth Barber on 15 March 1762 in Exeter, NH. She was born 24 March, 1739, a daughter of Robert Barber who was killed by the Indians. Captain Nathaniel moved to Gilmanton, New Hampshire the first week of March, 1769. Their children were eight sons: Warren, Robert, John, Nathaniel, John, Job, Levi, and Jeremiah. Captain Nathaniel was active and useful in promoting the settlement of the town, and did much to promote its civil and religious interest. He was also a spirited officer in the Revolutionary service, and was one of the five members organized into a Congregational church November 30, 1774. He was a ugood farmer and mechanic, an energetic and industrious man, a very worthy citizen and an exemplary Christian.0 He was a merchant in Lower Gilmanton from 1795 to 1800. He died 16 February 1819, aged 80. Mrs. Elizabeth Wilson died 12 March 1824, aged 85. In Gilmanton there is a small cemetery located on what used to be called Wilson Hill. In that place are stones for Captain Nathaniel and Elizabeth upon which is written "The death that cuts the sevard that binds man in his earth, but Christ has said, I go before him to heaven a mansion to prepare."
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Elder Nathaniel Wilson
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Elder Nathaniel Wilson, son of Captain Nathaniel, was born in Gilmanton, New Hampshire on 8 August 1769. He was an early settler of Barnstead, New Hampshire and lived on the "Sinkler Place" on Route 107 in 1800. He was a free will Baptist and preached in his barn for over 30 years. He was a farmer. He married (1) Elizabeth True, a schoolteacher in Gilmanton, New Hampshire. Their children were: Betsy (married John Page), and Nathaniel Jr. He married (2) Fanny Proctor September 1801 in Barnstead, NH and they had children: Fanny (Married William Demerett), Samuel T., and Abigail P. (married James Woods). Panthea, wife of James Woodhouse, is also listed as daughter of Elder Nathaniel in some reference works and among her children were Betsy, Fanny and Nathaniel, suggesting they were named for this family. She is not, however, mentioned in Elder Nathaniel's will. Elder Nathaniel died in Barnsted 17 December 1844 and his wife Fanny died in 1857.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Nathaniel Wilson, Jr.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Nathaniel Wilson, son of Elder Nathaniel, was born June 1797 in Gilmanton, New Hampshire. He married Mary J. Roberts on 15 November 1816. Mary was born 28 February 1795 in Strafford, New Hampshire. Their known children are Thomas, Jonathan and Elizabeth. The famijly moved to Meramera, illinois in 1835. Nathaniel Wilson died 26 June 1845, just several months after his father's death. Apparently Nathaniel had been sick for some time as Elder Nathaniel Wilson's will, dated 17 May 1844, provides for him to receive ten dollars and the property that Elder Nathaniel owned in illinois to be held in trust for
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Nathaniel Jr.'s children. None of his other grandchildren were mentioned in the will. Mary died 2 March 1885.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Thomas Wilson
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Thomas Wilson, son of Nathaniel Wilson, was born 4 March 1825 in Giln-ianton, New Hampshire. He was married to Josephine Sager on 8 September 1849. A family Bible records that they had children David A., Charles Milo, Alonzo (Lonnie) and Lorenzo (Lennie) who were twins, Mary, John T., Thomas Goodwin, Gertrude, Ben Sager, and Eliza Ellen (Nellie). Thomas was a farmer in illinois and all children were born either in Meramera, Wayne, or Mackinara counties. While in Illinois he became a good friend of Abraham Lincoln. Together, they made a table which was kept in the family for many years and was known as "the Lincoln table." Wife, Josephine died 20 December 1879. Thomas later married Malvina. Thomas died 1. February 1903.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Nellie (Eliza E.) Wilson Rose
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Nellie Wilson was born 5 March 1870 in Mackinaw, Illinois. Her mother died when she was 9 years old. She tried to maintain the household for a time, then moved to Olympia, Washington to live with her sister and brother-in-law, May (Mary) and Henry Hannah. Her brother Milo also moved west to British Columbia and worked in coal mines. There he met William de Ruchie Rose. de Ruchie, as he was known, was born 1 August 1864 in Portland, Maine. When he was in his early teens, his parents, James and Myra, died. His mother was a devout Catholic. After her death he moved to Quebec to live with "Aunt Francine." de Ruchie finished his schooling there and his Aunt offered him a small fortune to marry Daisy." He declined because of her reportedly tarnished reputation and then was disinherited by his Aunt. He then moved from her home. At least ten years later we find evidence of him in British Columbia. Milo brought de Ruchie to the church where his sister Nellie was practicing the organ for church services. He had a lovely tenor voice and he came down the aisle and sang with her. After this meeting and a period of courting, they were married 13 July 1897. They had five children:
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Clarence de Ruchie
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Clarence de Ruchie, born 8 April 1898, Ontario, CA; married Gertrude Swenson l931; died 23 August 1864, Whittier, CA. Dorothy Louise, born 25 December 1899, New Denver, British Columbia; married Elton Don Vanderburg 1 May 1918, Fullerton CA; died 28 February 1966, Lebanon, OR. Margery Mae, born 4 July 1903, Tumwater, WA; married l-J.B. Eastland, 2-Herb Curtis. Esther Myra, born 14 June 1906, Seattle, WA; married Douglass Grandy, 1 September 1927. Helen Lillian, born 28 October 1908, Santa Ana, CA; married Burnell Obernolte, 25 December 1929.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Nellie was ill for many years and died 28 February 1917. de Ruchie subsequently married second Leila Lockwood who died 20 November 1917 and third Mae Pierce. He died 11 February 1930 in Compton, CA.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Paternal Ancestry
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following genealogy of Neil Vanderburg ' s paternal ancestry, compiled by his daughter, Mary Stone, traces the family's migration from New Amsterdam, (New York) to Oregon over a 240-year period.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: The Vanderburg Family
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 1. LUCAS DIRCKSEN VANDERBURGH (also known as Luycas Diricksen or Dircksen)
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Lucas Dirchson Vanderburgh was the first American ancestor of the Vanderburgh family. Some records find him referred to as "Luycas Dircksen, known also as Vanderburgh". He was born about 1620 and married to Annete Cornelise, date unknown. Their children were:
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Cornelis baptized May 11, 1653 Hendrick baptized April 18, 1655 Arent baptized March 26, 1656 Johannes baptized February 28, 1657 Margarite baptized May 26, 1658 Dirck baptized March 13, 1661 Elsie baptized November 22, 1662
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The earliest records of Lucas (from 1658) identify him as a sergeant in the service of the Dutch West Indies Company. This may have been the motivation and the means of his immigration to the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam. Through the next years he acquired several pieces of land along the North, or Hudson River as well as along the South, or Delaware River.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: On February 16, 1654 he petitioned for and received a license as tavern keeper, and two years later Sergeant Dircksen asked for and was granted his discharge from the Dutch West Indies Company and given leave to settle at the South River (documents show that Lucas owned extensive property in what is now the state of Delaware).
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: There are ten documents preserved in the J. Pierpont Morgan Library in NY, NY regarding Lucas Dircksen. One of these is his naturalization paper, dated in 1659, written in Dutch. This may lend credence to the recorded tradition that the VanDerBurgh family lived in England for several generations prior to immigrating the New Amsterdam. Another document lists him as one of the residents of New Amsterdam entitled to the burgher right,
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: that is the right to hold office and the privilege of full citizenship. Other documents record agreements and various transference of deeds.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Dissatisfaction with Dutch rule increased and the power of the Company decreased in the next few years. When the British demanded the surrender of New Amsterdam, Lucas was one of those who swore allegiance to the Duke of York October 21-26, 1664.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: In 1666 Lucas was operating an inn, or tavern, named, "Sign of the Fort Orange". Fort Orange was one of the first Dutch settlements on the Hudson River named for Holland's unselfish hero, William of Orange. Fort Orange was renamed "Albany" after English acquisition. The tavern was at the present site of 16 Stone Street and his home was at the present site of 21 Broadway in New York City. This property remained in the family until 1715.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Lucas died prior to April 13, 1670, as we find at that time his widow Annetje was remarried to Jacob Fabritius.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 2. DIRCK VANDERBURGH (also known as Dircksen VanDerBurgh)
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Dirck was baptised at the Dutch Church in New Amsterdam, New Netherland (now New York City, New York) on 13 March 1661.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: He married Reymerig VanNostrand. (The VanNostrands were a founding family of Brooklyn.) His will, dated 1709, mentions two children:
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Henry born about 1685, married Magdalena Knight Anna Marie born about 1690, married Thomas Lewis, October 24, 1714 Dirck added much to the properties inherited from his father, purchasing additional land on and near Broadway. Numerous references are made to Dirck in Colonial manuscripts regarding land acquisitions; work as tax collector (1692); obtaining a pardon for his negro slave Jack, who was convicted of burglary and sentenced to death (1698); as an alderman (1704-6), surveyor of city (1705), Justice of the Peace (1704).
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Dirck was listed as a merchant during the time he was an alderman, but there are many records of his petitions for payment for building projects. Of note are his employment in building "His Majesty Chapel with several other buildings in and about His Majesty Fort William Henry" Ca. 1695 and work on Trinity Church for which he is credited with the exterior design Ca. 1699. In addition to monetary payment for his work on Trinity Church in Manhattan, Dirck received a silver tankard, "of ye value of 12 pounds".
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Shortly after 1700 Dirck purchased several tracts of land in Dutchess County; One tract was just south of Poughkeepsie, another bought in partnership with Samuel Statts along the Hudson River between Hyde Park and Rhinebeck. The town of Staatsburgh is named for Dirck's partner and the cove along the river between Staatsburgh and Rhinebeck is known as VanDerBurghs' Cove. Dirck never came to Dutchess County to live, but died in New York
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: City in 1710 leaving his Poughkeepsie land to his son Henry.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 3. HENRY VANDERBURGH
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Henry was born about 1685 and married Magdalena Knight (b. Ca. 1694, d. Ca. 1752). (Knight is the English translation of Ritter - the original family name.) Magdalena at One time was a lady-in-waiting at Queen Anne's Court. Their children are as follows:
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Hester bap. March 8, 1711, French Church, NY Anna Maria bap. April 12, 1713 Dutch Church Richard bap. May 18, 1715, Dutch Church, NY Henry bap. April 3, 1717, Poughkeepsie, NY John bap. February 11, 1721, Poughkeepsie, NY Pieter bap. September 11, 1723, Poughkeepsie, NY Susanna bap. June 11, 1725, Poughkeepsie, NY James bap. September 4, 1729 William bap. October 3, 1731 Stephen Magdalen
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: After inheriting his father's land, Henry settled in Poughkeepsie in 1712 and in a few years became a prominent and influential citizen. He was one of the assessors for 1717-1718, a supervisor 1719-1721, and then County Clerk. He served in the Colonial Militia. He was a warden in Christ Church. Two known documents also ascribe to him the title "Gentleman".
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Henry's will is dated 12 January 1737/8. At that time he describes himself as being "weak in body', though he did not die until 1750.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 4. COL. JAMES VANDERBURGH
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: James VanDerBurgh was born September 4, 1729. He married, September 29, 1753, Margaret, daughter of Bartholomew Noxon of Beekman, where he had recently moved from Poughkeepsie. Their children were:
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Henry (Capt.) b. 28 February 1756 Bartholomew (Ensign) b. 8 November 1757 James b. 16 October 1759 Magdalenna b. 5 July 1761 Peter b. 5 March 1763 Elizabeth, b. 16 May 1764 Stephan b. 4 January 1765
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Margaret Noxon died August 8, 1766. October 6, 1767 Col. James married Helena Clark who bore him eleven more children:
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: William b. 18 August 1768 Margaret b. 26 April 1770 Richard b. 26 May 1772 Gabriel Ludlow b. 20 August 1774 Egbert Benson b. 8 December 1776 Clarissa b. 25 March 1779 George Washington b. 24 May 1781 Paulina b. 5 December 1783 Almira b. 20 December 1785 Federal b. 11 May 1788 Caroline b. 21 February 1793
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Col. James purchased a tract of land on the road leading from Poughquag to Gardiner Hollow and built the first substantial dwelling house in that vicinity. It was built of stone and wood with a broad, covered verandah across the front The basement contained quarters for slaves. This house remained standing over a century, having been torn down in 1860.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: He engaged in farming and also kept a general store. He was active in the civil and military life of the county, serving several terms as assessor and supervisor of Beekn-ian. When in 1775 the War of the Revolution was fast becoming inevitable he ardently espoused the cause of the Colony and was commissioned Lieut-Colonel of Col. William Humphrey's Fifth Regiment, Dutchess County Militia on 17 October 1775 and became a colonel on March 10, 1778. He was a deputy to the third Provincial Congress, 1776, which ratified the Declaration of Independence. He, with his regiment, took an active part in the building of fortifications and forts in the Highlands and in their defense. He was Justice of Peace for many years.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: He held the friendship of Governor George Clinton and General George Washington. In his diary for May 1781, General Washington mentions the fact that he was the guest at the house of Col. VanDerBurgh May 18 while on a trip to New England and again on his return May 25 making note of the pleasure these visits gave him and of the fine hospitality of his host. Helena had given birth to a son the night before, and Washington named him, (George Washington VanDerBurgh) and gave him his silver knee buckles for his name. When Washington stayed there, at night they kept his horse in the basement in the slaves' quarters so that it would not be stolen by the Tories (This report from Old Deyon, a slave who refused to take her freedom when they were set free).
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Also entertained in his home were Rochambeau and LaFayette. On one of LaFayette's visits, while out riding, LaFayette remarked that the country looked much like his farm in France (LaGrange), due to this the area became known as LaGrangeville, later shortened to LaGrange.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Once during the war when the Colonel was ill, the Tories attempted to capture him but Helena barricaded the door with a heavy bedstead and with the help of the slaves defended him so well that they gave up the fight. The Colonel furnished much of the equipment for the regiment. The muskets were stored in the attic of the old house for years and the younger children often played with them.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: One interesting note, Col. James' brother Henry held important offices in Dutchess County under the Colonial Government and at the beginning of the Revolution was Justice of the Inferior court. His sympathies were strongly Loyalist and remained so. He used his "best endeavors to suppress the rebels in their evil designs." He was arrested, placed on board a prison ship lying in the Hudson River, from which he escaped after three months. He lived in the woods for some time but was forced to surrender due to "age and infirmities".
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Colonel VanDerBurgh, like his father and brother, was a strong adherent to the Church of England.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Col. James died 4 April 1794. his gravestone bears a Masonic emblem which shows that he was a member of that order. His wife, Helena Clark, who survived him twenty-six years is buried beside him in the family burying ground at Poughquag.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 5. JAMES VANDERBURGH, JR.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: James Vanderburg, Jr. was born 26 Oct. 1759 in Beckman (now Beacon), Dutchess County, NY. He married first Jane Rosecrans. Their children were:
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Polly (never married) Phoebe married Dr. House James ifi Henry born in Poukeepsie, Dutchess Co. NY
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: James married second Margaret (Polly) Jessup. Their children were:
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Jane m. Sylvanus Caulkiins Lewis J. b.1 Aug 1806, d. 15 Sept 1863 Webbs Mills, Chemung Co., NY, m. (1) Salome Smith 10 Dec 1831, d. 25 June 1842, and (2) Desire Cady 7 Oct 1844. Caroline m. Jesse Maxfield Clarence Federal b. Nov 1813, m. Sarah Maxfield
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: James Jr. appeared in Columbia County court on 4 Feb 1834 (age 75 yrs) to make application for pension provided for by congress in 1832 for those who served in the Revolutionary War. At that time he was a resident of the town of Austerlitz, Columbia County, NY. He states that he enlisted for a period of nine months in the army at Beekman, Dutchess Co., NY, on April 1776, as a private in the company commanded by Capt.; John Durling. Shortly after he joined Col. Cornelius Humphrey's Regiment and George Clinton's Brigade at Fort Montgomery. His primary work there was in construction of the fort. He recollects returning home in January 1777, crossing the Hudson on ice.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: On 15 Sept 1778 he enlisted for three months under Capt. Israel Vail. They were organized at his father's inn and marched to White Plains joining with either Col. Livingstone's or Col. VanRenscelaer's regiment, camping 8 or 9 miles from Fort Independence, then in possession of the enemy. On the offensive,, while climbing a steep

chapters.title: Bucking Timber On The Siletz In 1943
chapters.label: Appendix B.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Appendix B. Bucking Timber On The Siletz In 1943
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Neil Vanderburg wrote the following recollection of his timber falling career along the Siletz River in Lincoln County, Oregon.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The reason that our saw was called a "swede fiddlet' was because the work was very hard and a lot of Swedes came out to the northwest to work in the woods. The men came from M.innesota and other states that were logged out. In the early days of logging they wanted to get the trees off of the ground so they could farm it. I have been back in Minnesota and seen where the logging barons have logged and not reseeded, or left the ground with seed trees to replant it. When you see the way they did it back east you can see why people from back there are so concerned with the clear cutting out here. They don't realize that we are replanting with hybrid trees that are going to make lumber much faster than the trees that were native to this country. Even so, with seed trees there is a lot of timber that has regrown that I helped cut that is a lot bigger than it was when we cut it originally.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I got off in another direction than I originally intended to go. Back to the big Swedes. I worked in the woods in 1943 before I went into the Marines. I worked for Werner Timber Co. out of Cutler City, which is part of Lincoln City now. We had to leave the office at 4:00 in the morning to go up the Siletz River until we got on the west side of Valsetz. We would get up to the landing, which was as far as the crummie (an old six- cylinder Dodge bus) went. We would get to the landing at about 8 o'clock in the morning.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We figured that we carried about 120 pounds of tools on our backs. We carried our lunches and a one-gallon canteen on long straps that would go over our shoulder and hang at or a little above the waist. We carried a seven-foot bucking saw with a handle on it. We carried two bucking wedges. Everything was steel then, they hadn't invented plastic yet. They were carried on a rope with a six-pound maul on the other side to balance them. We carried a double bit ax. One side of the ax was sharp enough to shave with. If you were doing any falling, all of the under cuts were cut with the ax. You asked Donald how we cut the limbs off. We used the duller side of the ax for that as well as for cutting brush around the cut to make a place to stand. After we ate lunch each day we would talk and sharpen our ax.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We carried an oil bottle with us to lubricate our saw, and if we got into a pitchy tree, to wash the pitch off; it had diesel in it. It was made out of an old ketchup or wine bottle. It had a hook wired to it with fine wire wrapped around it several times to hold the hook solid. The hook was used to hook the bottle on the tree close to the cut. We had to be careful that we didn't run out of oil before quitting time or it really slowed you down.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then we carried an under cutter. That was a piece of flat metal with a roller with grooves in it so we could put the saw on it upside down so we could cut up from under the bottom of the log. We used the under cutter if a log was laying with one end up in the air to keep from splitting it. We also had to build a stand for it to come down on to keep from splitting the log.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was beautiful old growth timber about three foot in diameter on the stump. I cut one tree up there that had 14,000 feet in it. I almost got fired one time when my legging slipped out and I split a log that was about 30 inches across and 16 feet long. The boss said that log was worth almost $200.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A man ran the saw all by himself. For several reasons: one being that as often as not one side of the Cut would roll down the hill and the log would roll over you, if you were on the bottom side. On the bigger trees the end of the saw would go into the tree so you couldn't have a handle out there. Also, when we got down close to the bottom of the cut we would saw with the end of the saw, so if we got into the dirt we just dulled the end few teeth. You can't do that with a chain saw. We only got two sharp saws a week, so when the time was about half up you put the handle on the other end and had a sharp saw again.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We got paid by the thousand so this job separated the men from the boys. When I went into the Marines I had a 46-inch chest and a 30-inch waist and weighed 205 pounds. The Marines sure liked to get the loggers from the northwest.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As to where the big Swedes went, that is three generations back and they are all mixed up with other nationalities.
entries.chapter_ref: 4. The Coote and Weinert Mill Site

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: - Neil Vanderburg Independence, Oregon December, 1990
